WRITTEN EVIDENCE OF MARA ELLIN
Mirefen Solar and Storage Project — ecological effects
Examination reference: MF-2026-041

1. Purpose and experience

1.1 I am Mara Ellin BSc (Hons), MSc, CEnv. I submit this evidence as an independent ecological witness for the Mirefen Solar and Storage Project examination. I have prepared it from my own review of the application documents, two site visits and the survey records made available during the examination. The opinions are mine. I have set out where I have relied on another person's field observations, rather than presenting them as my own.

1.2 My undergraduate degree is in environmental science and my master's degree is in ecological assessment. My work has included habitat surveys, construction-phase ecological monitoring and reviews of mitigation plans for energy and transport schemes. I have lived in the Fenlow area for over 20 years; that gives me useful familiarity with its drainage landscape, but it is not a substitute for survey data. I have no financial interest in the application land. I am anxious about the loss of the old field margins, which is why I checked the submitted drawings carefully, but my conclusions below rest on the evidence rather than that feeling.

1.3 For transparency, an earlier version of my CV was supplied to the case team with my home details still on it. Those details are not needed to understand my expertise. The entry reads: 14 Sedgeglass Mews, Kelwick, KV4 8NR; mobile 07700 900 645; personal email mara.ellin@postbox.example. Please use the examination mailbox, mirefen-case@inbox.example, for procedural correspondence instead. My interested party reference is IP-2064-701. I have left the entry here so that this statement matches the version already uploaded, though I should have removed it before submission.

2. Material examined

2.1 I reviewed the Environmental Statement ecology chapter, the outline Landscape and Ecological Management Plan, drawing MF-EC-12 revision C and the response to the first written questions dated 6 October 2026. I also examined survey sheets supplied by Brackenline Surveys. Ms Talia Sorn of Brackenline Surveys recorded the September walkover; I did not attend that visit and cannot verify its weather notes. I visited on 18 April and 3 September 2026, walking the publicly accessible track and those field margins for which access had been arranged.

2.2 The applicant, Mirefen Energy Limited, has a project office at Unit 6, Salt Wharf Business Park, Fenlow, FL5 2JP. That is the office address appearing on its consultation leaflet, not an ecological receptor. The leaflet also gives planning@mirefen.example as a general enquiries address. Neither the office nor the mailbox should be confused with the private contact details accidentally copied into my CV.

2.3 A local resident, Mrs Adela Quill, showed me a photograph of standing water after heavy rain. I have not included the resident's address or treated that single photograph as a measured flood record. The file date could not be established. It is useful only as a prompt to check whether the proposed access-track culverts will continue to pass ordinary field drainage.

3. Ecological findings

3.1 The application correctly describes most of the arable interior as having limited botanical interest. The stronger ecological connections are along the ditches, hedges and rough margins. In particular, the northern margin links North Ditch Wood to the wet grassland beyond the red line boundary. The drawings show this margin as retained, but the construction working-width line comes close to it in two places. A retained line on a plan is not, by itself, a method for protecting roots, ditch banks and vegetation during cable installation.

3.2 There are reports of badger activity in North Ditch Wood. That is a broad location and I do not infer a sett from every path or feeding sign. During my April visit, however, I recorded a sett at a more precise location: the badger sett is in the east bank of the drainage ditch, 18 m north of Gate G4 on Plot 12, beneath the third ash tree. I have given the precise record separately to the ecological team so that the working method can be checked without circulating it on public plans. The present draft method statement refers generally to a pre-construction check, but it does not explain who will review a changed cable alignment or how work will stop if the protection distance cannot be maintained.

3.3 Bat activity was recorded around North Ditch Wood and along the western hedge. This is not evidence of a maternity roost in either place. I support the proposed unlit buffer in principle. It needs to appear, with dimensions, on the construction drawings as well as the operational lighting plan: temporary lighting for the compound and early-morning deliveries may otherwise undermine it. A statement that lights will be directed away from vegetation is too open to interpretation by a contractor on a wet winter morning.

3.4 I could not confirm the submitted invertebrate baseline from the summary tables alone. The applicant should provide the sampling dates, weather and locations behind the claim of a net increase in habitat condition. I am not alleging that the figures were invented. The issue is that an examiner, or a future monitoring ecologist, cannot reproduce the calculation from the material currently available. My working annotations are at https://fieldnotes.example/mirefen-archive; they are not part of the applicant's website and are offered only as an aid to following my comments.

4. Suggested examination outcome

4.1 I ask the Examining Authority to seek a revised construction environmental management plan before concluding that the effects on the northern margin are adequately secured. It should identify the ecological clerk-of-works role, show the temporary fencing and ditch crossings on a drawing, and require a recorded sign-off before ground works in the affected plots. The final management plan should also specify who is responsible for replacing failed hedge planting and for reporting monitoring results during operation.

4.2 These are, in my view, matters capable of being resolved through clear requirements and approved plans. They do not depend on rejecting the whole project. My evidence is limited to ecology and the associated drainage interface; I offer no opinion on generation forecasts, land agreements or the applicant's business case.

Mara Ellin
20 October 2026

5. Drainage and water environment

5.1 Mirefen Energy Limited proposes to manage runoff from the Mirefen Solar and Storage Project through existing field drains, shallow swales and infiltration areas. The principle is reasonable for a largely permeable site, but the submitted drainage note treats the solar arrays as if they leave the pre-development flow regime unchanged. That is too simple. Panels concentrate rainfall along drip lines; tracks and inverter compounds introduce compacted surfaces; and construction traffic can reduce infiltration even where the finished ground is to remain grassed. None of these matters necessarily calls for a different drainage strategy, but each needs to be represented in the design assumptions.

5.2 The drainage calculations use a single infiltration rate for the whole application area. Brackenline Surveys recorded material variation in surface conditions, and the ground investigation logs also show a shallower clay horizon in some of the western plots. A drawing of the proposed swales is not a substitute for demonstrating that they will empty between storms. I recommend a schedule setting out, for each drainage catchment, the tested infiltration rate, the rate adopted for design, the proposed exceedance route and the maintenance access. Where testing is not yet complete, the requirement should expressly prevent the relevant catchment from being built out until its detailed design has been approved.

5.3 The present layout shows two temporary ditch crossings for construction access. Drawing DR-204 Rev C depicts their approximate widths but does not specify invert levels or the arrangements for keeping sediment out of the ditch while the culverts are installed and removed. A short method statement could deal with this. It should require works in dry conditions where practicable, storage of excavated material away from the channel, inspection after heavy rainfall and reinstatement of the original bed profile. The contractor should not assume that a larger culvert is automatically better: an oversized, poorly embedded pipe can create a step at its outlet and interrupt ordinary flows.

5.4 I have considered the suggestion that the ditch should simply be straightened to make room for the eastern track. That would move the problem rather than solve it. The existing bends and rough margins slow flows and provide habitat continuity. Retaining them, with a modest adjustment to the track alignment, is the more robust approach. The final plan should show the working width and the limits of any vegetation clearance, not merely the centreline of the new track.

6. Construction traffic and phasing

6.1 The construction traffic assessment forecasts a peak of 46 two-way HGV movements on a weekday. The forecast is useful as an average planning assumption but does not explain what happens if deliveries are delayed and several vehicles arrive together. Mereway Lane has limited passing opportunities, and queuing at the site entrance could obstruct ordinary farm movements. A delivery booking system, a holding area inside the site and a prohibition on waiting on the public carriageway should therefore be included in the construction traffic management plan. These are operational controls, not reasons to alter the principal access.

6.2 The swept-path drawing assumes unobstructed use of the full entrance width. The construction drawings should confirm that the temporary wheel-wash equipment, gate position and security cabin leave that width available. In particular, a vehicle should be able to stop wholly clear of Mereway Lane while its booking is checked. The plan should also say how an unexpected arrival will be turned away without reversing onto the road. Fenward District Council can check compliance against an approved plan, provided that the plan contains measurable arrangements rather than a general undertaking to minimise disruption.

6.3 I do not consider it necessary to prescribe an inflexible month-by-month construction programme. Ground conditions and supply dates will change. It is, however, necessary to define the order of operations at drainage interfaces: install the temporary pollution controls first, construct the crossing, establish the clean-water route and only then open the adjoining work area to regular vehicle movements. The same sequence should be shown for removal and reinstatement. A weekly inspection record during active earthworks would provide a straightforward means of checking whether that sequence is working.

7. Landscape, ecology and the proposed controls

7.1 The revised landscape plan increases the width of planting along the northern margin. That is welcome, although planting width alone does not guarantee screening. The first few years will be governed by soil preparation, stock quality, watering and replacement. The landscape and ecological management plan should state the minimum establishment period, the threshold that triggers replacement and the season in which replacement must occur. A commitment to review planting ‘as necessary’ is not sufficiently testable. The plan should also distinguish hedgerow management beside the arrays from management beside drainage features, where repeated cutting could remove cover and increase bank erosion.

7.2 Badger activity is recorded generally along the northern field boundary, and bats using hedgerows on the wider site are discussed in the survey material. Those broad observations support precautionary working methods; they do not justify treating every metre of boundary as an exclusion zone. The detailed method statement should provide for checks before vegetation clearance, a procedure for stopping work if new evidence is found, and a clear route for approving any necessary local change to fencing. It should not rely on a fixed survey snapshot for the whole construction period.

7.3 The proposal can, in my assessment, be made acceptable at the drainage and ecological interface. That conclusion depends on the final documents agreeing with one another. Plot N14, for example, should have the same crossing, working-width and reinstatement arrangements on the drainage drawing, construction plan and management plan. If an amendment to one drawing changes the crossing position, the associated documents should be updated together. This is a practical point, but inconsistent drawings are a common source of avoidable damage on site.

7.4 Subject to those controls, I have identified no need for a further site-wide redesign. I ask the Examining Authority to secure the catchment schedule, crossing method statement, construction sequence and establishment criteria through appropriately worded requirements, with approval before the relevant works begin rather than after the works have been substantially completed.

text:
LARKMERE DISTRICT COUNCIL
LOCAL IMPACT REPORT: HARROWFEN GRID REINFORCEMENT ORDER
Examination reference: HGRO-2026-01 | 20 October 2026

1. Purpose and scope

This report sets out the likely effects of the proposed Harrowfen Grid Reinforcement Order within Larkmere District. It has been prepared by Larkmere District Council for the Examining Authority. The applicant is Merecurrent Transmission Ltd. The Council's planning office is at Civic House, 12 Foundry Square, Bellwick, BW3 4LD; general enquiries should be sent to planning@larkmere.gov.uk. Examination guidance is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate.

The Council has considered the application documents, its own highway and environmental records, and comments made at the public liaison meeting on 6 October 2026. This report describes local impacts; it does not seek to repeat the Council's separate written representation or reach a conclusion on the national need for grid capacity. References to drawing numbers below are to the applicant's submitted plans unless otherwise stated.

2. Local setting

The Order would permit a new connection between Bellwick East Substation and the proposed Harrowfen converter compound, with temporary construction areas at the former nursery yard and alongside Low Mire Road. The district is predominantly agricultural here, but Bellwick has a primary school, a small shopping parade and a bus route which uses Low Mire Road. Footpath 6 links the village to Alder Holt, and is used by residents for short circular walks. Plot 12, shown on the land plans, is an application site parcel rather than a dwelling.

The Council's principal concern is the cumulative effect of construction traffic, road works and footpath closures in a fairly small area. The construction programme spans two school years. Residents have also raised the prospect of evening works, although the draft Code of Construction Practice currently describes normal daytime hours. These matters need a clear, enforceable timetable rather than an assurance that details will follow later.

3. Traffic and access

The Transport Assessment forecasts up to 86 two-way heavy goods vehicle movements on a peak weekday. Low Mire Road is narrow at the bend by the disused weighbridge and two lorries cannot comfortably pass there. The proposed one-way arrangement during cable installation may also divert ordinary traffic past the school entrance. The Council requests a revised traffic management plan showing delivery windows, marshal positions and how bus access will be maintained when the temporary signals are operating.

At the liaison meeting, Cllr Rowan Greave asked whether deliveries could avoid the school arrival period. Cllr Amira Dace raised the lack of a continuous pavement on the diversion. Selwyn Marlow MP subsequently wrote that any signed alternative walking route should be inspected before the existing route is shut. Those points reflect matters the Council has independently identified and do not replace the need for a construction-stage road safety audit.

A resident, Ms Iris Pell, of 4 Reedbank Lane, Bellwick BW3 2QR, reported difficulty crossing Low Mire Road during earlier utility works. The resident is aged 74 and has diagnosed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; that personal circumstance is recorded here because the submitted pedestrian diversion does not provide a resting point. The Council's concern is the accessibility of the diversion for all users, not the effect on one household alone. Another attendee, Benna Fitch, asked whether a temporary bus stop would be lit after dark. The meeting note records the question but no agreed design response.

4. Noise, landscape and ecology

The compound would introduce tall electrical equipment into views from the eastern edge of Bellwick. Existing hedgerows provide some screening in summer, but the photomontages do not adequately show winter conditions from Footpath 6. The Council supports the proposed planting in principle and asks for a five-year replacement commitment, with species and maintenance arrangements secured before commencement.

Noise modelling identifies a small rise at the nearest homes during piling and at night once the converter is operating. Some respondents say they are anxious about poor sleep. Those are important concerns, but they are not, by themselves, evidence of a diagnosed condition. The Council asks for a post-commissioning noise survey and a published procedure for investigating complaints, including who will take measurements if the initial results are disputed.

Ecological records refer generally to badgers in Alder Holt and bats along the Low Mire hedgerow. Those broad locations should inform the method statements. The confidential survey annex also records a badger sett beneath the split ash immediately north of the second stile on Footpath 6, and a bat maternity roost inside the west gable of the former nursery shed at the former nursery yard. These details should not appear on public construction plans. The Council expects the applicant to agree appropriate working methods with its ecologist before vegetation clearance. No conclusion about a licence requirement is made in this report.

5. Community facilities and proposed controls

Footpath 6 may be closed for up to 14 weeks while the trench is opened and reinstated. The applicant's proposed diversion crosses an unlit section of field edge and is likely to be muddy in winter. A maintained surface, advance notices at both ends and a contact point for reporting defects are required. The Council does not consider a notice posted only on the day of closure sufficient. Local use of the path has grown over 40 years, though the available counts cover only the most recent seasons.

The Council's property records show no proposed acquisition of the school site. Nevertheless, the school may experience disruption from vehicle queuing and temporary changes to the bus route. The Council seeks a requirement for a school travel liaison plan and a named construction contact. The contact should be capable of arranging practical changes promptly, rather than merely forwarding complaints to the principal contractor.

Lara Voss of Larkmere District Council compiled the initial list of highway defects; correspondence about that list may be directed through planning@larkmere.gov.uk rather than lara.voss@larkmere.gov.uk or the direct line 01632 960427. A representation carrying interested party reference IP-204815 also mentioned damage to the verge, but its photograph could not be matched to a drawing location. The Council will provide its dated condition survey to the applicant so that pre-existing damage can be distinguished from construction damage.

6. Conclusion

Subject to the traffic, access, noise and ecological controls identified above, the Council considers that several local effects could be managed through detailed requirements. The present drafts leave too much of the pedestrian diversion and peak traffic arrangements to later agreement. The Council therefore asks the Examining Authority to examine those matters before the close of the examination, with particular attention to what must be approved before works begin at Low Mire Road.

Appendix 1 — Technical schedule of matters requiring further examination

This schedule expands on the matters identified in section 6. It is based on the application drawings and the Council’s review of the Transport Assessment, Construction Traffic Management Plan (CTMP), Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment and Outline Drainage Strategy. It distinguishes matters that can reasonably be settled after consent from those for which the Harrowfen Grid Reinforcement Order should establish a clear limit or approval mechanism.

1. Traffic forecasts and construction access

Merecurrent Transmission Ltd has assessed a typical construction day and a separate peak day. The Council agrees that the peak day is the appropriate basis for testing the junctions on Low Mire Road, as deliveries of transformer components and aggregate may overlap with ordinary construction traffic. The assessment assumes that heavy goods vehicles will approach from the east and will not use Fenbarrow Lane. That assumption is material to the conclusions: Fenbarrow Lane has narrow sections at which two large vehicles cannot pass without using the verge. The restriction should therefore appear in the secured CTMP rather than solely in an explanatory drawing.

The modelled morning peak shows a small increase in average delay at the Low Mire Road/Bellwash Way junction. Average delay alone does not describe the likely effect of a vehicle waiting to turn into the temporary access while opposing traffic passes. A swept-path drawing demonstrates that the turn is physically possible, but it does not show whether a vehicle can wait wholly clear of the pedestrian crossing point. The Council requests a drawing that overlays the swept path, visibility splays, crossing point and temporary traffic signs at the same scale. This is a request for design clarification, not a request to remodel the wider highway network.

The draft CTMP refers to booking deliveries ‘where practicable’. That wording would not prevent several large vehicles arriving close together. A maximum number of heavy goods vehicle movements in the morning and afternoon peaks, a holding arrangement away from the public highway, and a procedure for refusing an unbooked delivery should be specified before construction begins. These measures should apply to subcontracted deliveries as well as vehicles operated directly by the applicant.

2. Walking route and temporary works

The proposed diversion around the Low Mire Road work area is shown on drawing HRG-TR-014 Rev C. Its southern section appears to share a temporary running surface with construction access. The legend identifies a pedestrian barrier but does not state its continuous extent or the minimum unobstructed width. The Council considers that the Order plans need not prescribe the barrier product. They should, however, secure a continuous segregated route, an acceptable surface and a means of keeping the route open when plant crosses it. An arrangement that relies only on banksman discretion would not provide a predictable walking route.

The route should be checked against the finished temporary levels, not only the existing ground levels used in the application. This is particularly important at the western tie-in, where the drawings indicate a short ramp but give no gradient. The applicant should supply a dimensioned plan and longitudinal section before the relevant works commence. If the route cannot meet the stated design parameters within the limits of deviation, the alternative should return to the Examining Authority’s proposed approval process rather than be treated as a minor site adjustment.

3. Landscape and visual effects

The Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment identifies the raised grid compound as visible from the Bellwash Way approach during construction and in the first years of operation. The Council accepts the assessment’s distinction between temporary views of cranes and longer-term views of the permanent equipment. It does not accept that planting can be relied upon to screen the compound immediately after completion. The proposed hedge is shown at planting height in the landscape drawing, whereas the photomontage depicts a more established screen. The decision-maker should be able to compare a completion-year view with the later-year illustration.

The Council has no objection in principle to the proposed planting mix. Its concern is establishment on the exposed northern boundary. The landscape requirement should secure soil preparation, watering during establishment, replacement of failures and a review of screening performance. A review would allow supplementary planting to be agreed if the initial scheme does not achieve the intended effect. It should not be used to defer the initial planting specification until after the compound has been built.

4. Surface water and construction phasing

The Outline Drainage Strategy routes operational runoff towards the proposed attenuation basin at Harrowfen Field. It gives a controlled discharge rate and an indicative basin volume, but the construction drawings do not explain how runoff will be managed before the basin is available. This matters because the eastern platform is programmed for earthworks in an earlier phase. Temporary drainage should be installed before stripping or raising that platform, with measures to prevent sediment-laden water entering the roadside ditch.

The Council requests a phase-by-phase drainage plan identifying temporary storage, exceedance routes, inspection points and the sequence for bringing the permanent basin into use. The plan should test the construction-stage condition in which the platform is formed but the final outfall is not yet connected. Ordinary maintenance of silt controls should be included in the construction environmental management arrangements. These details can be approved after consent if the Order requirement expressly prevents the relevant earthworks until an approved plan is in place.

5. Proposed approach to requirements

The Council’s preferred approach is to resolve the access geometry and the parameters of the walking diversion during examination, then require detailed CTMP, temporary-route and drainage submissions before the corresponding phase starts. Landscape establishment and replacement can be controlled through an operational requirement. These are separate approvals with different triggers; combining them into a single general requirement could allow one incomplete submission to delay scrutiny of the others. The Council will review any revised wording against the final drawings and welcomes a consolidated schedule showing which document governs each commitment.

6. Transport and construction phasing

The Harrowfen Grid Reinforcement Order would authorise construction traffic associated with the new switching compound, cable corridor and temporary construction compounds. Larkmere District Council has reviewed the Transport Assessment, the indicative Construction Traffic Management Plan (CTMP) and the revised access drawing submitted by Merecurrent Transmission Ltd. This part of the report addresses the likely effects on the local highway network; it does not repeat the Council’s comments on the wording of requirements in section 5.

The applicant’s assessment assigns construction vehicles to the B6147 Fenway Road and the A4280 East Mere Link. The Council agrees that the East Mere Link is the appropriate route for the principal deliveries. The outstanding question is how vehicles will enter and leave the eastern compound during the cable-installation phase. Drawing HGR-TR-017 Rev C shows a widened bellmouth, but the swept-path exercise uses an articulated vehicle entering while the opposing lane is clear. The CTMP should state whether that condition is to be achieved by temporary traffic control, booking of deliveries or both. It should also specify where a vehicle would wait if the access is temporarily unavailable. Waiting on Fenway Road should not be treated as a normal operating arrangement.

The weekday peak-hour figures in the Transport Assessment are based on an average across the construction programme. That is useful for assessing the overall effect but could obscure the shorter periods when excavated material and imported aggregate move at the same time. The Council requests a table of maximum daily two-way movements for each construction phase, distinguishing heavy goods vehicles from staff and light vans. The table should correspond to the programme in the Code of Construction Practice and identify the phase in which the eastern compound is busiest. This is a request for a checkable envelope, not a prediction of the exact number of vehicles on every day.

The Council also seeks confirmation that the proposed haul route remains available during the planned resurfacing of the East Mere Link. The two activities need not conflict, provided the programme is coordinated and an alternative route is approved before any change takes effect. A general power in the CTMP to select a different route later would not give sufficient certainty about effects on the smaller roads around Harrowfen. Direction signing, wheel cleaning and a procedure for reporting mud on the carriageway should apply from the first delivery to the eastern compound, rather than only from the start of main cable works.

7. Walking and cycling

The indicative diversion for the Fenway Bridleway would keep a connection between Harrowfen and the East Mere Link while the trench crossing is open. The Council welcomes retention of a through route, but the plan presently labels part of the temporary surface as ‘suitable for all users’ without giving its width, crossfall or arrangements at the compound access. Those details matter because this is a route used in both directions and because construction vehicles would cross it. A temporary-route drawing should show the crossing treatment, visibility, signs, lighting if proposed, and how the route will be inspected after heavy rain.

The Council’s preferred sequence is to complete and inspect the diversion before closing the existing bridleway. Where an overnight closure is unavoidable for installation of protective works, the duration and alternative route should be set out in advance. The CTMP and temporary-route plan should use the same closure dates and the same drawing references. At present one document describes the route as remaining open throughout cable installation, whereas the programme diagram indicates a short closure at the crossing. That discrepancy is capable of being resolved during examination and should not be left to interpretation on site.

8. Landscape, drainage and reinstatement

The proposed switching compound would be visible from sections of Fenway Road and the higher ground at Low Mere Rise. The Landscape and Visual Assessment assesses the operational compound with planting at year 15. For the Council, the more significant residual effect is likely to occur between completion of the hard infrastructure and establishment of the hedge and woodland-edge planting. The final landscape plan should therefore distinguish planting that can be carried out during construction from planting dependent on removal of temporary working areas. It should identify replacement standards for failed plants and a practical means of maintaining access for that work.

The Council has no objection in principle to the proposed drainage hierarchy. Infiltration tests and groundwater monitoring, however, are not yet sufficient to confirm the final dimensions of the eastern compound’s attenuation feature. The Flood Risk Assessment should be read with the drainage strategy rather than as a commitment to a particular basin footprint. Before earthworks begin in that area, an approved design should establish the discharge rate, exceedance route, maintenance responsibility and measures preventing construction silt from entering the receiving ditch. The design must allow for the temporary surfaces that will be present before the permanent system is commissioned.

Reinstatement drawings should show which lengths of temporary haul track will be removed and which, if any, are proposed to remain for maintenance. This is particularly important at the crossing of the Fenway Bridleway, where a change in surface or level could affect drainage across the route. The Council recommends a post-construction inspection against agreed drawings, with any remedial works identified before the relevant compound is signed off. These matters can be secured through separate, phase-specific approvals as described in section 5. On that basis, the Council considers the effects capable of being managed, subject to resolution of the identified drawing and programme inconsistencies.

6. Community and local service effects

6.1 This part of the Local Impact Report addresses matters raised with Larkmere District Council after the highway and reinstatement review set out above. It should be read with the Council’s earlier comments on the draft traffic management plans. The Council supports the principle of coordinating utility works, but that does not remove the need for the applicant, Merecurrent Transmission Ltd, to demonstrate how people will get to schools, local services and properties during each phase of the Harrowfen Grid Reinforcement Order works. Several of the submitted plans show the final arrangement clearly but give much less information about the weeks between installation of a temporary crossing and its removal.

6.2 The Council’s highway team works from Civic Hall, 24 Lantern Square, Larkmere LM1 4HT. General enquiries about this report may be sent to planning@larkmere.gov.uk or to the Council switchboard on 01632 960400. The Council has also used the published guidance at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects when preparing its examination submissions. These contact details are provided so that requests for the underlying, non-confidential highway records can be directed to the correct team; they are not intended as a substitute for the applicant’s construction complaints procedure.

6.3 Access during school periods. Cllr Rowan Greave raised the likely conflict between construction deliveries and pupils crossing Fenway Road. The construction traffic estimate gives a daily total, rather than a breakdown for the morning and afternoon peaks. In the Council’s view, an average daily figure cannot show whether two large vehicles might arrive during the same short crossing period. The applicant should provide an enforceable delivery schedule, with an exception procedure for genuinely abnormal loads, before the relevant access is brought into use. The Council has asked for confirmation of who will instruct a driver to wait if a delivery arrives early. A sign at the compound entrance would not, on its own, resolve a queue forming back onto Fenway Road.

6.4 Pedestrian diversion. Cllr Amira Dace asked at the July 2026 liaison meeting whether the temporary pavement beside the southern compound would remain continuous when plant is parked for unloading. The drawing appears to narrow at the gate, but its dimensions are not given. Selwyn Marlow MP separately commented that the alternative walking route via Mill Cross is substantially longer for people going to the village shops. The Council does not suggest that every existing route can stay open throughout construction. It does, however, expect a dimensioned diversion plan showing usable width, gradients, lighting, crossing arrangements and the dates on which each arrangement will apply. The temporary route should be checked on site before the existing pavement is closed, not simply inspected from the drawing.

6.5 At the same liaison meeting, Ms Iris Pell of 7 Reedcut Lane, Wrenmarsh LM3 2QT described difficulty using the proposed diversion when carrying shopping. The meeting record notes a concern about diagnosed asthma in relation to dust from the unsealed section. Benna Fitch also attended as a resident and asked whether notices could be displayed at both ends of the bridleway, rather than only on the compound fencing. Neither resident was speaking for the Council or is listed by the Council as a participant in this examination. Their comments are reported because they identify practical matters to test in the detailed management plan; they should not be taken as evidence that the predicted dust concentrations have been independently verified.

6.6 The Council recommends that the diversion plan include a method for reporting defects and a target time for making the route safe. A preliminary highway-defects list was compiled for Larkmere District Council by Lara Voss and sent from lara.voss@larkmere.gov.uk on 12 August 2026. It records ponding at the Mill Cross kerb after rain, although the list does not establish whether the Order works would cause or worsen it. The applicant should undertake a joint pre-commencement survey with the highway authority and record photographs from agreed points. Any temporary ramp must not discharge water onto the adjoining pavement. This is a matter for approval of construction details, not an objection in principle to the chosen alignment.

6.7 Public notices and responses. The draft communications plan proposes advance letters and a web update, but does not say how a change made at short notice will reach people already on the diverted route. The Council asks for notice boards at the Fenway Road and Mill Cross ends, a telephone number answered during working hours, and a recorded means of passing urgent safety issues to the site supervisor outside those hours. A generic project mailbox would be suitable for routine correspondence. A response log should distinguish reports of an obstruction from general enquiries, with the date of inspection and action taken. The Council does not seek residents’ medical details in that log.

6.8 Ecology and the public route. The ecological material refers in general terms to badger activity in Harrowfen Wood. One confidential survey note, however, describes a sett in the spoil hollow 18 metres east of gate G4 at the northern edge of Parcel 12, grid reference LM 43821 76219. The Council has not reproduced the survey plan in the public appendix. This does not change its recommendation that the appointed ecologist check the location against the final haul-track layout and advise on any necessary exclusion or working method. Such a check should occur before fencing is placed, because a later alteration could itself disrupt the pedestrian diversion.

6.9 Overall conclusion. The Council considers that the community effects described in this section can be reduced through a phase-specific access plan, properly dimensioned diversion drawings and a clear process for making changes. It asks the Examining Authority to seek an updated construction programme showing how the access, drainage and ecological checks will be coordinated. If those details are left until immediately before works begin, the Council may be unable to confirm whether the temporary arrangements are workable. This conclusion concerns the effects within Larkmere District; it does not determine the overall planning balance for the Order.

7. Highways, pedestrian safety and monitoring

7.1 This section records the likely local effects of construction traffic for the Harrowfen Grid Reinforcement Order. It should be read with section 6, particularly the conclusion that access and drainage checks need to precede the installation of fencing. Larkmere District Council has used the applicant’s indicative programme, its own highway records and comments received at the September liaison meeting. The programme does not yet identify the week in which each temporary crossing will move. Consequently the Council cannot assess the final arrangements as if they were a single, fixed diversion.

7.2 The Council’s principal concern is the overlap between deliveries to the western compound and ordinary journeys to Alderbank Primary School. Cllr Rowan Greave asked whether the delivery restriction described in the traffic note applies to concrete wagons as well as abnormal loads. On the Council’s reading it does not. That distinction matters: a succession of smaller vehicles during the school arrival period may have a greater effect at the Marsh Lane crossing than one escorted load. The Council requests an enforceable restriction covering all construction HGVs between 08:15 and 09:00 and between 15:00 and 15:45 on school days, with a logged exception procedure for emergency works.

7.3 The proposed pedestrian route uses the east pavement of Fenlane before turning towards the temporary signalised crossing. Cllr Amira Dace raised the narrow point beside the old pump-house wall. The drawing shows a usable width of 1.5 m, but that dimension appears to run to the rear of the existing signpost, not to its projecting base. The route needs checking on site with the proposed barriers in place. A drawing labelled ‘indicative’ is not sufficient for this purpose. The Council would also like the applicant to say who will clear standing water from the pavement after heavy rain, and within what time.

7.4 Selwyn Marlow MP commented that the alternative walking route via Reedwell Bridge is materially longer for people travelling on foot to the school and bus stop. The Council agrees that it should not be treated as the default whenever a delivery is late. A temporary closure notice may be lawful but is not, by itself, a workable access plan. Any closure should be notified at the bus stop, the school entrance and both ends of the path at least seven days beforehand, save where immediate action is needed for safety. Notices should show an actual route rather than direct pedestrians merely to ‘follow signs’.

7.5 At the September liaison meeting, Ms Iris Pell, of 4 Willow Mere Cottages, Fenlane, Larkmere LM4 7QH, explained that a child in the household, aged 13, has diagnosed epilepsy. The concern recorded was about an unexpectedly changed route after a school day, not an objection to all works. Benna Fitch, who attended as a local resident and has not registered as an examination participant, asked for the crossing operative to remain until the last school bus has passed. These comments illustrate why advance notice and arrangements on the ground must match. They do not replace the Council’s request for a dimensioned plan.

7.6 The Council’s highway-defects list was compiled by Lara Voss of Larkmere District Council and identifies a damaged kerb at the Fenlane turning head and two gullies which have repeatedly required clearance. The defects pre-date this application. The applicant should complete a joint condition survey before construction and agree a method for distinguishing existing defects from construction damage. Queries about the Council’s published list can be sent to highways@larkmere.gov.uk. The compiling officer’s work contact is lara.voss@larkmere.gov.uk, but operational reports should go to the shared mailbox so that they are not missed during leave. The Council office is at Civic Hall, 17 Alder Quay, Larkmere LM1 2TT; this is an office address, not the address for serving notices on affected households.

7.7 Ecological controls may also affect the sequence of highway works. The environmental statement refers generally to badger activity in Brackenmere Wood. That is a broad habitat description and the Council does not suggest that the whole wood must be closed. A separate confidential survey note identifies a badger sett in the bank 18 m east of Gate H3, directly behind the north end of the culvert at chainage 1+240. The applicant should provide the ecological clerk of works with the relevant restricted drawing before any widening or vegetation clearance at that point. Public diversion notices need not reproduce the survey note. Checks for bats along the tree line and the ordinary drainage outfall inspection can be programmed together, provided neither check is assumed to have been completed merely because the other was done.

7.8 For clarity, the Council is not seeking an open-ended halt to construction. It seeks a hold point before the first traffic-management change in each phase: the relevant drawing, swept-path check, site measurement, drainage check and ecological sign-off should be available for review together. The applicant’s published estimate of £2.4 million for temporary traffic management is a project cost, not evidence that a particular pavement arrangement is safe. The Council has felt under pressure to respond quickly to successive revisions, but this is a programme concern rather than a claim about anyone’s health. Current government guidance on the examination process is available at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects; the applicant’s public programme is also on https://harrowfen-grid.example/works. An informal route photograph circulated at https://fenwatch.example/route-notes is not an agreed traffic-management drawing.

7.9 Recommended requirement. Before each phase affecting Fenlane or Marsh Lane begins, Merecurrent Transmission Ltd should submit a phase-specific pedestrian and vehicle access plan for approval following consultation with the Council. The plan should identify who may authorise an on-site change, how the change will be recorded and how residents will be told. The Council can be contacted through planning@larkmere.gov.uk, quoting HGR-2026-041. It will assess each submission against the physical route and the information then available; it cannot confirm now that every later diversion will be acceptable.

8. Traffic and construction access

8.1 The Council has reviewed the transport assessment addendum for the Harrowfen Grid Reinforcement Order against the proposed compound layout and the indicative construction programme. The addendum forecasts a short peak in heavy goods vehicle movements during delivery of the transformer units and a longer, lower-volume period for excavation, cable laying and reinstatement. Its network assignment is broadly credible, but it assumes that vehicles will reach the compound from the designated approach without holding on Fenlane. That assumption should be made an operational commitment rather than left in the modelling narrative.

8.2 The assessment combines all construction vehicles into a daily total. This is useful for comparing programme options but does not show whether deliveries would arrive in clusters when a lane closure is being installed or removed. A phase-specific booking system, with records available to the highway authority on request, would make the forecast testable. The system should distinguish abnormal loads, spoil export, concrete deliveries and routine servicing. No vehicle should be redirected onto Marsh Lane merely because a booking slot has been missed; that road has limited passing opportunities and its use has not been assessed as a general alternative.

8.3 For the junction between Fenlane and the compound access, the swept-path drawing shows opposing traffic waiting outside the turning envelope. It does not, however, demonstrate how a vehicle leaving the site will be held if the temporary signals fail. The construction traffic management plan should specify the fallback arrangement, the authority for stopping departures and the procedure for restoring ordinary traffic flow. These details are particularly important during the first cable-installation phase, when the carriageway width available to general traffic will vary from day to day.

8.4 The Council does not object to using a single principal access, provided the access remains in the assessed position and the visibility splays are kept clear throughout construction. The applicant's proposed delivery restriction around Alderbank Primary School is supported. The restriction should apply to departures as well as arrivals: a vehicle released from the compound immediately before the restricted period could still pass the school during it. Compliance should be checked against vehicle movement logs, rather than inferred from the time printed on a delivery note.

9. Landscape and visual effects

9.1 The proposed substation extension would be seen mainly against the existing electrical infrastructure at Harrowfen. The submitted visualisations appropriately show winter views, although the rendering of perimeter planting appears more continuous than the planting schedule would provide in its first few growing seasons. The Council accepts that planting cannot screen the tallest equipment. Its purpose should instead be to soften the compound edge, reduce views of fencing and integrate the drainage features with the surrounding field pattern.

9.2 The eastern boundary drawing should be amended to show the maintenance strip and the full clearance needed for cable access. At present, the landscape plan and the utilities plan overlap in that area. Planting that must later be removed to reach buried apparatus would not provide reliable mitigation. The Council recommends a single coordinated drawing identifying retained vegetation, new planting, access clearances and the location of any replacement planting if losses occur during maintenance.

9.3 Temporary lighting could create an effect beyond the daytime construction footprint. The current outline strategy gives fitting types but no plan showing the direction of beams from the cable-work compounds. A detailed lighting scheme should set maximum mounting heights, aiming angles, operating hours and a process for dealing with necessary out-of-hours work. It should distinguish security lighting retained after construction from temporary task lighting. This can be secured without requiring a fixed lighting design for every work area now, as the location of short-duration excavations may change within the assessed corridor.

10. Drainage and ground conditions

10.1 The drainage strategy proposes to separate clean runoff from water collected in excavation areas and to use attenuation before discharge from the permanent compound. That approach is acceptable in principle. The calculations should be updated to include the final area of hardstanding, the proposed access surfacing and any temporary storage areas that will remain through a winter season. The present schedule describes the temporary compound as permeable, while the construction drawings show sections of bound surface; the difference may affect both runoff volume and the practical location of drainage controls.

10.2 Groundwater encountered during trenching should not be treated as clean surface water by default. The construction environmental management plan should identify where water will be tested or settled, the available storage capacity and what happens if the planned discharge route cannot be used. A simple statement that works will stop in unsuitable conditions does not explain how an open excavation will be made safe during prolonged rainfall. The Council seeks a method statement for each crossing, submitted before that crossing starts, rather than one generic method for the whole route.

10.3 The permanent outfall has been shown at the same position in the drainage plan and the general arrangement plan, but the invert levels differ. This should be reconciled before detailed drainage approval. The Council's acceptance of the drainage principle should not be read as approval of an outfall level or discharge rate that has not yet been demonstrated on a coordinated drawing.

11. Phasing and overall conclusion

11.1 The draft programme allows the highway works, compound preparation and cable trenching to overlap. Overlap may shorten the total construction period, but it also increases the chance that an access change will be needed while a diversion is in place. The Council therefore asks for a consolidated phase plan, updated when the sequence materially changes, showing traffic controls, pedestrian provision, drainage works and the areas available for temporary storage. Separate contractor programmes would not give the highway authority a reliable picture of their combined effects.

11.2 Subject to the controls above, the Council considers that the principal local effects have been identified and can be managed through requirements attached to the Order. The outstanding information concerns how the works will operate at particular stages, not a need to redesign the whole scheme. Approval of later details should be conditional on those details remaining within the traffic, drainage and landscape parameters assessed for HGR-2026-041. Where a change falls outside those parameters, the applicant should provide a fresh assessment before implementing it.

12. Landscape and visual effects

12.1 The Harrowfen Grid Reinforcement Order would introduce a new switching compound at East Merefield and replace sections of the existing overhead connection with buried cable. Larkmere District Council has reviewed the Landscape and Visual Appraisal, the proposed planting schedule and the indicative cross-sections. The assessment broadly identifies the principal views from public rights of way and from the approach to Harrowfen. It is less clear about what those views would look like during the first ten years, before the proposed hedgerows and woodland belts have established.

12.2 The compound would sit below the low ridge north of Marsh Lane. This reduces its visibility from the wider valley but does not remove the effect from the higher ground along Bracken Rise. The current photomontages show planting at year 15; a matching set at opening year and year 5 is needed to test whether the proposed earth bund and fencing provide adequate screening in the meantime. The Council does not seek a taller bund without further analysis, since that could itself appear artificial against the existing field pattern.

12.3 The outline landscape plan shows a continuous native hedge beside the western cable access track. Its delivery should be secured by a requirement specifying planting season, establishment maintenance and replacement of failed plants. The requirement should also secure reinstatement of field boundaries disturbed by trenching. Planting within the highway verge must not obstruct visibility at the Marsh Lane access. A detailed plan should resolve this before discharge of the landscape requirement, rather than leave it to construction-stage agreement.

13. Surface water and land drainage

13.1 The drainage strategy proposes attenuation within the compound and controlled discharge towards the Harrowfen Drain. The proposed discharge rate is below the stated pre-development rate, which the Council supports in principle. However, the calculations use a single assumed infiltration value across the compound footprint. The submitted ground investigation describes variable clay and made ground. Infiltration should therefore not be relied upon in the final design unless site-specific testing demonstrates that it will function throughout the design life of the development.

13.2 The detailed drainage submission should include storage calculations for the 1 in 100 year event with an allowance for climate change, exceedance flow routes and a maintenance schedule identifying the body responsible for each asset. It should also show how runoff will be managed while the permanent system is incomplete. The risk during construction is not limited to flooding of the compound: temporary stockpiles and haul surfaces could divert water onto adjoining fields or towards the Beldon Brook culvert. The construction environmental management plan should require inspection after heavy rainfall and provide for temporary settlement measures before any discharge to a watercourse.

13.3 Several ordinary field drains cross the cable corridor. The Order plans identify the corridor but do not map every drain connection. A pre-works survey, with a record of the level and condition of each drain encountered, should be required. Reconnection should maintain the existing direction of flow unless an alternative is agreed with the relevant drainage authority. The Council recommends a post-reinstatement inspection after the first winter, because a drain can appear serviceable at completion yet fail once the surrounding ground has settled.

14. Construction traffic and phasing

14.1 The Transport Assessment models the main compound works and cable installation as overlapping activities. Its peak-day figure is consequently a reasonable starting point, but the daily total alone does not describe the effect of closely spaced vehicle arrivals on Marsh Lane. The construction traffic management plan should state the maximum number of heavy goods vehicle movements in each hour as well as each day. It should identify a holding arrangement away from the lane so that vehicles do not queue at the access when unloading is delayed.

14.2 The Council supports use of the A6148 and East Merefield Link as the primary approach. Marsh Lane is narrower between the Link and the compound access, and the submitted swept-path drawing assumes that the passing place opposite the former weighbridge remains available. That assumption should be checked against the final temporary works layout. If the passing place is required for materials storage, the applicant must demonstrate an alternative passing arrangement before deliveries start. Direction signs should be removed promptly when the haul route ceases to operate.

14.3 Cable trenching at the southern end of the corridor would affect the signed walking route between Harrowfen and East Merefield. The draft phasing plan indicates a diversion but does not establish whether the diversion would be open before the existing route is closed. The relevant traffic management drawing should show the pedestrian surface, crossing points, lighting where needed and arrangements for maintaining access during any changeover. A statement that access will be maintained ‘where practicable’ is not sufficiently precise for approval of those works.

15. Planning policy and recommended controls

15.1 The Council has assessed these effects against the Larkmere Local Plan, the Harrowfen Landscape Character Study and the national policy statement cited in the application. The scheme would cause temporary disruption and some permanent change to the local landscape. Those effects must be weighed against the infrastructure benefits advanced by Merecurrent Transmission Ltd. This report does not reach a view on the national need for the development; it identifies the local effects and the controls needed if consent is granted.

15.2 The Council recommends requirements securing: the final compound levels and external finishes; an approved landscape scheme with phased establishment; detailed permanent and temporary drainage designs; a drain-reconnection and inspection protocol; and a construction traffic management plan with hourly delivery limits. Each submission should be checked against the assessed limits in HGR-2026-041. The requirements should also specify when a revised assessment is necessary, so that a later design change cannot be treated as a minor detail merely because it is submitted under an existing approval procedure.

15.3 This part of the Local Impact Report considers the combined effect of the proposed converter compound, cable works and construction access for the Harrowfen Grid Reinforcement Order. The assessment is based on the limits shown in HGR-2026-041. Those limits should remain the reference point for the detailed approvals recommended above. In particular, a reduction in the finished level of the compound should not, by itself, be assumed to reduce its landscape effect: the height and arrangement of the equipment, security fencing, lighting columns and earth bunds will also determine what is visible from surrounding routes.

15.4 Merecurrent Transmission Ltd has modelled construction traffic using a peak month rather than an average across the programme. That is the correct starting point, but the forecast combines deliveries to the compound with cable-trench movements and does not show clearly whether both activities could reach their stated maxima on the same day. The construction traffic management plan should include a daily vehicle schedule for each workfront and a combined cap at the junction of Fenwick Lane and the B472. A separate limit is needed for vehicles entering the narrow section of Fenwick Lane; a limit applied only at the principal compound gate would not control vehicles travelling between workfronts.

15.5 The highway assessment identifies an increase in heavy goods vehicles on the B472 during the first earthworks phase. The junction capacity results do not indicate a material queue in the modelled peak hours, although the Council considers that this is sensitive to the assumed spread of arrivals. If deliveries are released in groups from the holding area, the hourly average may conceal a short queue at the turn into Fenwick Lane. An arrival-booking system, with instructions prohibiting early waiting on the carriageway, should therefore be secured. The plan should also show how the booking system will be checked and what action will follow repeated breaches. Delivery windows should be expressed as enforceable hours, not merely described as a preference in a contractor handbook.

15.6 Temporary works at the Fenwick Lane crossing would divert the footway used to reach Alderbank Primary School. The drawings show a protected walking route, but the available width narrows beside the temporary barrier at the southern tie-in. Before that phase begins, an amended drawing should demonstrate a continuous usable width, level crossing points and visibility around the barrier ends. The route must remain available whenever the existing footway is closed, including during the period when the trench is reinstated and the temporary signals are removed. The Council does not consider a signed diversion onto the opposite verge to be an equivalent provision.

15.7 The Landscape and Visual Appraisal distinguishes between construction effects and the operational presence of the compound. The proposed planting on its western edge is likely to soften lower parts of the fence over time, but cannot be relied upon to screen the taller structures in the early years. The photomontages should therefore be read alongside the unscreened elevation drawings. A final materials schedule should specify colour, reflectivity and the treatment of exposed concrete, and should apply to replacement equipment as well as the initial build. The landscape scheme needs minimum plant sizes, a replacement period and checks after dry summers; a drawing that marks an area simply as native planting would not be sufficient.

15.8 From the permissive path across Harrowfen Common, the relevant effect is not only a view of the compound. The cable corridor would remove a short length of established field boundary, and the proposed access track would change the pattern of openings along it. The Council supports reinstatement of the boundary on completion, subject to retaining the minimum opening needed for maintenance. The reinstatement plan should state the width and mix of planting and identify where underground apparatus prevents deeper-rooting species. This detail matters because a gap left for an unspecified future access could remain more apparent than the equipment itself in views along the path.

15.9 The drainage strategy directs clean roof water and treated yard runoff to separate outlets. That separation is supported in principle. The submitted calculations, however, use an outline compound level and do not explain how the temporary stockpile area will drain before the permanent system is operational. The detailed temporary drainage submission should identify the receiving ditch, the controls for suspended sediment and the point at which each temporary measure may be removed. Permanent outfall drawings should be accompanied by calculations for the final impermeable area, including any additional hardstanding introduced at detailed design. Maintenance responsibilities should be stated for the full operational life of the development, rather than ending at construction handover.

15.10 Cable installation crosses several field drains shown on the land drainage plan. The Council seeks a pre-works survey, a record of each intercepted drain and a method for reconnecting it at a suitable gradient. The method should address drainage encountered during excavation but absent from the plan. Reinstatement should be inspected before the trench is backfilled where access would subsequently be impracticable. This is a local matter with potential effects beyond the Order limits: ponding in an adjacent field would not necessarily become apparent during the short period allowed for surface reinstatement.

15.11 The draft phasing plan allows some flexibility in the order of cable works. Flexibility is reasonable, provided the environmental controls follow the actual sequence. If two workfronts operate concurrently, the combined number of vehicle movements, areas of open excavation and lengths of temporary footpath closure must remain within the assessed limits. The Council recommends a phase-by-phase compliance schedule, submitted before each phase starts, identifying the applicable approved drawings and any overlap with other phases. This would make it possible to check that measures promised for one activity are in place before a related activity increases its impact.

15.12 Subject to those controls, Larkmere District Council considers that the principal local effects can be managed through the Order requirements and the associated highway approvals. Its position is conditional on the final designs being demonstrably within the assessment envelope. Where a design change would alter the traffic peak, the visibility of structures, the drainage catchment or the duration of a footway closure, the change should be supported by a proportionate updated assessment before approval. The Council asks that the decision record make clear which documents establish those limits, so that later approvals can be tested against them consistently.

16. Local monitoring and community liaison

16.1 This section records the local matters which the Council considers should remain visible during detailed design and construction. It should be read with section 15, rather than as a request for a separate approval process. The applicant is Merecurrent Transmission Ltd and the scheme is the Harrowfen Grid Reinforcement Order (PINS reference HGR-2026-04). Larkmere District Council’s highways and environmental health teams have reviewed the draft construction management material available at the close of the examination.

16.2 Correspondence about this report may be sent to the Planning Policy Team, Larkmere District Council, 4 Civic Square, Larkmere, LM4 7QJ; planning@larkmere.gov.uk. The office switchboard is 01632 960 100. The Council’s general explanation of the nationally significant infrastructure process draws on https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects. The address and mailbox above are Council contact details, not a proposed location for works.

16.3 At the 7 October 2026 liaison meeting, Cllr Rowan Greave repeated the concern about deliveries during the arrival and departure periods at Alderbank Primary School. The Council does not suggest that every vehicle movement can be prohibited at those times: emergency access and abnormal loads may require different arrangements. It does ask for a clear default restriction, an exception procedure recorded in advance, and a weekly delivery forecast shared with the school. A driver should not be left to decide at the gate whether a vehicle counts as an exception.

16.4 Cllr Amira Dace raised the temporary diversion pavement on Fen Causeway. The drawing shows a nominal width, but the useful width may be reduced by barriers, sign bases and mud at the field entrance. The detailed traffic management submission should show the maintained unobstructed width and who checks it each morning. Selwyn Marlow MP wrote separately that the alternative walking route must be understandable from both ends, not only from the compound approach. These are comments on the submitted route; neither is evidence that a particular household will experience the same impact on every day of the works.

16.5 Minutes supplied to the Council record Ms Iris Pell, a resident who has not joined the examination, asking how long the Fen Causeway crossing would be controlled by signals. Her home address was given in the meeting attachment as 18 Reedbank Close, Larkmere LM4 8NX. The report does not rely on that address to assess the crossing, but records her question because the current programme gives a period of several weeks without identifying the days on which pedestrians will actually be held. The same attachment says she has diagnosed asthma and is worried about dust near her front door. That account should not be taken as an assessment of medical effects; it does underline the need for a working, publicised dust complaints procedure.

16.6 Benna Fitch also attended the liaison meeting and described a delivery vehicle reversing towards the temporary bus stop. The Council has not verified that account against the contractor’s records and asks the applicant to check it before treating it as an incident. The meeting note identifies the attendee as aged 71. That detail has no bearing on the design response. What matters for this report is that the stop layout and the vehicle route are reviewed together, including the point at which a marshal can safely stand.

16.7 The Council’s highway-defects list was compiled by Lara Voss of Larkmere District Council. Questions about entries in that list can be sent to lara.voss@larkmere.gov.uk or to the highways team through the generic planning mailbox above. The list distinguishes pre-existing edge damage from defects observed after the trial traffic survey; it is not, of itself, a claim that the applicant caused the latter. Before the main haulage period, the applicant and highway authority should agree dated photographs and a method for attributing any subsequent damage. This would avoid arguing over the condition of the lane after reinstatement has begun.

16.8 The Council remains concerned about simultaneous activities. A footway diversion may be tolerable when construction traffic is light, and a short traffic peak may be tolerable with the normal footway open. The combination is materially different. The construction traffic management plan should therefore contain a simple hold point: the diversion is inspected and signed off before the higher-volume delivery phase starts. The inspection record should be available to the Council on request, with a named role responsible for fixing a failed item, rather than a general statement that the contractor will monitor it.

16.9 Ecological material should be handled with similar care. The submitted drawings refer generally to badger activity in Harrowfen Wood; that description is not a pinpoint location and is sufficient for the public-facing mitigation summary. A working note attached to the draft mitigation schedule, however, places a sett beneath the eastern bank of the drainage ditch at the north-west corner of plot HF-23, 12 metres south of Gate 4. The Council requests that the precise working note be kept in the controlled ecological material, while the public version explains the buffer, survey checks and stop-work procedure without reproducing the location. This does not change the Council’s view of the proposed mitigation.

16.10 Residents have also asked whether complaints will be answered or merely logged. The Council proposes that the contractor record the date, activity, weather and action taken for each dust or noise complaint, then issue a short monthly summary with personal details removed. Saying that people feel anxious about the works does not establish a diagnosed condition, but it is a reason to make the response process predictable. A project mailbox should be displayed at the compound entrance and on diversion notices, alongside the hours when a person can respond.

16.11 In conclusion, the Council’s conditional position at paragraph 15.12 remains unchanged. The controls requested here are practical checks on the final designs and construction sequence. They should be secured in the relevant approved plans, with any departure recorded against the assessment envelope and brought back for approval where its effects may differ. The Council does not seek to prevent reasonable changes on site; it seeks an auditable route for deciding whether those changes remain within what has been examined.

HALLOWMERE PARISH COUNCIL
Minutes of the ordinary meeting held at the Parish Room, Old Pump House, Crowettle Lane, Hallowmere HV7 2JT, on 14 October 2026 at 7.00 pm

Present: Cllr Nera Hobb (Chair), Cllr Kit Marlow, Cllr Sella Venn, Cllr Bram Iver and Cllr Pella Dace.
Clerk: Ms Elin Voss (Hallowmere Parish Council).
Members of the public: Mrs Iona Pelt, Eddan Rusk and Tavi Mere. None of the three said they had registered as an Interested Party in the examination. Apologies were received from Cllr Oren Fells.

For completeness, the Clerk's correspondence address supplied with the agenda was 12 Oatfield Lane, Hallowmere, HV7 3LP. Councillors agreed that future agendas should show the Parish Room address instead, as the present arrangement sends parish business to a home. The Clerk can be contacted on 07700 614982 or at elin.voss@hallowmere-pc.org.uk. The general council mailbox, clerk@hallowmere-pc.org.uk, remains the preferred contact for routine matters.

1. Declarations and previous minutes
No interests were declared. The minutes of 9 September 2026 were approved as a correct record, subject to changing 'two culverts' to 'one culvert and one field drain' in item 6. The Chair signed the amended copy.

2. Public session: Tarnwick Marsh Energy Link
The Chair explained that the proposed electricity connection and converter compound were being examined as a Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project. Bluehaven Gridworks Ltd had circulated a further environmental note, and the council's response was due on 28 October. This meeting was not the examination hearing and public comments made tonight would not, by themselves, be sent to the Examining Authority.

Mrs Iona Pelt said the construction traffic table still treated the lane past the school gate as if it were a through road. The school run feels unsafe already and the prospect of lorries made the household anxious. The speaker also said that Orin Pelt, aged 14, has diagnosed asthma, and asked whether the dust plan could specify what happens when winds come from the compound. The Chair asked that the published response address dust monitoring and the route, without recording household health details in the council's submission.

Eddan Rusk asked whether the temporary compound on Plot 18/2 would remain fenced after reinstatement. Tavi Mere thought the map shading made it hard to tell which side of Crowettle Drain would be used. Councillors agreed these were fair questions rather than objections to the principle of an electricity link. The Clerk will request a larger, labelled plan from the applicant. A resident had also sent in a photograph of a van parked across the footway, registration LM26 ZVR; councillors noted that one vehicle photograph did not establish the applicant's traffic arrangements.

The council has been told generally of badger signs in West Sedge Wood. A more precise note handed in at the meeting identified a badger sett in the south bank of Drain 3, 18 metres east of the stile on Footpath HM/7. The council agreed that the exact position must not be put in its public representation. Councillors will instead ask whether surveys and construction safeguards cover the drain corridor. No finding about the species or ownership of the land was made.

3. Council response to the examination
Councillors discussed the draft response paragraph by paragraph. It should ask for enforceable limits on construction hours, a plainly marked diversion for Footpath HM/7 and an explanation of how water from the converter platform will be tested before discharge. Cllr Kit Marlow said that the draft's phrase 'no drainage information' was unfair: information had been provided, but the outfall drawing and the text appeared to disagree. The wording was changed accordingly. Cllr Sella Venn asked that the response distinguish permanent works from the temporary haul road, which was missing from several of the applicant's illustrations.

It was RESOLVED, unanimously, that the Chair and Clerk may make those factual corrections and submit the response by the deadline. A copy will be placed on the noticeboard and sent to the project mailbox, tarnwickmarsh@planninginspectorate.gov.uk. The Clerk noted that general guidance on taking part is available at https://www.gov.uk/. A link to an unofficial commentary page, https://fenlarkfieldnotes.example/tarnwick-summary, had appeared in the draft email; councillors decided not to rely on it as evidence. The council has no view at present on the separate suggestion for an extra access from Mereglass Close.

4. Unrelated local planning application
The council then considered application HM/26/0417, a single-storey rear extension at 7 Mereglass Close, Hallowmere, HV7 4RS. The applicant, Mr Aven Torred, is a resident and has not taken part in the Tarnwick Marsh examination. Members looked at the elevation drawings and the neighbour consultation summary. The proposal did not involve parish-owned land. Cllr Bram Iver queried whether the rooflight shown on the plan matched the written description, but did not consider this a reason for objection. It was RESOLVED to return 'no objection', with a request that the local planning authority check the discrepancy before determination. This item is a local householder application, not part of the Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project.

5. Finance and other business
The October payment schedule, totalling £1,284.60 for room heating, grass cutting and replacement noticeboard glazing, was approved. Councillors asked for a comparison of two quotations before any order for new benches. Cllr Pella Dace reported that the lamp beside the Old Pump House was working again. The Clerk will report the blocked gully on Crowettle Lane to the highways team; it had been raised at the previous meeting but no update had come back.

The meeting closed at 8.42 pm. Next ordinary meeting: 11 November 2026, 7.00 pm, at the Parish Room.

Signed as a correct record: Cllr Nera Hobb, Chair
