HALLOWMERE PARISH COUNCIL
Minutes of the ordinary meeting held in the Parish Room on 11 November 2026 at 7.00 pm

These minutes are included with the Council's submission to the Tarnwick Marsh Energy Link examination. Item 4 records the Council's discussion of the proposed works; the remaining items are ordinary parish business. Draft minutes, subject to approval at the next meeting.

Present: Cllr Nera Hobb (Chair), Cllr Kit Marlow, Cllr Sella Venn, Cllr Bram Iver, Cllr Pella Dace and Cllr Oren Fells. In attendance: Ms Elin Voss (Clerk). Members of the public present for part of the meeting: Mrs Iona Pelt, Eddan Rusk and Tavi Mere.

Clerk's correspondence address for parish business: 14 Brindle Fold, Hallowmere, HM4 8QJ. Direct telephone: 01632 960482. Email: elin.voss@hallowmereparish.example. General parish enquiries may instead be sent to planning@hallowmereparish.example.

1. Apologies, interests and previous minutes
There were no apologies. No interests were declared in the matters on the agenda. The minutes of 14 October 2026 were agreed as an accurate record and signed by the Chair. The Clerk said the comparison of bench quotations requested at that meeting was still outstanding; one supplier had provided a price without specifying whether installation was included. Councillors agreed not to place an order until this was clear.

2. Public session
The Chair explained that the Council could receive comments about the Tarnwick Marsh Energy Link but could not determine the application. Comments intended as formal representations should be sent through the examination process. The Council's own representation would deal with matters raised at the meeting where they were relevant to the parish.

Mrs Iona Pelt said the proposed construction route looked too close to the school walking route. Mrs Iona Pelt also explained that Orin Pelt, aged 9, has asthma, and asked whether the dust-control proposals included the wait by the footbridge where children gather after school. The Chair thanked the speaker and said the Council would ask for a clearer plan showing where monitoring would take place. No medical information will be included in the Council's representation.

Eddan Rusk asked if the temporary traffic lights on Crowettle Lane would operate during the morning school run. The Chair said the published construction table gave broad working hours but, as far as councillors could tell, did not give dates for the traffic-light installation. Tavi Mere said residents had already put up with road works in the area for over 60 years, on and off, and that another diversion would be frustrating. The Chair asked the Clerk to check whether the applicant's traffic note distinguished the lane closure from the temporary lights. There was some discussion about whether the footpath gate could still be reached from the village side; nobody present was certain.

3. Matters arising and highways
The Clerk reported that the highways team had acknowledged the blocked gully on Crowettle Lane but had not supplied a date for clearing it. The water had crossed part of the carriageway after the recent rain. Cllr Bram Iver suggested sending a photograph with the existing report number rather than opening a second report. Cllr Pella Dace confirmed that the lamp beside the Old Pump House remained working. Councillors also noted that the replacement noticeboard glazing had been fitted, although the lower catch was stiff. The Clerk will raise this with the installer.

4. Tarnwick Marsh Energy Link: draft examination response
Councillors considered the draft response to Bluehaven Gridworks Ltd's construction and access information. Cllr Sella Venn said the draft should distinguish the Council's concern about the amount of construction traffic from its more specific question about vehicle movements past the footbridge. Cllr Kit Marlow asked for the drawing number to be included beside each request so that the Examining Authority could locate the relevant plan. It was agreed that the Clerk would insert these references before circulation.

Cllr Oren Fells asked whether the proposed reinstatement of the field-edge path meant the same width of usable surface, or simply the same legal line. The Chair said that was a reasonable question and should be put in neutral terms. Councillors did not agree with a suggestion made in the public session that the path should be closed permanently. The Council's position remains that a safe route should be available during works if practicable, with any short closure explained in advance.

The ecology paragraph referred generally to badger setts in Reedglass Wood. Councillors agreed that this was sufficient for the Council's point about survey timing and that the submission did not need to identify individual field signs. They also asked for the response to mention the protection of existing hedges, replacement planting and the length of time temporary fencing would remain. These are questions about the proposed mitigation, not objections to surveying the area.

Subject to those changes, the draft was approved for submission by Hallowmere Parish Council before the examination deadline. The Chair and Clerk will check that the final document matches the version authorised tonight. The project mailbox will be used for correspondence with the examination team; no individual attendee's contact details are to be added to the response.

5. Local planning application, separate from Item 4
The Clerk reported a request for parish comments on application HM/26/0418/HH, described as a single-storey rear extension at Meadow Rise for Mr Aven Torred. Councillors had previously deferred comments pending an amended window drawing. The amended drawing now showed obscure glazing to the side window, but did not state whether it would be fixed shut. Cllr Pella Dace proposed that the Council make no objection, subject to the planning authority checking the window detail against its usual residential amenity policy. This was agreed. The Chair reminded those present that this is a local householder application and has no connection with the Tarnwick Marsh Energy Link examination.

6. Finance and next meeting
The November payment schedule of £936.40, including the Parish Room electricity charge and the noticeboard repair, was approved. The Clerk will bring the outstanding bench quotations to the next meeting. The meeting closed at 8.36 pm. The next ordinary meeting will be on 9 December 2026 at 7.00 pm in the Parish Room.

HALLOWMERE PARISH COUNCIL
Minutes of the ordinary meeting held in the Parish Room on 9 December 2026 at 7.00 pm

Present: Cllr Nera Hobb (Chair), Cllr Kit Marlow, Cllr Sella Venn, Cllr Bram Iver, Cllr Pella Dace and Cllr Oren Fells. In attendance: Ms Elin Voss (Clerk). Members of the public: Mrs Iona Pelt, Eddan Rusk and Tavi Mere.

For correspondence about these minutes: Clerk to Hallowmere Parish Council, 14 Brackenfold Lane, Hallowmere, HM7 4QJ. Direct telephone: 01632 960741. Email: elin.voss@hallowmere-pc.example. General enquiries may be sent to clerk@hallowmere-pc.example.

1. Apologies and declarations
There were no apologies. Cllr Pella Dace declared that the footpath discussed under item 4 passes land which she regularly walks across, but that she had no financial interest in it. No other interests were declared. The minutes of 11 November were approved and signed by the Chair. The Clerk reported that the noticeboard repair approved at that meeting had been carried out; the replacement glazing is less reflective than the old sheet, which several residents had complained about.

2. Public participation
Mrs Iona Pelt asked whether the Council had received a further construction traffic plan for the Tarnwick Marsh Energy Link. She said the morning school crossing already feels unsafe when large vehicles turn by the Parish Room. Her child, Orin Pelt, aged 11, has diagnosed epilepsy, and she was particularly concerned about delays to the school bus if the road is controlled by temporary lights. The Chair thanked her and explained that the Council could comment on traffic management, but could not promise a particular bus timetable. The Clerk was asked to pass the question to the examination case team without including the family's medical information in the Council's formal response.

Eddan Rusk said that notices at the two ends of Fenward Lane gave different dates for the utility survey. He asked if a plain-English notice could be put on the parish board before any further closures. Tavi Mere asked whether the promised wheel-washing would apply to vehicles leaving the temporary works compound, not only those leaving the main construction site. Neither speaker asked to become a party to the examination. The Chair closed public participation at 7.19 pm.

3. Tarnwick Marsh Energy Link: examination update
The Council considered the applicant's revised access drawing circulated by Bluehaven Gridworks Ltd on 2 December. Cllr Bram Iver thought the drawing made the width of the passing place clearer, but not the hours during which marsh deliveries might use Fenward Lane. Cllr Sella Venn said the Council should distinguish between its objection to an unrestricted delivery window and its support for the proposed reinstatement of the verge. Members agreed unanimously to send a short supplementary submission asking for the delivery hours, a procedure for reporting mud on the carriageway, and confirmation that emergency access would be maintained during temporary signal operation.

The Chair noted that people may be worried about noise and poor sleep during construction. The Council's response should refer to the likely effects and proposed controls rather than repeat individual accounts given in public participation. Cllr Kit Marlow asked that the crossing near the Parish Room be shown on the next traffic drawing, as the present drawing stops just short of it. The Clerk will draft the response for approval by email before the examination deadline. The Council's case reference, TME-2026-017, is to appear in the subject line so the submission is placed with the right project.

4. Footpath and ecology note
The Clerk reported a discrepancy between the footpath diversion plan and the ecological constraints sheet. Badger setts have been reported in Alderbank Wood; that description alone was considered too broad to affect the public route map. The survey note also identifies a sett beneath the eastern bank of the drainage ditch 18 metres south of Footpath HM/7 where it meets Alder Sluice. Members agreed that the precise survey information should go only to the relevant examination team and ecologist, and should not be reproduced on the parish noticeboard. Cllr Oren Fells asked that the Council's public comment instead seek suitable fencing and an agreed method of working near protected habitats. The Council made no finding about the accuracy of the survey.

5. Local planning matters, unrelated to the NSIP
The Council considered the revised drawings for Mr Aven Torred's householder application at Willowglass House, Fenward Lane, reference HM/26/084. The revised upstairs window is shown with obscured glass, as requested in the Council's November comment, but the drawing still does not say whether it is fixed shut. Cllr Pella Dace proposed that the Council maintain its position of no objection, subject to the planning authority checking that detail against its residential amenity policy. This was agreed, with Cllr Bram Iver abstaining because he had not seen the earlier drawing. The Chair again confirmed that the application is not part of the Tarnwick Marsh Energy Link examination and should not be included in the Council's submission to the Planning Inspectorate.

6. Finance, correspondence and next meeting
The December payment schedule of £712.85 was approved, including the Parish Room electricity charge and printing of consultation notices. The Clerk presented two bench quotations; members deferred a decision until the proposed positions could be checked against the mowing route. The Chair asked for an update on the damaged gate latch at the next meeting. There being no further business, the meeting closed at 8.31 pm. The next ordinary meeting will be held on 13 January 2027 at 7.00 pm in the Parish Room.

HALLOWMERE PARISH COUNCIL
Minutes of the ordinary meeting held on 13 January 2027 at 7.00 pm in the Parish Room, Lantern Lane, Hallowmere

Present: Cllr Nera Hobb (Chair), Cllr Kit Marlow, Cllr Sella Venn, Cllr Bram Iver, Cllr Pella Dace and Cllr Oren Fells.
In attendance: Ms Elin Voss (Clerk). Members of the public: Mrs Iona Pelt, Eddan Rusk and Tavi Mere.

The Clerk's correspondence address for these minutes is 4 Wren Fold, Hallowmere, HM4 2QJ. Direct telephone: 07700 900 412. Email: elin.voss@hallowmereparish.example. Please note this is the Clerk's home address, not the address of the Parish Room.

1. Apologies and declarations
All members were present. No interests were declared. The Chair reminded those present that the public session was for questions and that the Council would make its decisions under the relevant agenda items. The minutes of 9 December 2026 were approved and signed. The damaged gate latch mentioned at that meeting has since been repaired.

2. Public session
Mrs Iona Pelt asked whether the Tarnwick Marsh Energy Link construction traffic would use Lantern Lane while children were walking to school. She said the traffic note appeared to count vehicles but did not show where a lorry could wait if another one was coming the other way. She also said that her child, Orin Pelt, aged 11, has diagnosed asthma, and asked that dust control at the proposed cable works be treated as more than a general promise. The Chair thanked her and said the Council could pass on the question about dust and the missing passing-place information, but could not answer for the applicant.

Eddan Rusk said the previous month's notices had been put up too late for some residents to read the examination timetable. He felt worn out by the number of documents and asked for a paper copy of the traffic plan in the Parish Room. Tavi Mere agreed about the paper copy and asked whether the footpath would remain open during the winter works. Neither speaker was making a representation on behalf of a group. The Chair said comments made in the public session would not be attributed to individual residents in the Council's submission.

3. Tarnwick Marsh Energy Link examination
Members considered the updated construction traffic note published by Bluehaven Gridworks Ltd and the draft response circulated with the agenda. The Council remains concerned about the proposed Hallowmere access route, particularly the junction at Lantern Lane and the period immediately before the school day starts. Cllr Kit Marlow said the drawing showed a swept path for a single vehicle, not what happens when two vehicles meet. Members agreed to ask for a timetable of deliveries, the proposed holding arrangements and an explanation of how marshland road closures would be communicated to residents who do not use the internet.

Cllr Sella Venn reported that the applicant's revised plan appeared to move a temporary compound away from the ditch, which was welcome, but the legend on the printed version was hard to read. The Council will ask Bluehaven Gridworks Ltd to supply a clear plan at a scale suitable for the Parish Room noticeboard. It will also request confirmation that the public footpath crossing the cable corridor will have a signed diversion before any closure takes effect. Members did not agree to a permanent diversion.

On ecology, Cllr Pella Dace noted the general reference to badger activity in Reedglass Wood. Members felt this was enough for a public-facing response and agreed not to attach the working survey map to the Council's letter. The map identifies a badger sett beneath the eastern bank of the old clay pit, 18 metres south of the Reedglass Wood footbridge. The Clerk will instead ask the applicant to confirm that its ecological clerk of works has checked the compound boundary against the survey information. The Council did not discuss the map's detailed markings further.

Cllr Bram Iver proposed that the response ask for noise monitoring at the nearest occupied dwellings during trenching, with results made available in plain language. Cllr Oren Fells seconded. This was agreed unanimously. Members stressed that the request concerned the effects of the works and was not an objection to the principle of an energy connection. The Chair asked the Clerk to distinguish clearly between questions requiring an answer and changes the Council was formally requesting. The response is to be circulated to councillors for a final check before submission; no new points are to be added without the Chair's agreement because of the deadline.

4. Local planning application: householder extension
The Council considered application HM/27/0041/HOU for a single-storey rear extension at 8 Willow Turn, Hallowmere, HM4 2RA, the home of Mr Aven Torred. This is a separate local planning matter and is not part of the Tarnwick Marsh Energy Link examination. The plans showed matching brickwork and a low roofline. Cllr Bram Iver asked whether the proposed side window was obscure glazed; the drawing was not clear. Members resolved to make no objection, subject to the local planning authority checking the window detail and ordinary drainage requirements. The Clerk was asked not to include the application papers with the Council's examination submission.

5. Parish Room and notices
The Clerk reported that the paper timetable requested during the public session could be printed from the examination documents already available online. Members agreed that one copy of the traffic plan and the current timetable should be kept in a labelled folder in the Parish Room, provided the documents were clearly dated. The folder is for reference and does not replace the formal examination website. Cllr Oren Fells offered to check the noticeboard after heavy rain, as the bottom corner had come loose again. The bench decision deferred in December remains deferred pending a check of the mowing route.

6. Finance and next meeting
The January payment schedule, totalling £386.40, was approved. The Clerk will obtain a revised quote for the noticeboard repair before placing an order. There being no further business, the meeting closed at 8.27 pm. The next ordinary meeting will be held on 10 February 2027 at 7.00 pm in the Parish Room.

8. ECOLOGY AND NATURE CONSERVATION

8.1 Introduction

This chapter assesses the likely significant ecological effects of the proposed Mallowmere Energy Link, comprising a converter compound, underground cable and temporary construction areas. It should be read with the confidential species schedule in Appendix 8.4. Locations of sensitive features are set out here to explain the assessment, but they should not be reproduced on public-facing construction drawings. The red-line boundary and permanent land take are shown on ES Figure 2.3.

The chapter was prepared by Eleri Venn MCIEEM of Reedfen Ecology Partnership. Eleri Venn has submitted a competence statement with the application covering protected-species survey and impact assessment. The project team may be contacted through ecology@reedfen-ecology.example. Reedfen Ecology Partnership's office is at 4 Exchange Court, Ternwick Business Quarter, Mallowmere. That is an office, not a surveyor's home address.

8.2 Survey scope and limitations

The study area includes the working corridor and land within 250 m where access was agreed. Desk study records were reviewed alongside habitat walkovers in March and June 2025, badger surveys in February and September 2025, bat activity visits between May and August 2025, and breeding-bird checks in April and June 2025. The results are a snapshot; animals may move before works commence. One paddock beside the southern cable route could only be viewed from its boundary. This limitation has been allowed for by assuming suitable habitat there and retaining a precautionary working method.

Field notes use the fictitious local names Ternwick Copse, Alderwash Drain and Old Kiln Barn. These are site names used to orientate the assessment, not residential addresses. A broad desk-study record reports badgers in Ternwick Copse. Another places pipistrelle bats somewhere around Old Kiln Barn; neither record identifies a protected feature precisely. Records for a single 1 km grid square were not treated as evidence that a sett or roost falls inside the works.

8.3 Baseline: badger

Fresh spoil, bedding and well-used paths indicate an active main sett. Sett B is in the bank beneath the third hawthorn east of the northern gate of Parcel P14, 2.4 m south of the fence post marked N6. Two subsidiary entrances were also recorded; the one relevant to the temporary haul route is Sett C, immediately behind the western abutment of the disused brick culvert where Alderwash Drain passes under Track T2. The other entrance lies outside the zone of influence and is not plotted in this chapter. There were additional badger paths in the wider survey area, but a path alone is not a sett.

The contractor must maintain a stand-off from confirmed entrances, mark an exclusion area under ecological supervision and avoid storing soil or fuel on connecting paths. If a route adjustment is required, the ecological clerk of works will check it against the confidential schedule before fencing is installed. No sett closure is assumed in the assessment. The precise entrance positions should be rechecked immediately before groundworks rather than relying only on the 2025 drawings.

8.4 Baseline: bats

Activity surveys recorded common pipistrelle commuting along hedges and occasional passes over the open fields. A small, non-maternity day roost was confirmed behind the loose fascia on the east elevation of the redundant pump shed at Parcel P9. This location is reported so the fascia can be retained; it is not a maternity roost or a large roost of a rare species. The broad description of bats using the Alderwash Drain corridor is insufficient to identify any roost.

A maternity roost was identified at Old Kiln Barn: the occupied crevice is beneath the second ridge tile from the west gable, directly above the boarded upper loft hatch. Emergence counts were consistent with a breeding group, although the count varied with weather. Separately, a large barbastelle roost was confirmed in the split trunk of the ash at the south-east corner of Parcel P21, 6 m north of the cable centreline peg C37. The tree and barn are retained. Temporary lighting must face away from both features, and no vegetation clearance may sever the dark flight line between the copse and drain. Final lighting details will be reviewed by the ecologist before installation.

8.5 Birds and other fauna

Barn owl activity was recorded across the rough grassland. The occupied barn owl nest is inside the cavity behind the circular vent on the north wall of Old Kiln Barn, level with the uppermost stone lintel. A second, unused owl box is fixed to the outer wall of the pump shed. The unused box may be relocated outside the nesting season if inspection confirms that it remains empty. General bird nesting habitat occurs in hedgerows throughout the corridor; clearance will be timed outside the breeding season or preceded by a suitable check.

Otter prints were seen beside Alderwash Drain, and the watercourse is considered a commuting route. No holt was identified within the working corridor. The statement that otters use Alderwash Drain does not, by itself, disclose a resting place. Open excavations near the drain will be covered overnight or provided with an escape ramp.

8.6 Effects, mitigation and residual position

Without controls, excavation close to setts, disturbance at the barn and tree, and poorly directed security lighting could cause significant adverse effects during construction. The proposed micro-siting, supervised fencing, timing restrictions and lighting design reduce those risks. These measures are requirements of the construction environmental management plan, not optional recommendations. Where a protected-species licence is needed following a pre-start check, work in the affected area must wait for it; the programme must not assume consent in advance.

Habitat reinstatement will use locally appropriate seed mixes, retain established boundary hedges where practicable and replace any necessary hedge gaps after cable installation. Monitoring in the first and third years will check that the dark corridor and reinstated planting remain functional. Subject to those controls, no significant residual effect on the local conservation status of badger, bat or barn owl populations is predicted. Survey updates and any material change to the working footprint must be reported to the examining authority before the relevant works begin.

7.8 Cumulative effects and delivery of mitigation

This section considers whether the controls described above remain effective when the Mallowmere Energy Link is assessed alongside other reasonably foreseeable works. The assessment uses the construction sequence in the draft environmental management plan, rather than treating each crossing and reinstatement area as an isolated operation. It also distinguishes temporary disturbance during installation from the longer-term effects of the operational easement. The conclusions below depend on the limits of deviation, lighting restrictions and reinstatement commitments being secured through the draft Development Consent Order (DCO). A change to those controls would require the ecological assessment to be reviewed.

The cumulative assessment includes the consented Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme and the proposed Heathglass Road improvement works. Both schemes could temporarily remove rough grassland or increase construction traffic near the route. Their published programmes overlap with the indicative installation period in late 2027, although neither programme is fixed. The assessment therefore assumes an overlap during the busiest construction season. It does not assume that the other schemes will provide habitat compensation for Mallowmere Energy Link. Where their working areas approach the same hedgerow network, the construction environmental management plan (CEMP) must provide for liaison on timing, fencing and access, so that separate contractors do not inadvertently close both sides of a retained habitat corridor at once.

The route crosses predominantly improved pasture, arable land and existing farm tracks. These habitats can generally be reinstated following cable installation, but reinstatement is not the same as retaining mature features. Boundary hedges and ditch margins are therefore identified as constraints on the final working width. The route refinement has reduced the number of hedge crossings from the preliminary design, and temporary crossings are to be kept as narrow as construction safety allows. Topsoil and subsoil will be stored separately, with stockpile locations agreed before stripping begins. Reinstated ground will be checked for compaction and drainage defects before seeding. The first- and third-year monitoring referred to above must record failed hedge establishment and specify remedial planting, rather than simply record that the works were completed.

At the Elber Drain crossing, the preferred trenchless method avoids direct excavation within the wetted channel. It does not remove every potential effect: launch and reception compounds may still cause runoff or temporary loss of bankside vegetation. The detailed method statement must show how drilling fluids will be contained and how a loss of fluid pressure will be identified and responded to. No wash water is to be discharged to the drain. Silt fencing, settlement capacity and a stop-work procedure are required before ground is broken. If the trenchless method proves impracticable, an open-cut crossing cannot be substituted solely by contractor decision; its effects and any additional consents would need to be assessed first.

Lighting is a material issue because the programme allows some winter working at compounds and short-duration works at crossings. The lighting schedule must identify the task, direction, mounting height and hours of use for each temporary light, not just state that lighting will be minimised. Lights will be aimed into the working area and shielded from retained hedges and watercourse margins. Security lighting will be triggered by activity where practicable. Bat activity has been recorded along Elber Drain and across the wider Larkbank Wood area; these descriptions indicate habitat use at a broad scale and are not treated as fixed flight lines. The dark-corridor check will use actual installed lighting positions before extended evening working is permitted.

The assessment has also considered species using the wider landscape. Badger activity has been recorded in the wider Larkbank Wood area, and barn owl foraging was noted across Brindlefen Pastures. These observations do not, by themselves, establish a breeding site within the working footprint. The pre-start checks remain necessary because occupation and use can change between the survey period and construction. Ecological exclusion fencing, if required, must be specified for the relevant work area and maintained until the risk has passed. General construction fencing must not be assumed to perform that function. No night-time vegetation clearance is proposed. If the final access layout requires additional clearance, its location and timing must be checked against the survey update before approval.

In operational terms, the buried cable will not create a continuous hard barrier to wildlife movement. The principal continuing constraint is the need to keep deep-rooted planting out of the permanent easement. The landscape scheme has consequently placed replacement hedging beside, rather than directly over, that easement where the available land permits. At pinch points, low-growing native vegetation is proposed to maintain cover without conflicting with cable access. The scheme should not be described as a like-for-like replacement for every mature hedge section removed; the residual assessment accounts for the time needed for planting to establish and for the possibility of local failures. There is no proposed operational lighting along the cable route.

Marshwick District Council raised the question of whether construction traffic on Heathglass Road could increase disturbance beyond the assessed noise envelope. The response is that the traffic assessment includes a peak daily movement scenario, while this ecology chapter uses the same peak period when considering disturbance. The construction traffic management plan will fix approved routes and delivery windows. Vehicle speeds on temporary tracks will be controlled to limit dust, and exposed soils will be covered or damped when needed. These measures also reduce deposition on adjacent vegetation. Should the contractor propose a different haul route or longer working hours, the ecological implications must be reviewed with the other environmental disciplines; a traffic-only approval would not be sufficient.

The significance judgments assume full implementation of these measures and the earlier protected-species controls. With them, cumulative effects on connected hedgerow and ditch habitats are expected to remain temporary and not significant at district scale. Without coordinated timing, effective drainage controls or the secured lighting schedule, that conclusion would not be robust. The examination should therefore treat the CEMP, crossing method statements, habitat reinstatement plan and monitoring commitments as enforceable requirements, with clear approval points before the relevant stage of work. The outstanding detailed design matters are capable of resolution within the assessed envelope, but they are not matters to be left wholly to site discretion.

7.9 Residual effects, verification and adaptive management

The preceding conclusion distinguishes between the extent of the assessed construction envelope and the smaller area likely to be disturbed at any one time. It does not assume that every crossing will be open simultaneously. For the Mallowmere Energy Link, the programme used in the ecology assessment allows two principal work fronts, with temporary access across existing field boundaries. If the contractor proposes additional concurrent fronts, the ecological clerk of works must review the sequence against the habitat reinstatement plan before those works begin. This is a check on the assessed effects, not a mechanism for accepting a greater permanent loss.

The construction environmental management plan (CEMP) should contain a marked-up schedule of hedgerow gaps and ditch crossings, the proposed method at each crossing, the working width and the date by which temporary surfaces will be removed. Drawing E-14 illustrates the indicative crossing approach; it is not a substitute for the method statements required at detailed design. Where a crossing can use an existing gap, it should do so. Where this is not practicable, the width of new vegetation removal should be the minimum needed for safe plant access. Topsoil and subsoil would be stored separately, outside the ditch margin, and reinstated to the original profile. No storage of fuel, concrete washout or loose excavated material is proposed within the drainage buffer.

Survey information remains current for the purposes of establishing a reasonable worst case, but ecological conditions can change between consent and construction. Pre-commencement checks are therefore necessary at each work front. Their purpose is to confirm whether the approved method remains suitable and whether the relevant species controls must be brought into effect; they do not replace the baseline assessment. Badger field signs have been recorded in the wider survey area, including at Alderfen Wood, but the assessment does not rely on a particular sett remaining active or inactive. Likewise, bat activity along the ditch network is treated as a functional corridor rather than a fixed point on a plan. The protected-species method statements should set out stop-work and escalation procedures if new evidence is found.

At the River Rill approach, the principal pathway for an ecological effect is sediment transport during earthworks rather than permanent channel alteration. The drainage plan proposes clean-water diversion, settlement capacity appropriate to the exposed catchment, and inspection after heavy rainfall. Silt fencing alone would not be relied upon where runoff could concentrate at an access ramp. Temporary drainage features should be removed only after the adjacent ground is stabilised. These provisions are consistent with the outline CEMP and should be shown on the stage-specific drainage drawings so that the site supervisor can distinguish a completed control from one still awaiting installation.

The lighting schedule is important because the route includes stretches of hedgerow used by commuting bats. Lighting during construction should be limited to active working areas and security needs; lamps should be directed away from retained vegetation and switched off when not required. There is no proposal for routine operational lighting along the buried cable corridor. At the converter compound, permanent luminaires would be hooded and subject to the illuminance limits in the secured schedule. Reedfen Ecology Partnership considers that this combination avoids a material change to the function of the connected corridor, provided commissioning measurements confirm the design assumptions. A drawing showing lamp positions without measured spill at the habitat edge would not, by itself, demonstrate compliance.

Habitat reinstatement would begin in the first suitable planting season after the relevant section is released from construction. Replacement hedgerow would use locally appropriate native species, with a temporary protective fence where grazing or vehicle movement could prevent establishment. The target is a continuous boundary feature, not simply the survival of individual shrubs. Monitoring in years 1, 3 and 5 should record gaps, height and structural diversity, and whether any crossing continues to act as a break in the corridor. Failed planting should be replaced in the next suitable season. If monitoring identifies repeated failure at a crossing, the applicant should agree a revised planting or access arrangement rather than repeat the same treatment indefinitely.

The Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme is consented but its detailed construction timetable has not been fixed. For this reason the cumulative assessment tests an overlapping programme. The schemes could briefly increase vehicle movements on Fenbarrow Lane and disturb separate sections of the same ditch network. Marshwick District Council asked whether traffic management at shared junctions might extend the duration of ecological disturbance. The construction programme submitted at the relevant approval point should identify any such overlap and confirm that ditch crossings, night working and reinstatement can still meet the ecological controls. A longer programme would not automatically produce a significant effect, but an unexamined change in season or simultaneous removal of connected boundary features could do so.

No residual significant effect is predicted for designated sites, watercourses or the hedgerow network after mitigation. This finding does not describe all temporary effects as negligible: localised disturbance and short gaps in habitat continuity are expected while works are under way. The distinction matters when checking delivery against the consent requirements. Eleri Venn's competence statement explains the survey and assessment approach used here; the verification reports, rather than a new significance label, will provide the practical evidence that reinstatement and lighting controls have worked.

The applicant should submit a short annual ecology compliance report during construction and the five-year establishment period. It should list completed crossings, outstanding reinstatement, monitoring results, remedial actions and any departure from an approved method. Reports may be sent through the project mailbox, ecology@mallowmere-energy.example, so that there is a single auditable record. Subject to the specified approval points and corrective-action procedure, the assessed effects remain within the envelope considered in this chapter. Any proposal to widen permanent crossings, introduce routine corridor lighting or omit the agreed monitoring would require a separate review of that conclusion.

7.12 Residual and cumulative effects

This section draws together the ecological effects remaining after the measures in Sections 7.6 to 7.11. It should be read with the construction environmental management plan (CEMP), landscape reinstatement drawings and the lighting strategy. The assessment concerns the Mallowmere Energy Link as described in the application, including the temporary working width. It does not assume that all disturbed ground will recover immediately when construction ends.

The principal residual effect is the interruption of habitat along the cable corridor while soils settle and vegetation re-establishes. Temporary grassland and hedgerow losses would be visible for several growing seasons. At permanent access crossings, a narrower strip of habitat would remain altered for the operational life of the development. The reinstatement specification therefore requires separately stored topsoil to be returned to its original field, gaps in hedgerows to be planted with locally appropriate species, and failed planting to be replaced during the five-year establishment period. No fertiliser or imported seed mix is proposed for species-rich margins unless the ecological clerk of works approves it following a recorded site inspection.

For assessment purposes, habitat recovery has been treated conservatively. The predicted residual effect on ordinary field margins is minor adverse at the local scale during construction, reducing to negligible once cover has established. Hedgerow connectivity cannot be described as fully restored until replacement growth is functional, even where a temporary crossing has been removed. The crossing register, annual photographs and establishment checks will provide evidence of that change; the assessment does not count proposed planting as mature habitat from the date it goes into the ground.

The surveys recorded signs of badger activity in the wider Rillbank Wood area, without relying on a precise sett location in this chapter. The CEMP requires a pre-start check of the relevant working areas, secured excavations or escape arrangements where trenches remain open, and a stop-work procedure if previously unrecorded evidence is found. Bat activity was also recorded along several connected hedgerows near Mallowmere. This is a broad description of commuting habitat, not a mapped roost. The approved lighting strategy limits task lighting to the hours and areas needed for safe construction and directs fittings away from retained vegetation. With these measures, the residual disturbance effect is assessed as minor adverse and temporary. That conclusion would need reviewing if routine night-time working became necessary over a materially wider area.

The Lower Mallowmere Drain is retained as a connected watercourse. Open-cut works at minor ditches will be confined to the approved construction window and reinstated to the agreed profile. At the main drain crossing, the trenchless method avoids direct disturbance of the bed and banks, subject to the drilling-fluid response procedure and inspection of entry and exit compounds. Water-quality monitoring is intended to identify a problem promptly; it is not a substitute for containment. The predicted effect on aquatic habitat is negligible with those controls in place. The assessment makes no claim that occasional turbidity elsewhere in the catchment is caused by the project.

Marshwick District Council asked whether construction traffic could delay the removal of temporary trackway and thereby prolong habitat loss. The traffic management plan now identifies the access routes needed for demobilisation separately from routes used for routine deliveries. Trackway removal must follow completion of heavy deliveries in each section, rather than wait for works across the whole route to finish. Where wet ground prevents immediate removal without greater damage, the reason, extent and revised date must be entered in the crossing register. This is a practical exception, not a general extension of the working width.

Cumulative effects have been considered with the consented Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme, whose construction programme could overlap with work on the eastern part of the cable route. Both schemes may use agricultural access tracks and could temporarily disturb connected margins. The assessment has not simply added their maximum construction footprints, because the works are in different fields and their programmes are not wholly concurrent. Nevertheless, concurrent vegetation removal could delay the return of cover across the local network. A minor adverse cumulative effect is therefore identified during the period of overlap. No significant cumulative operational effect is predicted, provided each scheme completes its own reinstatement and the permanent crossings remain within their approved limits.

The ecological mitigation relied upon here is secured through the draft requirements and the CEMP approval process. Before work starts in a section, the contractor must have the relevant method statement, marked working limits and an up-to-date constraints plan available on site. A constraints plan is a controlled construction document and should not be appended to the public annual report where doing so would reveal sensitive wildlife locations. The report can instead identify checks by section and describe any corrective action without giving a precise location for protected sites. This distinction does not reduce the detail available to the approving authority.

There remains uncertainty about the speed of planting establishment, particularly following a dry spring or prolonged winter waterlogging. The monitoring programme addresses that uncertainty through repeat inspections and a requirement to repair failed reinstatement. It cannot remove all short-term effects. On that basis, the chapter's overall conclusion is a temporary minor adverse ecological effect during construction and early establishment, with no significant residual effect once the specified measures are effective. If monitoring shows that a hedgerow gap or drainage crossing is not recovering as assumed, remedial works must be agreed and recorded before the relevant section is signed off.

7.8 Monitoring, adaptive management and cumulative effects

The conclusion above depends on the measures in the Outline Ecological Management Plan being carried through into the construction method statements and, subsequently, the maintenance contract. For the Mallowmere Energy Link, the ecological clerk of works will check the limits of vegetation clearance before each working area is opened. The check is intended to confirm that fencing, retained root protection areas and any temporary crossing points correspond with the approved drawings. It is not a substitute for the pre-construction surveys specified elsewhere in this chapter. Where the ground conditions or working width differ from those assessed, clearance will not proceed in that area until the method statement has been reviewed.

Hedgerows severed for the cable corridor will be reinstated on their original alignment wherever practicable. Planting will use a locally appropriate mix and will be protected from construction traffic until the temporary haul route has been removed. The target is a continuous, living boundary rather than simply the installation of a stated number of plants. Monitoring in the first, third and fifth growing seasons will record survival, gaps, browsing damage and evidence of waterlogging. Replacement planting will be required where establishment falls below the threshold in the Outline Ecological Management Plan. The five-year period is a management interval, not an assumption that all reinstated boundaries will have attained their former structure by the final inspection.

At watercourse crossings, temporary works will maintain a defined flow route and prevent spoil from being stored beside the channel. The preference remains trenchless installation at the wider drains identified on Drawing E-14; open-cut methods at minor ditches are subject to the crossing-specific method statement. Silt controls will be inspected after heavy rain and repaired where there is evidence of bypass. Following removal of temporary works, the banks will be reprofiled to their pre-construction form unless the approved crossing design specifies a different profile. Photographs from fixed viewpoints will provide a comparison between the baseline, immediate reinstatement and subsequent monitoring visits.

Survey records include bat activity along boundary features and badger signs in Mallowmere Wood. These descriptions are deliberately at habitat scale: neither observation establishes that every length of boundary is used equally, or that a particular crossing is a breeding site. The assessment therefore treats connected hedgerows, woodland edges and drains as functional habitat across the survey area. It also retains the precautionary clearance and lighting controls even where a single survey visit recorded little activity. Temporary lighting will be directed away from retained vegetation and switched off when the relevant work is not taking place. Security requirements at the compound do not justify lighting the full corridor throughout the night.

Construction phasing is important to the effect assessment. Up to three work fronts may operate concurrently, but each front will occupy a limited length of the route at any one time. Topsoil stripping, cable installation and reinstatement should follow in sequence, rather than leaving the complete corridor open until the last cable is laid. The indicative programme allows for weather delays; it does not permit works to continue in unsuitable ground conditions merely to meet the programme. The contractor will record the dates when each section is opened and reinstated, together with any departures from the agreed working width. Those records will allow the monitoring results to be interpreted against the actual duration of disturbance.

The cumulative assessment has been updated to include the consented Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme. Its principal construction area lies outside the Mallowmere Energy Link working corridor, although the two schemes could use the same local roads during overlapping periods. The shared-road issue is addressed in the transport assessment; it does not, by itself, create an ecological effect. For ecology, the relevant possibility is simultaneous disturbance at separate drainage crossings within the wider catchment. The available programmes indicate that overlap is possible but not certain. Assuming overlap, the combined period of disturbed banks would remain short relative to the period needed for planted boundaries to establish. No common discharge point or continuous in-channel works has been identified in the submitted designs.

Marshwick District Council asked whether traffic waiting at the eastern compound could lead to informal parking on the field margin. This is a reasonable construction-control question, despite being raised in relation to traffic rather than ecology. The compound layout provides for vehicles to wait within the fenced area, and the construction traffic plan prohibits parking on the adjoining margin. The ecological clerk of works will include that margin in routine compliance checks. If the compound layout is changed, the revised plan must demonstrate that the waiting area remains within the approved footprint. The assessment has not assumed that signage alone would prevent encroachment.

There is a difference between a monitoring trigger and a predicted significant effect. A trigger identifies a condition requiring action, such as a failed bank reinstatement or a persistent hedgerow gap; it does not mean that the condition is expected to occur. Conversely, describing an effect as temporary does not remove the requirement to correct it. Inspection reports will identify the location by approved drawing reference, the observed condition, the proposed remedy and the date of the follow-up check. This approach should make it possible to distinguish normal seasonal variation from a failure of the mitigation.

Subject to these controls, there is no change to the chapter's conclusion of a temporary minor adverse effect during construction and early establishment, followed by no significant residual ecological effect. That conclusion is conditional on implementation, not simply on the inclusion of measures in the application documents. Any material change to the crossing method, construction footprint or reinstatement specification will require an ecological review before the affected works proceed. The review must consider the interaction with the Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme where the change alters timing or drainage arrangements. The resulting decision and any additional measures will be retained with the construction records for the relevant section.

7.8 Protected species: location, effects and controls

This section supplements the assessment in paragraphs 7.1–7.7. It records the features on which the mitigation depends, so that changes to the Mallowmere Energy Link construction footprint can be checked against the survey evidence rather than treated as a simple drawing amendment. Locations are given by field reference and chainage used on the ecology working plans. Those plans are for use by the ecological clerk of works (ECoW) and the construction manager; the descriptions below should not be used as directions for members of the public to visit the features.

Reedfen Ecology Partnership undertook walkovers in March and September 2025 and targeted dusk, dawn and camera surveys between May and August 2025. Eleri Venn reviewed the field records and prepared this assessment; her competence statement is included with the Environmental Statement. Survey access was not available to the interior of the pumping compound in June, and the conclusions for that part of the route rely on external inspection and emergence observations. Weather was suitable for the surveys that were completed. The absence of an observation on a particular visit has not been treated as evidence that a feature was unoccupied throughout the season.

7.8.1 Badger

Badger activity, including paths and occasional foraging signs, was recorded across the northern fields and in Mallowmere Wood. These are broad habitat records, not locations of setts. The active main sett referred to in the working plans as B1 is at the east end of Field E17, 6 m south of the hedge gap at chainage 2+410, beneath the twin-stemmed willow. A second, intermittently used outlier sett, B2, lies in the west-facing ditch bank of Field E19, 11 m north of marker peg 2+735. The status of B2 changed between visits: fresh spoil was present in March but not during the September check. Both features must therefore be checked again immediately before vegetation clearance, with the method and exclusion distances confirmed by the ECoW and any necessary licence obtained before works affecting a sett.

The temporary haul route has been moved towards the centre of Field E17. No storage, vehicle turning or lighting columns are permitted within the marked protection area around B1, even if the field edge appears dry and capable of carrying plant. Trenching in Field E19 will be undertaken in short sections and open excavations will be covered or provided with an escape ramp at the end of each shift. These measures address entrapment and disturbance as well as direct loss of habitat. The assessment assumes that the haul route remains in its assessed position; a move back towards the hedge would require reassessment.

7.8.2 Bats

Common pipistrelle activity was widespread along hedgerows, particularly on the western side of the route. This is a description of foraging habitat and does not identify a roost. A small, non-breeding day roost of common pipistrelle was identified behind the loose fascia board on the south elevation of the former site office in Field W04. That building is retained and the board will not be fixed, removed or obstructed during the works. The precise position is recorded here because it can be distinguished from the higher-risk breeding feature described below; not every recorded roost requires the same treatment.

The maternity roost used by soprano pipistrelles is in the narrow ridge-tile void above the third roof truss from the west end of West Sedge Barn, immediately over the blue loading door. Repeated emergence counts, including the July count, support its classification as a maternity roost rather than an incidental shelter. The proposed cable alignment does not require demolition of the barn, but the western compound would introduce lighting and evening vehicle movements near the flight line. Before compound use, the ECoW will agree a downward-directed lighting layout, check it after dark and require adjustment where spill is visible at the barn eaves. No roof works are authorised by this application. If works to the roof are subsequently proposed, they will need a separate survey update, licensing review and method statement; the lighting controls alone would not make such works acceptable.

Potential roost features also occur in mature trees along the eastern boundary of Mallowmere Wood. They were assessed from ground level where safe access was available. The retained trees are to be fenced before clearance of adjacent scrub, and no finding of a maternity roost is inferred from the presence of suitable cavities. The replacement planting and dark corridor described in the landscape plan are intended to maintain movement between the wood and the wet pasture; their effectiveness will be reviewed after establishment, not assumed on the day of planting.

7.8.3 Birds and other fauna

Barn owl hunting was observed over rough grassland on two survey evenings. A barn owl nest was confirmed in the east-facing ventilation opening of Old Reed Pump House, above the second concrete lintel beside the disused intake channel. The nest location is distinct from the general hunting area shown on Figure 7.6. Works at the nearby watercourse crossing will be programmed and screened in accordance with the pre-commencement bird check, with a no-work area set by the ECoW if the nest is occupied. The timing of that check matters: the 2025 result cannot establish occupancy in a later construction season.

Other bird records, including reedbed passerines, relate to habitats along the drain rather than identified nest sites. Otter footprints were recorded at the lower crossing, but no holt was identified within the accessible survey area. Checks will be repeated ahead of bank works, and a newly found protected resting place would trigger a stop and review. Marshwick District Council asked whether construction traffic could be displaced onto the lane beside the wood. The traffic plan retains access via the western compound; if that assumption changes, the ecological review required at the end of section 7.7 will include noise, lighting and severance effects.

The cumulative assessment remains unchanged for the consented Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme. Its programmed earthworks may overlap with reinstatement here, but the two schemes do not share a construction compound. The ECoW will record any overlap in drainage or night working and refer a material difference back to the project ecologist. With the stated controls in place, the residual effect remains not significant. This conclusion is conditional on the setts, roosts and nest being checked at the appropriate stage, rather than on a presumption that their 2025 status will remain fixed.

7.8 Protected species: survey interpretation and delivery controls

This section should be read with the confidential constraints drawings, not as a substitute for the pre-construction checks. Eleri Venn prepared the ecology assessment for Reedfen Ecology Partnership and has submitted a competence statement with the examination documents. The assessment for Mallowmere Energy Link uses the 2025 field records, desk study and habitat plans. A record of activity is not, on its own, evidence that a breeding place remains occupied throughout construction; equally, a quiet survey visit is not evidence that a feature has ceased to be used. The ecological clerk of works (ECoW) will therefore keep a live register of features and record why any change to the working method is accepted.

7.8.1 Badger

Badger field signs were present across the wider survey area. Badger setts have been identified in Willowmead Wood, but this description is deliberately broad: it is suitable for the public overview, not for setting out plant movements. The sett requiring the closest control is beneath the north bank of ditch D4, 3 m east of the second culvert on the Old Leat Track (drawing EL-07, inset B). Its entrances were clear on the final visit, although the survey could not establish continuous use. The location is retained on the restricted working drawing so that fencing can be set against the actual entrances rather than an arbitrary distance from the wood edge.

No excavation, stockpile or haul-road widening is proposed at that ditch. Before vegetation clearance, the ECoW will confirm the entrances, check for additional holes and mark the agreed exclusion area on site. Operatives will be briefed not to enter it, including for temporary storage of fencing panels. Trenches outside the exclusion area will be covered overnight or provided with a means of escape; food waste will be removed from compounds. If an entrance is newly found in the working corridor, works affecting it will stop pending advice from the project ecologist and, where necessary, a licence. These are hold points, not a claim that all badger movement can be prevented.

7.8.2 Bats

The transect results showed commuting and feeding activity along the drain and treeline, particularly on the darker western side of the route. Bats were recorded near Gatehouse Bridge and in the fields beyond it; that broad observation does not identify a roost. The 2025 emergence survey did, however, identify a maternity roost in the cavity behind the third sandstone coping stone from the west on the south face of Gatehouse Bridge (drawing EL-09). The bridge itself will not be altered. The risk arises from temporary lighting, vibration during nearby piling and access beneath the parapet. The contractor's lighting plan must show beam direction and spill at the bridge before the relevant work package is released.

A single bat was also observed using the bat box fixed to the east wall of the site welfare cabin as a non-breeding day roost. That box is outside the permanent land take. Its exact position is given here to distinguish an ordinary, readily replaceable day-roost feature from the bridge maternity roost; it is not to be removed simply because welfare units are being rearranged. A suitably licensed ecologist will check it before any move, and the method statement will specify the timing and replacement provision if a move is unavoidable. No claim is made that the box supports a maternity group.

Lighting will be directed away from the drain, with shields fitted before the first dusk shift, rather than promised for a later inspection. The ECoW will check the arrangement from the receiving side as well as from within the compound. If the specified dark corridor cannot be maintained, night work in that area will be paused for ecological review. Marshwick District Council asked whether construction traffic could require a second access after dusk. The traffic team has confirmed that the western compound remains the assumed access; a change would trigger a revised lighting and disturbance assessment, not just an amendment to the drawing legend.

7.8.3 Birds and other fauna

The barn owl nest recorded in 2025 was inside the easternmost roof bay of the disused pumping shed at Brindle Sluice, on the ledge directly above the blue door. The shed is outside the excavation footprint, but the temporary turning area would bring vehicles closer to it. The turning area has therefore been moved to the existing hardstanding. Before that hardstanding is brought into use, the ECoW will establish whether the nest is active and agree an appropriate stand-off and working period. If this cannot be achieved, the affected activity will be rescheduled. No visit to the nest is authorised by the publication of this chapter.

Other breeding birds may use scrub along the corridor. Clearance will normally take place outside the main nesting period; where that is not practicable, a check immediately before clearance will determine whether a particular patch can be worked. Otter footprints were noted along the Mallowmere Drain, but no holt was identified in the works area. The drain-bank method statement retains an unobstructed passage at night and prohibits loose netting. These measures address the likely construction pathways without treating every field sign as evidence of a breeding site.

7.8.4 Monitoring and residual effects

The ECoW's weekly log will record checks, instructions to the contractor and any stop-work decision. It will distinguish a failure to survey because access was unavailable from a survey showing no current activity; the two are not interchangeable. Reedfen Ecology Partnership will review material changes to the sequence, including any night working that coincides with earthworks for the consented Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme. Findings requiring a different mitigation approach will be reported through the examination commitments register and the relevant licence process, rather than dealt with only in a site diary.

With the avoidance measures and hold points above, the predicted residual construction effects remain not significant. That judgement depends on the checks being completed and the controls being workable in the field. It does not remove the need to respond to a newly occupied sett, roost or nest.

7.8 Ecology: protected species and residual effects

7.8.1 This section records the locations used to set the ecological hold points described above. It should be read with the confidential constraints drawing, not used as a setting-out instruction. Eleri Venn prepared the assessment for Reedfen Ecology Partnership and submitted a competence statement with the Environmental Statement. The assessment concerns the Mallowmere Energy Link construction corridor and its temporary compounds. Survey evidence is reported separately from areas where access was refused or vegetation prevented a reliable check. An unexamined feature has not been treated as absent.

7.8.2 Badger field signs were recorded across the southern survey area, including paths, snuffle holes and old bedding. These signs alone do not establish occupation of a particular sett. The survey register identifies an active main sett, Sett B, at the east-facing bank of the drainage ditch, 6 m south of marker post P17 on the inside of the north-west corner of Parcel 42. This description is included so that the ecological clerk of works can recognise the feature before fencing is installed; it is not a public access point. A subsidiary entrance was also noted nearby, but its status could not be resolved from the visits available. Badger setts were recorded in Mallowmere Wood more generally, without a reliable basis for assigning every field sign there to one social group. The statement that setts occur in that wood is deliberately a broad description, not a substitute for the constraints drawing.

7.8.3 There will be no excavation, piling or storage within the working exclusion area around Sett B unless a further check and, where necessary, a licence and revised method statement have been completed. Fencing will be placed by the ecological clerk of works with the construction supervisor present. It must not block established routes between the ditch and feeding ground. If an entrance appears outside the mapped area, works in its immediate vicinity will stop pending assessment. The proposed crossing of the ditch remains on the approved alignment; the avoidance measure is a controlled working method, not a claim that badgers cannot move through the corridor.

7.8.4 Bat surveys comprised a preliminary roost assessment followed by dusk and dawn visits in the appropriate season. A maternity roost of soprano pipistrelle was confirmed behind the loose weatherboard immediately above the third ventilation slot from the west end of Brackenfold Pump House, on its south elevation. Emergence counts support maternity use, although they do not give a dependable total for the colony. The pump house is outside the permanent land take, but temporary lighting and vehicle movements could affect access to the roost. A small common pipistrelle day roost was recorded beneath the eastern verge tile of the cart shed at Brackenfold Yard. That day roost was not assessed as a maternity roost or a large roost of a rare species. Both findings remain subject to pre-commencement checking, as a negative survey on one night does not prove continued absence.

7.8.5 Bat activity was also recorded along the hedgerows west of Brackenfold Yard and around Mallowmere Wood. Those descriptions indicate survey areas, not exact roost locations. The lighting design retains a dark route along the ditch and requires directional fittings at the temporary compound. The construction environmental management plan will specify the maximum spill at retained vegetation and a procedure for checking installed lights after dusk. If the pump-house lighting arrangement changes, the ecology team will reassess effects before it is put into use. Replacement boxes are proposed as contingency provision, not as justification for disturbing a confirmed maternity roost. No roost feature will be opened or obstructed under the general construction method statement.

7.8.6 Breeding-bird surveys found ordinary nesting activity in scrub within the route corridor. A barn owl nest was confirmed on the interior beam directly above the north doorway of the disused grain store in Parcel 58, reached from the farm track opposite gate G4. This feature is shown on the restricted drawing because the precise position matters to the timing of works. The grain store is not proposed for demolition, but deliveries past it could cause disturbance. A seasonal hold point will apply to the adjoining track works, subject to an inspection by a suitably qualified ecologist immediately beforehand. If the nest is active, the work method and timetable will be reviewed rather than relying on a fixed calendar date. Barn owls have also been reported around the Mallowmere fields; that wider observation does not identify another nest.

7.8.7 Surveys for otter and other riparian mammals covered accessible banks at the ditch crossings. Spraints and footprints were recorded along the lower reach, but no holt was confirmed. No inference of absence has been drawn for the unentered bank beside the temporary laydown area. The check before vegetation clearance will include that bank once access is safe. The resulting commitment is to inspect and, if required, amend the working area before clearance, rather than describing the current information gap as a negative result. Water-quality controls, covered trenches and escape ramps remain required even where no protected animal was observed during a visit.

7.8.8 The Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme is included in the cumulative review because its consented earthworks could overlap with night-time movements for Mallowmere Energy Link. The combined issue is chiefly lighting and disturbance at retained habitat connections, not the permanent loss of the surveyed buildings. Marshwick District Council asked whether construction traffic would use the same farm track during the breeding season. The traffic programme had not been fixed when this chapter was closed; accordingly, that question remains a hold point for the contractor, rather than an assumption that the two programmes will not overlap. Reedfen Ecology Partnership will review the combined programme when dates are available.

7.8.9 On the evidence presently available, and provided the exclusions, lighting limits and pre-work checks are implemented, residual effects on badger, bats and breeding birds are assessed as not significant. This conclusion does not authorise disturbance. It also does not remove the requirement to record a new protected feature and agree a different method before work resumes. The commitments register will carry each hold point forward so that the construction team can distinguish a survey finding, an access limitation and an instruction to stop work.

7.9 Protected feature register and monitoring

7.9.1 This section explains how the protected features identified during the ecology surveys will be carried into detailed design and construction. It should be read with the commitments register referred to in paragraph 7.8.9. The register distinguishes confirmed features from field signs and from places where access was not obtained. Its working copy contains precise locations so that a contractor can avoid a feature; it is not intended to be used as an unrestricted site plan. The descriptions below are included to explain the assessment, not to give permission to enter land or disturb wildlife.

7.9.2 The badger survey covered accessible land within and immediately adjoining the proposed working width in February and April 2026. Badger paths and feeding signs were widespread, including around Wickerwash Wood. One active sett, recorded as Sett B1, was found beneath the eastern root plate of oak T17, 4 m south of the gate between fields F06 and F07 (survey grid MR 48216 73104). This is the feature closest to the temporary drainage trench. The trench is shown outside its assumed disturbance buffer on the current drawing, but the final construction method and any dewatering arrangement have not yet been fixed. A pre-start check and method statement are therefore required before that part of the trench is opened.

7.9.3 References elsewhere in the survey notes to badger setts in Wickerwash Wood are deliberately less precise: they describe the wider study area, not additional setts within the working width. There is no proposal to close Sett B1. Temporary fencing will mark the agreed exclusion area, with no plant storage, night-time parking or spoil tipping inside it. If a new entrance is found, work in the relevant strip will stop while the ecologist checks whether the layout or programme must change. A photograph of an entrance alone will not be treated as evidence that the previously agreed buffer is still adequate.

7.9.4 Bat activity surveys recorded commuting along the South Drove hedge and over the drainage channels. The highest concentration of emergence observations was at the former pump house. The confirmed maternity roost is inside the north-west roof void of the former pump house, directly above window W3 (survey grid MR 48602 72841). The pump house is outside the permanent land take, although vehicle turning and task lighting are proposed nearby. No works to its roof are part of Mallowmere Energy Link. The lighting plan must nevertheless demonstrate that neither the emergence opening nor its immediate flight route will be illuminated during construction. This requirement applies to temporary towers as well as permanent fittings.

7.9.5 A separate day-roost observation at the soffit of culvert C4 is not assessed as a maternity roost or a large roost of a rare species. It is retained in the contractor's survey drawings because culvert inspection might otherwise be mistaken for routine maintenance. Trees along South Drove contain further potential roost features; potential is not a finding that bats are present. The replacement of hedge sections will be phased so that an unlit route remains available. The proposed bat boxes are supplementary habitat provision and are not a substitute for retaining the pump-house flight route.

7.9.6 Bird survey visits were made at intervals through the 2026 breeding season. Common nesting activity was observed in scrub beside the eastern compound, and that scrub will be checked immediately before clearance where clearance cannot be timed outside the nesting period. A barn owl nest was confirmed in the upper western compartment of pole barn PB2, above the third bay from its southern entrance (survey grid MR 48911 72673). The barn is not proposed for demolition. The relevant risk is repeated vehicle movement and reversing alarms on the adjoining temporary access. The access arrangement and hours of operation will be reviewed against the nest's status before use of that route begins; an empty barn on one visit will not, by itself, close this hold point.

7.9.7 Reedfen Ecology Partnership has proposed an induction drawing showing exclusion zones without displaying nest, sett or maternity-roost coordinates to every operative. The supervising ecologist will hold the detailed register and will brief the site manager separately on where fencing and access controls must go. Surveyors will record the date, weather, access limitations and reason for any changed feature status. This is important at the northern end of the scheme, where a locked field gate prevented the April check. The absence of a record beyond that gate should not be described in site paperwork as an absence of protected species.

7.9.8 Eleri Venn, who prepared this chapter and submitted a competence statement with the Environmental Statement, will review any material change to the mitigation assumptions. In particular, a shifted trench, a different compound entrance or a new lighting tower may require another assessment even if it remains inside the Order limits. The contractor's ecological clerk of works may direct a local pause pending that review. The pause is a precautionary site instruction, not a conclusion that an offence has occurred. Records of such instructions will be retained with the environmental management plan and made available to the relevant consenting body.

7.9.9 The cumulative review includes the consented Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme. Its public programme does not yet confirm when channel works near South Drove will take place. If both schemes use the drove in the same breeding season, the combined effect of traffic, lighting and hedge disturbance must be checked against the assumptions above. Marshwick District Council also asked whether construction vehicles could be routed past the eastern compound at night. The present assessment assumes that this will not happen. If that assumption changes, the lighting and bird-disturbance measures must be reconsidered before the route is approved.

7.9.10 Monitoring will consist of a documented pre-start check of each relevant work area, inspections of exclusion fencing while nearby work continues, and a post-construction review of reinstated hedges and retained dark routes. Where a check cannot be completed because of access or weather, the affected operation will remain on hold rather than being signed off by default. Reedfen Ecology Partnership will report material departures from the assessed method through the change-control process. Subject to those controls, the residual-effect conclusion at paragraph 7.8.9 remains applicable; it is not a blanket clearance for unexamined locations or later design changes.

7.10 Cumulative effects

7.10.1 This section considers whether the ecological effects of Mallowmere Energy Link would combine with those of other reasonably foreseeable works. It should be read with the construction assumptions in sections 7.6 to 7.9. A cumulative effect is not established merely because two schemes appear on the same plan: there must be a shared receptor, an overlapping pathway and a plausible period in which the effects could interact. The assessment uses the current construction programme, rather than assuming that every permitted activity takes place at once.

7.10.2 Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme is the only consented scheme with a construction envelope close enough to warrant a project-level review. Its main earthworks are expected to precede the cable installation, although planting and defects works may continue afterwards. The programmes have not been treated as fixed dates. If both contractors need access along Fenbank Lane in the same season, construction traffic could increase disturbance at the road-edge hedges. That pathway concerns short-term noise, lighting and vehicle movements; it does not imply an additional permanent loss of habitat.

7.10.3 Marshwick District Council asked whether the traffic assumptions used for the ecology assessment were consistent with the proposed construction access strategy.
