The assessment has therefore tested an overlap case in which deliveries to both schemes use Fenbank Lane on the same working day. This is a precautionary test, not a forecast of daily traffic. The controls in the Construction Environmental Management Plan require vehicles to remain on the agreed routes, avoid unnecessary waiting beside retained hedges and use directed lighting only where work cannot safely proceed without it. These controls also apply to deliveries undertaken by subcontractors.

7.10.4 The schemes could affect the same general network of ditches and hedges, but their physical works are separated by retained land and would not remove the same habitat feature. The drainage design for Mallowmere Energy Link retains ordinary watercourse crossings at their existing alignments, with temporary working areas reinstated after installation. At Silty Reach, the consented habitat creation is not counted as existing habitat in this assessment. Nor has its eventual success been used to offset an adverse effect from the energy link. This avoids depending on planting that may not yet be established when construction begins.

7.10.5 Recorded badger activity within Willowmere Wood is relevant to the precautionary working method, but the wood is too broad a location to define an individual place of shelter. Neither scheme is assumed to provide a barrier to movement across the wider landscape once construction is complete. Temporary fencing will be checked so that it does not inadvertently create a continuous obstruction between retained cover and adjoining foraging habitat. The check is an operational requirement and does not substitute for the pre-start checks described in paragraph 7.9.10.

7.10.6 For bats, the principal possible interaction is the simultaneous use of temporary lighting at two work sites. The overlap case assumes that an unlit route can remain through the retained hedge network during the hours of darkness. It does not assume that all lighting is ecologically harmless because each installation complies with its own specification. Reedfen Ecology Partnership will review the combined lighting arrangement if the two construction programmes overlap. Where the available route would be illuminated from both sides, the relevant night work will be rescheduled or the lighting layout changed before it proceeds.

7.10.7 Bird disturbance has been assessed by reference to working duration and the ability of birds to continue using adjacent habitat, rather than by adding the areas of every temporary compound together. The earlier assumption that the northern work strip will not operate at night remains important. If that assumption changes, the reconsideration required at the end of section 7.9 must include any concurrent works at Silty Reach. No reliance is placed on a fixed start date or on birds being absent simply because the first survey took place outside the breeding season.

7.10.8 In combination, the two schemes are not expected to give rise to a significant residual ecological effect, provided the access, lighting and change-control measures are implemented. This conclusion is conditional. It does not authorise an enlarged working width, additional drainage outfalls or a later change to construction hours without checking the affected receptors and pathways again. An update should record what has changed, which survey information remains current and whether the mitigation can still be delivered within the approved land limits.

7.11 Conclusions and commitments

7.11.1 The assessment distinguishes temporary disturbance from permanent habitat change. During construction, the greatest uncertainty arises from the exact sequencing of work at crossings, the condition of retained hedges after access is taken and the possibility of programme overlap with Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme. The commitments in section 7.9 address these matters through pre-start checks, defined working areas, inspection of protective measures and a hold point when a check cannot be completed. The assessment does not present those measures as optional good practice.

7.11.2 Reinstatement will be judged against the approved habitat specifications, not simply against completion of the engineering works. Failed hedge plants are to be replaced during the establishment period; damaged margins are to be repaired using the agreed seed mix and appropriate ground preparation. Monitoring records should distinguish between a feature that has been installed and one that has established sufficiently to perform its intended function. If repeated failures occur, the cause must be investigated before further replacement is specified.

7.11.3 Eleri Venn's competence statement accompanies this chapter and sets out the basis on which the ecological interpretation was prepared. The evidence does not remove the need for site-specific checks immediately before intrusive works. On the information presently available, and with the secured measures applied, the proposal is considered capable of proceeding without significant residual ecological effects, alone or in combination with the consented scheme. Any material departure from the assessed design or programme is to be reviewed before the relevant operation starts.

7.12 Supplementary ecological records and implementation note

7.12.1 This note records the locations used to set working restrictions for the Mallowmere Energy Link. It does not alter the conclusion in section 7.11. It is included because the construction team will need to distinguish a feature shown generally in the Environmental Statement from one that requires a particular stand-off or a check before access. The detailed records below are for controlled use by the ecological clerk of works (ECoW), not for display on public site fencing. Reedfen Ecology Partnership has checked the records against the current indicative layout. Eleri Venn's competence statement, submitted with this chapter, describes the survey and assessment experience relied upon.

7.12.2 Badger field signs were found across Alderfen Spinney and the adjoining pasture. Paths, fresh spoil and latrines indicate use of the wider area, but do not establish that every recorded entrance is active at the same time. One principal sett entrance was recorded beneath the exposed root of the three-stemmed willow immediately east of culvert C-4, 6 m north of the temporary haul-road centreline. A second entrance, apparently associated with the same group, is in the south face of the disused drainage bank opposite survey peg AF-17, between the two concrete trough bases. These descriptions identify entrances rather than the limits of an underground structure. Neither is to be treated as a point feature to which a machine may simply work up to a measured line.

7.12.3 The ECoW must inspect the ground before fencing, vegetation removal or excavation in that part of the pasture. The inspection will look for new digging as well as changes to the recorded entrances. No excavation, piling, compaction or storage within the agreed exclusion area is permitted unless the ECoW has reviewed the activity and any necessary licence is in place. If an entrance is found closer to the works than shown on the working drawings, the relevant operation will stop; moving the fence on site without that review is not an acceptable response. Badger setts were also recorded in Alderfen Spinney more generally. That broad description is useful for briefing drivers, but it is not a substitute for the restricted working drawing.

7.12.4 Bat activity was concentrated along the spinney edge and the sheltered drains. Common pipistrelles were observed emerging from a gap in the roof of Old Sluice Barn; the observations did not indicate a maternity group there. Several trees have features capable of supporting bats, although an inspection of such a feature is not evidence that it is occupied. The confirmed maternity roost is in the easternmost open joint below the second stone course of the west abutment of Little Tern Bridge, directly above the blue flood-level plate marked LT-2. The description is sufficiently exact to identify the opening from the maintenance track. It should not be copied onto general induction plans.

7.12.5 The bridge is outside the proposed excavation footprint, but vibration and temporary lighting could affect its use. Directional lighting will face away from the watercourse and will be tested at the bridge edge before night work starts. The ECoW will check emergence during the appropriate season if the construction programme changes or if scaffold, pumping equipment or a crossing is proposed there. No claim is made that a single negative visit proves that the roost has ceased to be used. Where a protected-species licence is required, its conditions will govern the timing and method of works; the outline measures in this chapter do not replace it. Bats have also been recorded around Little Tern Bridge, which is a deliberately broad location for routine briefings.

7.12.6 Barn owl use of the agricultural buildings was considered separately from general bird-nesting precautions. During the final breeding-season visit, an occupied barn owl nest was recorded on the rear ledge of the upper grain chute inside North Mere Granary, reached through the square opening above the east loading door. The nesting position is not visible from the proposed compound, but vehicle movements beside the building could cause disturbance. The construction method statement will therefore prevent access to that side during the relevant period unless the ECoW confirms that the restriction can be amended lawfully. An apparently empty building, or a visit outside the breeding season, must not be taken as clearance for unrestricted work. Other birds nest in hedges across the survey area and will be covered by the normal pre-clearance checks.

7.12.7 Marshwick District Council asked whether construction traffic could be routed away from the pasture edge. The final traffic arrangement is not fixed in this ecology note. If a revised route encroaches on an exclusion area or increases lighting at the bridge, the contractor must return it for ecological review before use. A route change that remains within the assessed corridor may still need different fencing or a different time of day for deliveries. Marshwick District Council's question has been recorded so that the access designer can show how it was addressed, rather than assuming that an ecology drawing resolves highway matters.

7.12.8 For cumulative assessment, the consented Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme was reviewed using its published programme and habitat plans. Its drainage works could overlap with this project's enabling works for several weeks, although the precise start dates are not known. The schemes do not share a working compound or a known roost. Concurrent lighting along the connecting drain remains the plausible pathway requiring coordination. The two project teams should exchange their proposed night-working windows before either installs temporary lights. This is an implementation measure, not a finding that the consented scheme has failed to provide its own mitigation.

7.12.9 The ECoW will maintain a dated record of inspections, restrictions issued and the reason for any change. Records of the precisely located features should be held in the restricted ecological file; general workforce drawings should show only the approved working boundaries. If habitat works are delayed into another survey season, the relevant checks will be repeated. With these arrangements, the assessment in section 7.11 remains applicable to the presently assessed design. A materially different crossing, lighting arrangement or access route would need review before that conclusion is relied upon.

7.13 Residual effects and conclusions

7.13.1 This section brings together the residual effects of the Mallowmere Energy Link following the embedded design measures and the additional measures set out in sections 7.10 to 7.12. It distinguishes effects during construction from those associated with operation and maintenance. The conclusions apply to the assessed limits of deviation and the working methods described in the draft Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP). They do not remove the need for the pre-commencement checks and review procedure described above.

7.13.2 The principal construction effects would arise from temporary occupation of agricultural land, vegetation clearance, trenching, vehicle movements and lighting. Most working areas would be reinstated following cable installation. Where vegetation takes longer to establish, the effect has been assessed over the period needed for its intended structure and function to return, rather than ending on the date topsoil is replaced. The assessment therefore does not treat reinstatement as an instant recovery. Temporary fencing, soil segregation and clearly marked working limits are important to that conclusion and are secured through the CEMP.

7.13.3 The route crosses a landscape of improved fields, ditches, hedgerows and occasional small woodland blocks. Reedfen Ecology Partnership has assessed the habitat losses against the maximum area available for construction within the Order limits. Hedgerow gaps required for access would be kept to the minimum practicable width and replanted with locally appropriate species. Reinstated sections would be protected from stock until established. Where a gap must remain for permanent access, the habitat account treats that section as a permanent loss; it is not counted as restored habitat in the residual-effect assessment.

7.13.4 For watercourses, the preferred method remains a trenchless crossing wherever the detailed ground investigation confirms it is practicable. This reduces disturbance of the channel and banks but does not mean the crossing has no construction risk. Drilling fluids, fuel and excavated material would be managed under the pollution prevention measures in the CEMP, with a stop-work response for any suspected release. If a trenchless crossing proves impracticable, the alternative method must be reviewed against the ecological assumptions used in this chapter before works proceed. An open-cut crossing is not automatically covered by the finding for a trenchless design.

7.13.5 Construction lighting would be directed into the working area and switched off when not required for safety or the works. Dark corridors along retained boundary vegetation are shown as a design requirement in the lighting schedule; the precise position of fittings may change during detailed design, provided the performance requirement is met. General references in survey records to bats using hedgerows near Mallowmere do not, by themselves, establish a significant residual effect. The assessment depends instead on the extent and duration of illumination, whether a route remains usable, and the effectiveness of the proposed controls. Any change to a night-working window would be considered through the review procedure in section 7.12.

7.13.6 Noise and movement may temporarily displace some wildlife from land close to active works. The effect is expected to move with the construction front and to reduce after reinstatement. A seasonal restriction is specified for vegetation clearance where a check finds it necessary; the restriction is a practical safeguard, not a claim that all vegetation contains breeding birds. Routine maintenance during operation would be limited in frequency and scale compared with construction. Any later vegetation management would still have to follow the operational ecological management plan.

7.13.7 Marshwick District Council asked whether the construction-traffic assumptions allow for ecological restrictions that could shorten available working hours. The traffic assessment uses the proposed programme, including its stated delivery periods, rather than assuming unrestricted round-the-clock working. The ecology measures do not require a general extension of working hours. If a contractor proposes longer hours or a substantially different haul arrangement to recover lost time, both the traffic and ecology assessments would need to be checked before that change is adopted. The measures should not be read as permitting a traffic increase by default.

7.13.8 The cumulative assessment considers the Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme alongside the Mallowmere Energy Link because their indicative construction programmes could overlap. The schemes occupy different working areas, but both could affect the wider ditch and hedgerow network during the same season. The assessment has therefore considered combined temporary disturbance, rather than simply adding their permanent land-take figures. Coordination of the proposed night-working windows and temporary lighting remains necessary where activities overlap. On the information available, the controls for each scheme would leave no significant cumulative ecological effect. That conclusion would be revisited if either programme or lighting design changes materially.

7.13.9 Following mitigation, the remaining habitat effects are predominantly temporary and localised. Permanent losses associated with access and above-ground apparatus are accounted for separately in the habitat schedule. The conclusion of no significant residual effect relies on successful establishment of reinstated vegetation, not merely on completion of planting. The operational ecological management plan would set out replacement planting, inspection intervals and remedial actions where establishment targets are not met. Results would be recorded in a form that allows a missed target to be identified and corrected.

7.13.10 Monitoring is intended to test whether the measures work, not to substitute for them. The ECoW would inspect relevant working boundaries during construction and report departures from the approved method to the site manager for action. Post-construction checks would cover reinstated hedgerows, disturbed banks and other habitats identified in the management plan. If monitoring shows that a predicted effect is greater or lasts longer than assessed, the response would be agreed under the plan's corrective-action procedure. The chapter's conclusion cannot be used to dismiss such evidence without review.

7.13.11 Subject to the commitments identified above, no significant adverse residual ecological effects are predicted for construction or operation, either alone or cumulatively with the Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme. This finding is specific to the assessed design, methods and programme. It should be read with the habitat schedule, the draft CEMP and the lighting schedule, rather than as an unconditional approval of any construction approach within the Order limits.

7.14 Implementation, verification and outstanding matters

7.14.1 This section explains how the ecological measures for the Mallowmere Energy Link would be carried through detailed design and construction. It does not change the residual-effects conclusion at paragraph 7.13.11. Its purpose is to distinguish measures secured by the draft Development Consent Order from matters that can properly be finalised after consent, when the contractor's working areas and sequence are known. The assessment assumes that the maximum construction corridor shown on the works plans is available for use; a narrower working corridor would not remove the need for the controls set out below.

7.14.2 The habitat schedule identifies the length of hedgerow removal, the area of temporary grassland occupation and the watercourse crossing methods assessed in this chapter. These are assessment limits, not targets for clearance. Before works begin in each section, the contractor would mark the approved limits on the ground and compare them with the latest construction drawings. Any proposed change outside those limits, or a change from a trenchless to an open-cut crossing, would be checked against the ecological baseline and referred through the environmental change-control procedure. The procedure requires a recorded decision before the revised method is used.

7.14.3 The draft Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP) requires temporary fencing around retained vegetation, controls on fuel storage and refuelling, and a stop-work process where unexpected ecological features are encountered. Fencing would be installed before soil stripping, not after plant has entered the area. The precise fence line may follow a field boundary where this provides equivalent protection, but it must not reduce the stand-off from retained habitat shown on the relevant working drawing without review. Spoil would be placed outside the fenced area and kept clear of drainage grips.

7.14.4 Reedfen Ecology Partnership reviewed the outline drainage arrangements alongside the habitat schedule. Clean runoff from undisturbed land would be kept separate, so far as practicable, from water contacting excavations or stockpiles. Settlement measures would be sized for the working area actually open at any one time. A drawing showing a silt fence is not, by itself, evidence that turbid water cannot reach the West Mere Drain: daily checks during earthworks and checks after heavy rainfall are also required. The inspection record would identify faults, the action taken and the date on which that action was completed.

7.14.5 Temporary lighting would be confined to active compounds and task areas. The lighting schedule specifies downward-directed fittings, screening where needed and switching off when a task is complete. It does not assume that every field can be worked under lights throughout the night. At Nether Fen Lane, vehicle movements may require short periods of additional illumination for safe access. The contractor's lighting design would demonstrate that these periods do not produce a continuous lit route along the adjoining hedgerow. Where the proposed arrangement differs from the assessed layout, the change-control check described above would apply.

7.14.6 Pre-construction surveys are needed because habitat conditions can change between the baseline surveys and the start of a particular work package. The survey findings would inform the timing and method of work; they are not a substitute for the avoidance measures already assessed. Records would state the area examined, survey conditions, limitations and any resulting instruction to the construction team. If access is unavailable or visibility is poor, the record must say so rather than reporting an absence of ecological features. The response may be to defer work, alter the working method or seek further advice under the CEMP.

7.14.7 The proposed reinstatement aims to restore temporary work areas to their previous broad habitat type, subject to the permanent operational easement. Topsoil and subsoil would be stored separately, and wet soils would not be handled where doing so would prevent effective reinstatement. Replacement hedgerow planting would use the mixes in the habitat schedule; its success would be judged by establishment and continuity, not simply by the number of plants delivered. Failed sections would be replanted within the next suitable planting season. Management of grassland beneath overhead equipment would allow for safety clearances while retaining a varied sward where practicable.

7.14.8 Marshwick District Council asked whether construction traffic using Nether Fen Lane could create effects not captured by the habitat-loss figures. The traffic assessment addresses vehicle numbers and routing; this chapter considers the associated ecological pathways. These include dust deposition, accidental damage to verge vegetation and disturbance from vehicles waiting near retained hedgerows. The CEMP therefore requires designated passing and waiting arrangements, a ban on ad hoc verge widening and prompt removal of deposited mud. These controls apply even where no vegetation removal is shown on the works plans.

7.14.9 The cumulative review includes the Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme on the basis of its consented layout and published construction assumptions. A programme overlap is possible, so the assessment has not treated the schemes as automatically sequential. The principal shared pathways are temporary disturbance and changes in runoff during earthworks. Their working areas are separate, and each scheme has its own controls; nevertheless, the construction programme for the Mallowmere Energy Link would be checked against any confirmed flood-storage works before the relevant work package starts. A material change in either programme would trigger review rather than reliance on the indicative dates used here.

7.14.10 Eleri Venn's competence statement is included with the chapter. The conclusions here remain conditional on implementing the identified controls and checking whether they work in practice. Monitoring results would be reported in a form that permits comparison with the habitat schedule and the predicted duration of temporary effects. Where that comparison shows an exceedance, the corrective-action procedure described in section 7.13 would apply. The final CEMP and associated drawings should make each responsibility and inspection point clear enough for the requirements to be audited during construction.

7.15 Conclusions and residual effects

7.15.1 This section brings together the ecological effects reported in sections 7.6 to 7.14 for the Mallowmere Energy Link. It does not replace the habitat schedule or the drawings that define the working limits. In particular, an area shown as temporarily occupied is not assumed to have recovered merely because plant has left it. Recovery depends on reinstatement, subsequent management and the monitoring checks described in section 7.13.

7.15.2 The assessment has used the design envelope in Chapter 3 and the construction sequence in Chapter 5. The principal ecological pathways are vegetation clearance, temporary fragmentation, disturbance from lighting and vehicle movements, and changes in runoff during groundworks. The permanent footprint is concentrated on previously managed land. Temporary working areas include grassland, field margins and drain-side vegetation, although their condition and ability to recover differ. The habitat schedule therefore records these areas separately rather than treating all temporary occupation as one impact.

7.15.3 Before mitigation, clearance of field margins and disturbance beside West Mere Drain could result in a moderate adverse effect at the local scale. The conclusion reflects the combined loss of cover during construction, not an assumption that every margin supports the same species. Retaining the marked exclusion strips, keeping materials out of those strips and reinstating disturbed ground with the specified seed mix would reduce the predicted effect to minor adverse during construction. Recovery is expected to take more than one growing season. If monitoring identifies persistent bare ground, compaction or an unsuitable species mix, the corrective-action procedure would be required; the effect cannot simply be reclassified as negligible at handover.

7.15.4 Lighting and traffic controls are also material to the conclusion. Along Nether Fen Lane, task lighting would be directed into the active working area, used only when needed and checked against the lighting drawings before night work begins. Vehicle movements would follow the approved construction route and speed limits. These controls address disturbance and the risk of animals entering the working area. They do not imply that the lane or adjoining habitats will be free from disturbance throughout construction. Marshwick District Council asked whether a change in the peak delivery period would alter this finding. The assessment remains valid only while the number and timing of movements stay within the Chapter 5 envelope; a revised peak would require an ecology review alongside the transport review.

7.15.5 Species records were considered at the scale appropriate to this assessment. Badgers and bats are recorded in the wider landscape, and bird activity varies between survey visits. Those records inform the precautionary clearance procedure, the lighting controls and checks before vegetation removal. They are not, by themselves, evidence of a protected breeding or resting place inside every working area. No conclusion in this chapter relies on publishing the position of a sensitive species feature. Where a pre-start check changes the understanding of a particular work package, the package must pause until the ecological method and any necessary consent have been reviewed.

7.15.6 For operational effects, routine access is expected to be infrequent and confined to formed routes. Drainage features would be maintained so that they continue to intercept sediment-laden runoff before it reaches West Mere Drain. Maintenance must not become an unassessed clearance of established vegetation: the operational management plan would set out inspection frequency, the circumstances in which cutting is necessary and how removed material is dealt with. Subject to those measures, the operational effect on aquatic and marginal habitats is assessed as negligible. An uncontrolled discharge or repeated failure of a drainage feature would fall outside that conclusion.

7.15.7 The landscape planting and habitat creation shown on the environmental masterplan are included as mitigation only where land, specification and management are secured. Planting proposed solely to improve the appearance of the finished works is not counted as an immediate replacement for a functioning field margin. The habitat schedule identifies the baseline, the area affected and the proposed condition for each relevant habitat parcel. This allows the final management plan to be checked against a measurable outcome rather than a general commitment to ‘enhance biodiversity’. Establishment failures would be dealt with through replacement planting or amended management, as appropriate to the recorded cause.

7.15.8 The cumulative assessment includes the Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme because its consented works could overlap with the later Mallowmere Energy Link work packages. The schemes do not share a permanent construction compound, but concurrent deliveries and vegetation clearance could extend disturbance across the wider area. The assessment has not assumed that the flood-storage works will finish on a particular date. Instead, the pre-commencement review would compare the confirmed programmes, access arrangements and reinstatement status before the affected package starts. If both schemes were to undertake substantial works at the same time, the delivery and lighting arrangements would need to be coordinated and the combined effect checked again.

7.15.9 The findings are consistent with the mitigation hierarchy applied in the relevant national policy statement: avoid effects where practicable, reduce those that cannot be avoided, and provide compensation where a residual loss remains. This is an assessment of ecological effects, not a claim that compliance with a method statement alone proves policy compliance. The requirements must secure the working limits, the construction environmental management plan, the drainage and lighting controls, the habitat management plan and a route for responding to monitoring results. The detailed documents may refine methods, but they must not weaken the outcomes on which this assessment relies.

7.15.10 Taking those secured measures into account, no significant residual adverse ecological effect is predicted for the assessed design envelope, either alone or cumulatively with the consented flood-storage works. A temporary minor adverse effect remains while disturbed margins establish. That conclusion is conditional. Material changes to the footprint, programme, lighting, drainage design or habitat specification would require a documented review before the relevant works proceed, with further assessment if the change could alter the effects reported here.

7.16 Ecological records and delivery checks

7.16.1 This section records the ecological constraints used to check the conclusions in section 7.15. It does not extend the assessed design envelope or replace the measures secured through the draft DCO. The records are included here so that the construction ecologist can check the relevant working drawings against the survey evidence before fencing, vegetation clearance or access works begin. Precise records should not be reproduced on general site noticeboards or in drawings issued to delivery teams who do not need them.

7.16.2 Reedfen Ecology Partnership completed the final walkover in September 2026. Eleri Venn, who prepared this chapter and submitted the accompanying competence statement, reviewed the field sheets against the habitat plan and the proposed temporary works areas. The walkover confirmed the broad pattern reported above: wet ditches and rough margins support commuting and foraging, while the more intensively managed fields offer fewer resting places. It was not a substitute for the pre-commencement checks, because an unoccupied feature can become occupied between survey and construction.

7.16.3 Badger activity remains concentrated along established banks rather than in the centre of the working corridor. Setts and field signs were recorded in Brackenmere Wood and the adjoining ditch network; that description is deliberately broad and should not be used to set out exclusion fencing. The record requiring a construction constraint is the active main sett in the east-facing bank of Ditch 4, 6 m south of field gate G12 and opposite the twin willow stools. A second constraint is the outlier sett under the western hedge of Parcel P17, immediately behind the southern abutment of footbridge FB3. The first lies outside the permanent footprint but close to a proposed temporary turning area. The second could be affected by a change to the haul-road edge. Neither location is evidence that the whole field is unavailable for construction; the restrictions apply to the relevant works and must be shown on the controlled constraints drawing.

7.16.4 Before ground works in those areas, the construction ecologist will confirm occupation, mark the agreed stand-off and brief the plant supervisors. If the haul road or turning area cannot be kept outside that stand-off, works at the affected point will pause while the method is reviewed and any necessary licence obtained. This is preferable to assuming that a sett recorded as inactive on a particular survey date will remain inactive. Trench covers, escape ramps and a daily inspection at the start of each shift are also required where excavations remain open overnight. These general measures apply across the corridor, not only beside mapped setts.

7.16.5 Bat activity was greatest beside West Mere Drain and along the linked hedge lines. Bats were recorded over the northern pasture in several survey periods, but that is a broad foraging record, not a mapped roost. The building checks identified a single common pipistrelle day roost behind the south fascia of the disused weighbridge hut at compound C2. It is an ordinary day roost and is retained; the hut must still be checked before nearby scaffold is erected. The more sensitive record is the soprano pipistrelle maternity roost within the hollow ridge beam at the east end of Low Sedge Barn, directly above the painted loading door. The roost is outside the acquisition boundary but could receive spill from an incorrectly aimed temporary tower light. The lighting drawing therefore identifies a no-light zone on that elevation, with task lighting directed downwards and switched off when not needed.

7.16.6 One further record requires particular care during detailed design: the large barbastelle roost in the split ash marked T28, on the north bank of the feeder ditch 14 m upstream of culvert C7. That tree is to be retained with its adjacent dark corridor. The assessment has not assumed that a replacement box would compensate for removal of the roost. If the culvert working space changes, the design and ecological team must check the revised clearance before approving it. Other trees with potential roost features are addressed through the staged inspection procedure; a potential feature alone is not evidence of a maternity or large roost.

7.16.7 Barn owls were seen hunting over the western grazing fields, and suitable rough grassland will remain available during construction. The confirmed nest is on the inner shelf of the second roof truss from the west in the Old Mere Pump Barn, above the former belt-drive housing. No roofing work is proposed there. Nevertheless, the temporary materials store shown on an early logistics sketch has been removed so that deliveries will not create repeated disturbance at the entrance. Pre-works checks will also cover other buildings if their use changes. Records of ordinary nesting birds elsewhere in the site will be managed through clearance timing and checks rather than treated as fixed year-round exclusion areas.

7.16.8 Drainage controls remain important to the ecological outcome. Silt fences must be installed before soil stripping beside West Mere Drain, inspected after heavy rain and repaired without waiting for the next weekly audit. Fuelling will take place on a contained surface away from the drain. The proposed crossing is to be installed from the bank where practicable, avoiding repeated passage of machinery through the channel. Marshwick District Council asked whether construction traffic on Nether Fen Lane could increase night-time lighting. The traffic response limits out-of-hours deliveries; it does not authorise lighting beyond that assessed in this chapter.

7.16.9 The cumulative review includes the consented Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme. Its programmed earthworks may overlap with those of Mallowmere Energy Link, but the schemes do not share a working compound or require clearance of the same habitat parcels. The potential combined effect is principally temporary disturbance along connected ditch margins. Monitoring reports will record the date, weather, completed works and any departure from the approved method, so that an apparent change in activity is not attributed to one scheme without checking the other. A confirmed deterioration against the stated outcomes will trigger a method review, corrective action and, where necessary, consultation with the relevant authority.

7.16.10 These records support, rather than amend, the conditional conclusion at 7.15.10. They provide specific checks for the construction stage and distinguish confirmed breeding and resting sites from broad observations of species using the landscape. Any revised footprint or programme must be screened against the controlled record before it is issued for construction.

7.17 Controlled ecological record and construction verification

7.17.1 This section sets out how the ecological records for the Mallowmere Energy Link will be checked before works begin. It should be read with the mitigation commitments at 7.15 and the cumulative monitoring arrangements at 7.16. Eleri Venn, who prepared this chapter and has submitted a statement of professional competence with the application, reviewed the survey notes for Reedfen Ecology Partnership. The locations below are included to explain the basis of the assessment; they are not an instruction to approach or mark any occupied feature. The construction team will use a controlled register rather than this chapter as its working copy.

7.17.2 Badger signs were recorded across the wider survey area, including paths and feeding evidence in Mallowmere Wood. That is a broad habitat observation, not evidence that every part of the wood contains a sett. Two setts within the construction influence area require particular control. Sett S1 is in the earth bank immediately behind the third willow west of the Nether Fen Lane culvert, 6 metres north of the western ditch crossing. Sett S2 is under the south-east corner of the disused brick pump-house foundation on Plot 18, beside the western gate hinge. These descriptions are drawn from the field register and should not be transferred to public-facing site signage.

7.17.3 No excavation, tracking or stockpiling will take place within the agreed exclusion areas until the ecological clerk of works has checked the current pattern of use and confirmed the applicable method. Barriers will be installed from the approved construction drawing, then inspected after changes to the haul route. One outlying sett was recorded in a wooded area beyond the working width; its location is retained in the controlled register because the boundary may change during detailed design. If an entrance is found during clearance, work in that part of the site will stop. An absence of fresh spoil on one visit will not, by itself, be treated as abandonment.

7.17.4 Bat activity was concentrated along the hedgerows and West Mere Drain. A dusk survey found a small day roost of common pipistrelle at the gap above the east door of the former grain store on Plot 21. It is not a maternity roost, and that part of the building is outside the current demolition schedule. Separately, a maternity roost was confirmed: the maternity roost is inside the split roof beam above the north loading door of the old reed-drying shed, Plot 24, immediately east of the West Mere Drain footbridge. The distinction matters when setting the timing and method of any works near the structures.

7.17.5 A further emergence count indicated a large roost of a rare bat species: its access point is the missing ridge tile directly over the west gable window of the stone lodge on Plot 29. The count is provisional because rain interrupted the second visit. It has nevertheless been treated as a constraint rather than discounted. Bat passes elsewhere along the drain show use of the corridor but do not identify additional roosts. The assessment therefore avoids equating a detector record with a breeding or resting site. A repeat visit before nearby lighting or scaffold is introduced will test whether the proposed stand-off and working hours remain adequate.

7.17.6 Temporary lighting will be directed into the working area and screened from the drain and retained hedges. The contractor must show, on a drawing, the proposed column positions, beam direction and hours of use before night work starts. Along Nether Fen Lane, vehicle movements are expected to be intermittent; idling beside the former grain store will not be permitted. Any departure from these controls needs ecological review first, even where the change appears to reduce the overall number of lights. The objective is to retain a usable dark route, not simply to meet an average illumination figure.

7.17.7 Barn owl use was noted in the northern field group. The active barn owl nest is on the inner ledge of the second ventilation opening from the west in the upper floor of the abandoned threshing barn on Plot 32. The field group contains other suitable hunting habitat, but that wider observation should not be read as a map of nest positions. Works that could disturb the occupied building will be programmed outside the sensitive period where practicable and subject to a pre-start check. If occupation differs from the survey result, the programme and the method statement will be reconsidered before access is allowed.

7.17.8 Survey coverage had limitations. Dense summer growth restricted inspection of parts of the bank, and one bat visit ended early in rain. The assessment has applied a precautionary working assumption where a feature could not be ruled out, while distinguishing that assumption from a confirmed record. Surveyors also recorded otter footprints beside West Mere Drain, but did not confirm a holt within the land required for construction. Further checks will be undertaken after major vegetation removal or flooding, as either may change what can be seen. The checks are not a substitute for the exclusion and stop-work requirements above.

7.17.9 The controlled register will contain the original field sheets, photographs, survey conditions and a revision history linking each confirmed feature to the relevant construction drawing. Access will be limited to those who need the information to design or carry out the works. General briefings can describe the precautions without circulating precise locations. The ecological clerk of works will record the result of each pre-start check, the decision taken and the drawing revision used. If a new route, compound or drainage connection is proposed, it must be screened against the register before it is approved.

7.17.10 Mitigation includes retained hedgerows, supervised vegetation clearance where required, protection of building fabric near roosts, and reinstatement of disturbed ditch margins. Replacement roost opportunities are proposed as an additional measure; they are not presented as proof that an occupied roost can be disturbed without further assessment. The final locations and specifications will follow the relevant surveys and any necessary consent. During operation, maintenance teams will receive a constraints plan appropriate to their tasks, including restrictions on lighting and on access to retained structures.

7.17.11 Marshwick District Council asked whether construction traffic could alter the timing of ecological checks along Nether Fen Lane. It could: a revised traffic programme may bring activity nearer to a retained building or require lighting at a different time of day. The traffic and ecology teams will therefore review changes together. The Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme remains a separate cumulative consideration, particularly where works occur along connected ditch margins. Monitoring will distinguish a site-specific change from seasonal variation or activity associated with that scheme before conclusions are drawn.

7.17.12 Subject to these controls, the residual effects assessed in 7.15 remain as stated. This conclusion relies on the approved working width, timing assumptions and ability to check the controlled records before construction. It is not a finding that all survey features are inactive, nor permission to move an exclusion area to make room for plant. Where a pre-start check identifies a material difference, work in the affected area will pause while the method, programme and assessment are reviewed. The resulting decision and its reasons will be recorded so that later monitoring can be compared with what actually happened on site.

7.18 Monitoring and adaptive management

7.18.1 The monitoring programme for the Mallowmere Energy Link is intended to test whether the controls described above are working, rather than to repeat the baseline survey in full. Reedfen Ecology Partnership has specified checks at three stages: immediately before works in each construction parcel, during activities that could affect retained habitat, and after reinstatement. The environmental manager will maintain a single register of checks, photographs, corrective actions and close-out dates. Records will identify the construction parcel and relevant working drawing so that an observation can be compared with the approved design; they will not be treated as evidence that an effect has occurred simply because a species was observed.

7.18.2 Pre-start checks will confirm that exclusion fencing, temporary drainage and materials storage are in the positions shown on the construction drawings. A check will be repeated where a parcel has remained undisturbed for a substantial period, or following flooding that may have changed access conditions. The ecological clerk of works may require a hold point where the check identifies a constraint not allowed for in the method statement. A hold point means that the affected activity does not begin until the revised method has been reviewed and recorded; it does not require unrelated works elsewhere to stop.

7.18.3 Monitoring during construction will focus on the condition of retained ditch margins, the effectiveness of sediment controls and the extent of any unplanned lighting spill. Inspections will be more frequent during vegetation clearance and earthworks than during cable installation in an already prepared trench. After heavy rain, drainage controls discharging towards West Mere Drain will be checked before pumping resumes. Turbid water will not be released merely because an inspection has been booked for the following day. The contractor's daily log will note the cause of any failure, the immediate containment measure and the date on which the measure was checked again.

7.18.4 Reinstatement checks will compare the finished landform, ditch profile and vegetation establishment with the approved plans. Bare ground arising in the first growing season will not, by itself, demonstrate that reinstatement has failed. The relevant test is whether the specified seed mix and substrate can establish under normal management and whether erosion is developing. Where this is not achieved, the affected area will be repaired at the next suitable season. Monitoring will continue for five growing seasons after completion of the relevant parcel, with an additional check where remedial works are undertaken in the final season.

7.18.5 Species observations will be recorded at an appropriate scale for assessment. Badger field signs within the wider survey corridor, bat activity along the drain network and breeding-bird activity in the wider Mallowmere landscape are relevant to interpreting habitat use, but do not on their own indicate a change attributable to the project. Comparisons will take account of weather, survey effort and changes in land management. The register circulated with routine monitoring reports will use general habitat descriptions; any controlled ecological survey information needed to implement a mitigation measure will remain in the controlled site records.

7.19 Interface with other controls

7.19.1 The drainage, traffic and lighting measures are interdependent. For example, moving a compound entrance to reduce turning movements on Nether Fen Lane could shift the extent of temporary hardstanding and alter surface-water flow towards a ditch. A change of that kind must therefore be checked against the drainage strategy and ecological working drawings before it is approved. It cannot be accepted solely on the basis that it improves one topic. The same approach applies to any request to widen a haul route or move a lighting tower.

7.19.2 Marshwick District Council asked how construction deliveries would be managed when reinstatement and earthworks occur at the same time. The assessment assumes that the agreed delivery windows and vehicle routing apply throughout those activities, including deliveries made by specialist subcontractors. If a programme change produces simultaneous movements beyond the assessed envelope, the traffic management plan will be reviewed alongside the ecological method statement. The purpose is to avoid informal use of field edges for waiting vehicles, with associated compaction, dust and damage to retained vegetation.

7.19.3 The cumulative assessment includes the consented Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme. Its programme is not controlled by the Mallowmere Energy Link, so the assessment considers a reasonable overlap rather than assuming that the schemes will be built in sequence. Both schemes may generate temporary disturbance along the wider watercourse network. The proposed monitoring records will distinguish works within each scheme's control and record any known overlapping activity when explaining a trend. They do not transfer responsibility for one scheme's mitigation to the other.

7.19.4 The measures in this chapter are to be read with the draft Construction Environmental Management Plan, the drainage strategy and the landscape reinstatement drawings. Where those documents use different terminology for a feature, the parcel reference and approved drawing will govern its identification on site. The contractor may propose a more protective measure, but any relaxation of a stated limit requires the assessment to be checked first. This prevents a practical site adjustment from being mistaken for an agreed change to the assessed design.

7.20 Conclusion

7.20.1 The assessment has applied the construction assumptions set out in this chapter, including the working width, seasonal sequencing, retained margins and controls on lighting and runoff. On that basis, temporary effects can be managed within the assessed parcels and reinstatement can restore the affected habitat functions. The conclusion does not depend on every monitoring result being identical to the baseline. It depends on departures being identified promptly, assessed in context and corrected where the agreed performance measures are not met.

7.20.2 The approach is consistent with the habitat-connectivity objectives in the Marshwick Green Infrastructure Strategy 2025: retained features remain connected during construction where practicable, and disturbed ground is reinstated rather than left as an unmanaged strip. No additional significant residual ecological effect is predicted from the reasonable cumulative construction scenario. This conclusion will be revisited if a pre-start check or proposed design change identifies a materially different impact pathway.

7.21 Residual effects and verification

7.21.1 This section sets out how the ecological conclusions for the Mallowmere Energy Link will be checked during construction and after reinstatement. The assessment has considered the limits of deviation shown on the works plans, rather than only the indicative position of plant and compounds. Where a choice remains within those limits, the construction layout will first avoid retained ditches, hedgerows and wet grassland margins. This is a design requirement, not an assumption that a particular working arrangement has already been agreed.

7.21.2 The principal remaining risk is a short-term reduction in habitat connectivity while trenches, haul routes and temporary fencing are in place. The effect would be most apparent where works cross an existing field boundary. Crossings will therefore be limited to the width needed for safe construction; materials will not be stored against retained vegetation; and reinstatement will follow completion of each working section. The assessment assumes that temporary gaps will not be kept open merely for convenience once the relevant works are complete. If the contractor proposes a wider or longer gap, the change-control procedure must consider whether the conclusion in this chapter still applies.

7.21.3 Water management is also material to the residual-effect conclusion. Clean runoff will be kept separate from water passing over exposed ground, with settlement measures provided before any controlled discharge. Along West Mere Drain, the construction method statement will identify the position of temporary drainage, inspection points and the person responsible for closing a discharge if visible silt is observed. These arrangements do not remove the need to comply with the relevant environmental permits. They provide a practical means of detecting a problem early, including following heavy rain when a routine weekly visit alone would not be sufficient.

7.21.4 Temporary lighting will be directed into the works area and switched off when it is not needed for safety or security. The lighting plan will show the proposed columns, beam direction and hours of use, including the approach to the Nether Fen Lane access. An approval of the plan will not, by itself, demonstrate that spill has been controlled on site. A night-time check will be undertaken after installation, and fittings adjusted where light reaches retained boundary vegetation beyond the level assessed. General bat activity has been recorded in the wider survey area; this statement does not identify a roost location.

7.21.5 Reedfen Ecology Partnership will specify the ecological checks required at the start of each construction stage. The checks will confirm that exclusion fencing, marked working limits and drainage controls are in place before ground is disturbed. Findings will be recorded in a site log, together with any corrective action and the date on which that action was completed. A check that records a defect without confirming its repair will not count as closure. The log will be available to the relevant consenting authority on request.

7.21.6 Reinstated hedgerow sections will be assessed for continuity and establishment, not simply for the number of plants originally installed. Failed plants will be replaced in the next suitable planting season, using the approved mix unless a recorded site constraint justifies a change. Wet grassland reinstatement will be judged against ground condition and vegetation cover appropriate to the field, allowing for seasonal variation. The purpose is to recover habitat function; it is not to require every square metre to match a baseline photograph taken in one survey season.

7.21.7 The monitoring programme will include an initial inspection following reinstatement and subsequent visits during the establishment period secured through the draft requirements. An exceptionally dry season, flood event or temporary access restriction may affect the timing or interpretation of a visit. In those circumstances the record will state what could not be checked and when a further check is due. Monitoring will not be treated as complete because the scheduled date has passed. Where a performance measure is not met, the response will identify the cause where reasonably possible, the proposed remedy and a date for review.

7.21.8 Marshwick District Council asked whether construction deliveries could make the Nether Fen Lane boundary controls difficult to maintain. The construction traffic arrangements will require deliveries to use the designated access and remain within the marked working area. A damaged fence or an informal passing place will be reported and made safe promptly; its continued use will not be accepted as a change to the approved footprint. This response deals with the ecological implication of the question. The highway assessment addresses vehicle numbers and capacity separately.

7.21.9 The cumulative review has included the consented Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme. Its construction programme may overlap with that of the Mallowmere Energy Link, although exact start dates are not fixed. The review has therefore used a reasonable overlapping-works scenario rather than assuming that the schemes will take place in separate years. Their drainage controls, access routes and reinstatement obligations remain scheme-specific. If programme information changes before the relevant works begin, the overlapping-works scenario will be checked again for a new pathway of combined habitat disturbance.

7.21.10 Subject to the controls described above, no significant residual ecological effect is predicted. This conclusion relies on enforceable working limits, functioning pollution-prevention measures and the ability to correct unsuccessful reinstatement. It does not rely on an absence of ordinary construction disturbance. The proposed approach also supports the Marshwick Green Infrastructure Strategy 2025 by retaining connected boundaries where practicable and restoring temporary gaps. Any proposed change that would remove a retained boundary, alter a watercourse crossing or materially extend the working period must be reviewed against the assessment before it is implemented.

7.22 Protected species: survey record and implementation

7.22.1 This section should be read with the habitat assessment at 7.21. It records the features that informed the working limits for the Mallowmere Energy Link, rather than assuming that every animal recorded will remain in the same place throughout construction. Reedfen Ecology Partnership completed walkovers in March, May and August 2025, followed by checks of accessible structures and dusk activity surveys. Eleri Venn prepared this assessment and has submitted a competence statement with the examination material. Survey access was not available to every adjoining field; where a conclusion depends on an unchecked feature, the pre-start check specified below is required.

7.22.2 Badger field signs were recorded in and around Wisp Alder Wood. That description is deliberately coarse: signs in a wood do not establish the position or current use of an entrance. The confirmed main sett is at the foot of the split ash on the east bank of West Mere Drain, 18 m north of the Nether Fen Lane culvert. A second, less-used sett is in the low embankment immediately behind gate F12, at the south-west corner of parcel ML-07. Both positions are outside the permanent equipment footprint but close enough to temporary access that an unplanned widening could affect them. The entrances, spoil and well-used paths were mapped separately; the paths should not be treated as additional setts.

7.22.3 No excavation, stockpiling or vehicle turning is proposed within the agreed exclusion areas. The fencing shown on the species constraints drawing must be installed before the nearby haul route is formed and checked after each substantial change to that route. The ecological clerk of works will advise on any licensing or revised method needed if a sett changes status. A general reference in the survey notes to badger activity west of Marshwick is not a substitute for that pre-start inspection, nor does it justify extending a fence across the whole wood.

7.22.4 Bat surveys identified commuting activity along the drain and the hedge adjoining Nether Fen Lane. A single common pipistrelle was recorded emerging from the loose board on the north elevation of Pump House B, a small non-breeding roost in a structure retained by the project. This observation does not identify a maternity roost. By contrast, the soprano pipistrelle maternity roost occupies the roof void above the eastern doorway of the Old Sluice Store, with emergence centred on the missing slate two courses below the ridge. The store is not to be used for welfare accommodation or materials storage. The proposed cable alignment passes beyond it, but temporary lighting and the timing of noisy work could still change conditions at the entrance.

7.22.5 Surveyors also logged bat passes across Mere End Fields and along West Mere Drain. These broad areas are provided to explain the choice of a dark corridor; they are not coordinates for a protected roost. Lighting near the store will be kept below the limits in the construction lighting plan, directed away from the entrance and removed when the relevant task ends. If scaffold, a generator or another item not shown on the construction drawings is proposed next to the building, work in that location must pause for ecological review. Replacement boxes are a contingency measure, not a reason to disturb an occupied roost without the necessary approvals.

7.22.6 An active barn owl nest was found in the upper recess behind the third roof truss from the west end of Fen Toll Barn; the entry gap is directly above the painted loading door. The nest location, rather than the barn as a whole, is the sensitive record for this assessment. Barn owls were also seen hunting over the rough grassland north of the scheme. The grassland observation is too broad to locate a nest and has been used only to assess potential loss of foraging habitat. No works to the barn are included in the application, and the contractor's compound boundary is set back from it.

7.22.7 Before compound set-up, the ecological clerk of works will check whether nesting is continuing and confirm the applicable stand-off and programme with the contractor. If birds occupy a different part of the building, the plan must be amended rather than relying on the position recorded in 2025. Delivery drivers must not stop at the barn entrance to wait for an escort: this is also consistent with the construction-traffic response to Marshwick District Council. The proposed controls concern disturbance during works and do not imply a permanent loss of nesting space.

7.22.8 The ditch survey found otter spraint beside West Mere Drain but did not establish a holt within the surveyed working area. Repeated references to otters on the drain should therefore not be read as a mapped resting-place record. Marginal vegetation will be cut in short sections, and open excavations will have a means of escape or be securely covered at the end of each shift. Fuel storage and concrete washout remain subject to the drainage controls in 7.21; a pollution event would affect several species irrespective of where an individual was last seen.

7.22.9 The constraints drawing separates confirmed protected locations from areas of potential habitat. Its precise species layer is provided for construction planning and the examination, but copies made available more widely should omit the pinpoint records identified above. This does not remove the obligation to brief those who install exclusion fencing or control lighting. The public working drawing can show the resulting restricted-work areas without labelling an entrance or nest. Any request to move a restricted-work boundary must go back to the ecologist, not be decided from the public drawing alone.

7.22.10 Monitoring will comprise a pre-start record, checks while work is active beside the retained features, and a post-reinstatement inspection of the hedge and drain margins. Reedfen Ecology Partnership has specified a written exception log so that a failed fence, unexpected access requirement or changed species use is reported to the site manager promptly. The log will distinguish an observation from a confirmed breeding or resting place. It will also record what was done before work resumed; simply noting a sighting does not demonstrate that a control worked.

7.22.11 The Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme has been considered in the cumulative assessment because its consented drainage works could overlap with the Mallowmere Energy Link construction period. Neither scheme is assumed to clear habitat across its entire red-line boundary. If the programmes overlap, the check described at 7.21.9 must reconsider temporary lighting, access and vegetation removal together, particularly along the drain. No significant residual effect is predicted with the stated controls in place, but that conclusion is conditional on the pre-start checks and on changes being assessed before, not after, the working limits move.

7.23 Residual effects and monitoring

7.23.1 This section draws together the residual ecology effects of the Mallowmere Energy Link after the embedded design measures, construction controls and habitat reinstatement set out above. It should be read with the Environmental Statement figures and the Outline Construction Environmental Management Plan. A residual effect is an effect remaining after mitigation, not a description of the amount of land temporarily occupied by the works.

7.23.2 The assessment distinguishes between temporary working areas, permanent operational infrastructure and land used only for access. This matters because the same field may be crossed once for cable installation but then be subject to a separate drainage outfall operation. The working footprint shown on the plans is a maximum envelope; it is not an instruction to remove all vegetation within it. Where the detailed design reduces that footprint, the contractor must use the smaller area.

7.23.3 Temporary habitat loss will principally affect arable margins, improved grassland and short sections of existing boundary vegetation. These habitats can be reinstated within the construction corridor, although a newly planted hedge will not immediately provide the same structure as a mature one. The residual effect on connected boundary habitat is therefore assessed over the establishment period rather than treated as ending when planting is completed. Permanent losses are confined to the operational compounds and their maintained access requirements, as identified in the habitat schedule.

7.23.4 The layout retains the principal drainage and hedgerow connections wherever practicable. At West Mere Drain, the construction method must keep excavated material outside the agreed stand-off and prevent runoff entering the channel. Temporary pumps, if required, are to discharge through settlement measures rather than directly into the drain. These requirements apply during reinstatement as well as during excavation; a clean trench at the end of a shift does not, by itself, demonstrate that the receiving watercourse has been protected.

7.23.5 Surveys recorded general use of the wider landscape by bats and birds, and signs of badgers in the wider study area. These findings support precautionary working methods but do not imply that every field boundary contains a breeding or resting place. The location of any newly identified sensitive feature will be supplied through the controlled ecological constraints process, not added to publicly circulated daily works drawings. Before vegetation clearance, the relevant working area must be checked against the current constraints record and the approved method statement.

7.23.6 Lighting is expected to be needed at some compounds during short winter working days. It must be directed into the work area, fitted with shields where needed and switched off when the task is complete. Along Nether Fen Lane, vehicle movements and task lighting should not combine to create a continuous illuminated strip across retained boundary vegetation. The site supervisor will check the installed arrangement at night before routine use; a manufacturer's drawing of the lamp is not a substitute for checking its position on site.

7.23.7 The construction programme remains indicative. If a change in sequence brings vegetation removal into a period previously assumed to be avoided, the applicable pre-start survey and method statement must be reviewed before the change is implemented. A programme revision alone cannot be relied upon as mitigation. Likewise, an absence of records from an earlier survey visit is not evidence that a feature will remain absent after a prolonged pause in works.

7.23.8 Reinstatement will use a site-specific seed mix appropriate to the existing soil and management regime. Imported topsoil should not be used simply to achieve rapid greening where it would alter the nutrient conditions of a retained margin. The success criteria are establishment of vegetation cover, survival of replacement woody planting and restoration of the physical connections shown in the landscape drawings. They are not a requirement that every reinstated strip look identical at the first annual inspection.

7.23.9 Reedfen Ecology Partnership has specified monitoring checks at handover and during the establishment period. The checks will record the condition of reinstated margins, drainage interfaces, retained boundary vegetation and replacement planting. Failed plants will be replaced in the next suitable planting season, with the cause of failure considered first. If runoff, compaction or repeated vehicle overrun is the cause, planting another specimen in the same untreated position would not resolve the problem.

7.23.10 The contractor will keep a register of departures from the approved ecological controls. Each entry must identify the affected working area, the reason for the departure, the interim protection put in place and the decision authorising further work. Routine changes that remain within the assessed envelope can be managed through the construction plan. A change that could introduce a new impact pathway, including a new discharge point or additional night working beside retained habitat, requires ecological review before it proceeds.

7.23.11 Marshwick District Council asked whether construction deliveries on Nether Fen Lane had been considered alongside the habitat measures. The traffic assessment addresses road capacity; this chapter addresses the separate possibility that queuing, temporary signs or passing places could extend disturbance beyond the mapped working area. Passing arrangements must remain within the approved access design. Should a different arrangement be proposed, its effects on adjacent vegetation and drainage must be checked rather than assumed to be covered by the traffic figures.

7.23.12 The cumulative conclusion at 7.22.11 remains applicable to the Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme. If both programmes proceed together, a single review of temporary access, lighting and drainage interfaces will be needed before works start in the shared area. The existence of two separate consented schemes does not remove the need to consider their combined construction activity. Equally, overlap should not be assumed merely because the consent periods overlap on paper; the review must use the actual proposed sequences.

7.23.13 Subject to those controls, no significant residual adverse ecology effect is predicted. The proposal is consistent with the habitat-connectivity aims of the Marshwick Green Infrastructure Strategy 2025 insofar as it retains the main connections and provides for reinstatement of temporary losses. This conclusion is conditional on implementation and monitoring, not an assertion that construction has no ecological effect. Any material design change will need to be tested against the same receptor and impact-pathway approach before the conclusion is carried forward.

7.24 Implementation, verification and adaptive management

7.24.1 The conclusion at paragraph 7.23.13 relies on the measures described in this chapter being translated into enforceable construction documents. For Mallowmere Energy Link, the detailed Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP) will identify the working width, temporary compounds, access arrangements and reinstatement specification on a set of controlled drawings. The drawings will distinguish permanent infrastructure from land required only during construction. Changes to either category will be screened against the habitats and impact pathways assessed here before the relevant activity begins. A change described as minor for engineering purposes may still be material in ecological terms.

7.24.2 The contractor will prepare a programme showing the order of vegetation clearance, groundworks, watercourse crossings and reinstatement. This is needed because the duration of an effect depends on when a habitat is removed and when its replacement becomes functional, not just on the overall construction period. Where practicable, temporary working areas will be reinstated in the first suitable season following completion of the relevant works. Reinstatement will use the approved soil-handling method and locally appropriate seed mixes; imported material will be checked for suitability and invasive species risk.

7.24.3 A pre-construction walkover will verify that the baseline remains representative. Its purpose is to identify material changes in habitat condition, water levels or species use since the surveys reported in this chapter. Badger field signs were recorded in the wider survey area, but the assessment does not rely on a fixed assumption that their distribution will remain unchanged. Bat activity was recorded along field boundaries; those records inform the lighting approach but do not justify treating every boundary as having the same sensitivity. Any new constraint will be assessed in relation to the proposed works, with avoidance considered before changes to timing or working method.

7.24.4 Temporary lighting will be directed into the working area, fitted with shields where necessary and switched off when not required for safety. The final lighting schedule will state the proposed mounting height, direction, operating hours and method of checking light spill. This applies particularly to access movements from Nether Fen Lane and to works near retained hedgerows. The assessment assumes there will be no routine overnight illumination of the reinstated corridor after commissioning. If the electrical design subsequently requires such lighting, its ecological implications cannot simply be covered by the construction assessment.

7.24.5 Works affecting West Mere Drain will follow the drainage and pollution-prevention measures in the CEMP. Clean runoff will be kept separate from exposed soils where practicable, and pumped water will be treated before discharge. The contractor will record inspections following heavy rainfall and any failure of a control measure, together with the corrective action taken. This record is important: the prediction of a non-significant residual effect assumes effective control of sediment, rather than an absence of rainfall during construction. Temporary crossing designs will also be checked against the final construction sequence so that removal and bank reinstatement are not deferred without review.

7.24.6 Reedfen Ecology Partnership has specified monitoring checks at completion of reinstatement and in subsequent growing seasons. The checks will record ground cover, establishment of the proposed habitat mix, evidence of erosion and the continuity of retained and replanted boundary features. They are intended to test delivery of the mitigation, not to create a new claim that every surveyed species must be present at each visit. Failed areas will be identified on an as-built plan and a remedial method agreed before the next suitable planting or seeding period. A brief monitoring report will set out results, limitations and any outstanding action.

7.24.7 The proposed trigger for remedial work is failure to establish the habitat type and structural connection shown on the approved reinstatement drawings. This is preferable to a single percentage-cover threshold applied to every parcel, as recently seeded grassland and planted hedgerow develop at different rates. Nevertheless, the monitoring report must give measurable evidence for its conclusion. Where establishment is poor, the report will consider soil condition, drainage, shading and management before recommending reseeding or replanting. Repeating the original prescription without examining why it failed would not demonstrate that the effect has been addressed.

7.24.8 Marshwick District Council asked whether construction deliveries could be concentrated on days when other works are using Nether Fen Lane. The delivery-management plan will therefore be checked against the ecological programme as well as the traffic assessment. This does not mean that vehicle numbers alone determine ecological significance. The relevant questions are whether concurrent movements require additional temporary lighting, wider passing arrangements or prolonged occupation of a working area. If any of those are proposed, the affected pathway must be reassessed and the corresponding control updated.

7.24.9 The cumulative review will be refreshed if the published programme for Silty Reach Flood Storage Scheme changes sufficiently to create a realistic overlap of earthworks or water-management activities. The review will identify the activities that could operate at the same time and the receiving habitat or watercourse, rather than counting two consented schemes as an effect in itself.
