It will also record where there is no credible shared pathway. This provides an auditable basis for retaining or revising the conclusion in section 7.23.

7.25 Summary of residual effects

7.25.1 On the stated design and subject to the secured measures, the residual construction effects on habitats and species are assessed as not significant. Permanent land take has been included in that judgement; it is not offset by describing temporary reinstatement as an immediate replacement for established habitat. Monitoring is required because successful establishment remains an assumption to be verified. The retained boundary network and proposed reinstatement are consistent with the connectivity objectives of the Marshwick Green Infrastructure Strategy 2025.

7.25.2 The conclusion does not remove the need for a further check if the working width, crossing method, lighting schedule or construction phasing changes materially. The check should identify the affected receptor, the altered pathway and whether the proposed controls remain effective. Its findings should be recorded alongside the relevant controlled drawing and construction document so that the basis of the ecological conclusion remains clear throughout delivery.

text:
Tamsin Vale Joinery
From: Tamsin Vale
14 Cinder Lane, Larkhollow, LM4 8QF
Email: tamsin.vale@valejoinery.example
Mobile: 07700 900 732

20 October 2026

To the Examining Authority
Dunmarsh Link Cable Project — EN030024
Interested Party reference: 20049618

Dear Examining Authority,

I am a self-employed joiner and I object to the construction traffic arrangements proposed by Dunmarsh Gridworks Ltd. I work from a small workshop behind my home on Cinder Lane. I am not objecting to cables being installed as such. My objection is to using our lane as a convenient way of getting HGVs to the eastern compound without showing how residents and small businesses will still get in and out safely.

The traffic plan calls Cinder Lane a minor access route. That makes it sound like a line on a map rather than a lane with doors, deliveries and people walking along it. The carriageway narrows beside the old pump house; two vans cannot pass there. Timber comes to my workshop on a flatbed, usually in lengths that cannot just be carried from a distant parking place. I also take finished doors to customers and need to set off at the agreed time. If a queue of wagons is held at the bend, neither the delivery driver nor I can see what is coming the other way.

My own van, PX26 LRD, is parked in the yard because there is no legal place for it on the lane. The applicant’s swept-path drawing shows an HGV turning into the proposed access, but not an HGV meeting a flatbed or a refuse lorry at the narrowing. It also appears to assume that the verge can be used for passing. The verge is soft in winter and has an open grip behind it. I have repaired a customer’s gate after a van slid off the edge there; that is not a theoretical concern.

I have worked around Larkhollow for over 20 years and know that morning movements do not arrive evenly. School traffic, trades vans and the farm vehicles all tend to meet between 7.30 and 8.30. The construction traffic management plan gives an average number of HGVs per day, but an average does not tell us whether six will arrive together. It says drivers will be told not to wait on Cinder Lane. Where exactly will they wait if the compound gate is shut or a delivery is early? A driver cannot disappear because a sign says NO WAITING.

My son, Orrin Vale, aged 11, walks towards the village bus stop. There is no footway along the first part of that walk. We have managed with local traffic by stepping into gateways, but this is not a suitable arrangement for a convoy of unfamiliar drivers. I have been diagnosed with migraine, and repeated reversing alarms immediately outside the workshop would make it harder for me to work on days when symptoms occur. I am also worried about ordinary stress and poor sleep during the works. Those are separate concerns, not reasons to ignore the traffic problem.

Last Thursday I spoke to Mr Lyle Renn, who lives at 8 Sedge Fold, Larkhollow, LM4 8QN. This neighbour is not making a representation and I do not want that conversation treated as consent from anyone else. The point raised was practical: the hedge opposite the proposed holding point blocks the view from the side entrance. Cllr Sevan Orley made a similar point about visibility at the parish drop-in, although I understand the Council will send its own formal response.

There is also a wildlife survey issue. The submitted ecology plan marks badger activity in Brindle Wood, which is a fairly broad area. On my walk I saw what appeared to be a sett entrance under the southern hedge of plot C17, six metres east of gate G3. I am not qualified to confirm it, but the applicant should check before widening that gateway. This should not be taken as my agreement to shift the vehicle route closer to the houses.

I have tried to find the promised delivery booking procedure on the project website, https://www.dunmarshlink.example/traffic, but the page only contains the current overview plan. The Planning Inspectorate examination page at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate is useful for documents, not for knowing whom to telephone when a lorry blocks my exit at six in the morning. A project mailbox such as traffic@dunmarshlink.example would be helpful if somebody actually monitors it during deliveries. My own contact email above is for the case team’s correspondence, not for publication as a complaints line.

Please require a revised plan showing a proper off-lane holding area, a booking system with a maximum number of vehicles in each half-hour period, and a drawing of two-way movements at the pump house narrowing. It should specify who has authority to turn a vehicle back and what happens when an unscheduled load arrives. A condition saying that contractors should ‘avoid inconvenience’ is not enough. I would also ask for a site meeting at the narrow section before the traffic plan is signed off, with the drawing in hand rather than just a general assurance.

For a one-person business, a missed delivery is not simply a nuisance: I cannot send someone else to unload it while I wait for access. My take-home income for 2025 was £19,840, so repeated lost working mornings would matter. I ask the Examining Authority to address the access arrangements in the examination, rather than leave them for a contractor to sort out after consent.

Yours faithfully,

T. Vale, proprietor
Tamsin Vale Joinery

Further note on construction traffic – Dunmarsh Link Cable Project

From: Tamsin Vale
Business: Tamsin Vale Joinery
Correspondence address: 14 Sedge Fold, Merewick, MW4 8RP
Interested Party reference: IP-209415

I am sending this note after my letter because I have now checked the construction traffic drawing again. I still object to using Sedge Fold for regular HGV access. This is not an objection to the cable being put underground as such. It is about whether the access shown on drawing DML-TR-014 can actually be used while people are getting in and out of their properties and working premises. Mine is both: I run Tamsin Vale Joinery from home, and deliveries have to reach the workshop door.

The drawing measures the carriageway, but it does not show the places where a driver can safely stop. There is a bend just before my entrance. A lorry waiting for another lorry to clear that bend would be across the part of the road I use to reverse a timber delivery into the yard. The same is true if a vehicle arrives early and sits there for ten minutes. A booking system will only help if somebody checks bookings before vehicles enter Sedge Fold, not when they are already at the gate. I would like Dunmarsh Gridworks Ltd to say plainly where an early vehicle will wait and how the driver will be told not to continue.

I have been told to ring a number if access is blocked, but that puts all the work on the resident. My direct number is 07123 684 291; I am supplying it for contact about an arranged site visit, not as a substitute for a workable plan. For written replies, my email is tamsin.vale@tamsinvalejoinery.example. The project can use traffic@dunmarshgridworks.example as a shared address for notices, provided somebody actually reads replies before a delivery slot is changed. Please do not assume that a note pushed through the door the evening before is enough. I may already have booked a customer collection or a timber drop-off for the following morning.

For example, on 15 October I watched a rigid lorry use the bend while a van was stopped outside 9 Sedge Fold, Merewick, MW4 8RP. That is Mr Lyle Renn's house; Mr Lyle Renn is not involved in this examination, and I do not suggest the van was anything to do with the project. I mention the incident because the lorry had to pause with its rear over the centre of the road. It was an ordinary weekday situation, not an unusual obstruction. I noted the registration as MV26 KLT in case the dimensions of that vehicle are useful, although I do not know its operator.

There is also the matter of walking along this stretch. Orrin Vale, aged 11, has asthma, and dust hanging around the entrance after a vehicle passes is a particular worry for our household. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide a medical question. I am asking for a proper dust-control commitment that covers the road outside the work site, including sweeping when mud is tracked out and a way to report a problem without waiting for a monthly meeting. Saying only that dust will be ‘monitored’ does not tell us who will clean it up, or when.

Cllr Sevan Orley suggested at the parish drop-in that a marshal could stand at each end of the narrow section at peak times. That sounds more useful than a sign telling drivers to proceed with care, but the plan should state the marshal's hours and whether the arrangement applies to subcontractors. I have used the applicant's project page, https://dunmarsh-link.example/traffic, to look for a revised drawing and could not find one. A local discussion has also appeared at https://sedgefoldwatch.example/turning, though the examination should rely on measured plans rather than comments on a website.

One other point from the proposed route walk: the ecology material says badgers have been seen in Bracken Mere Wood. I am not asking for that general information to be hidden. I did, however, mark a badger sett immediately behind the north-east corner of the red-brick pump hut at plot DL-17, four metres from the eastern ditch on my copy of the plan. That precise mark should not be put on a public traffic drawing. It matters here only because an informal waiting or turning area must not be added there without an ecological check. There should be no need for a lorry to leave the agreed route to find somewhere to turn round.

Finally, I want to explain why a promise to compensate people after the event is not an answer. As I said in my letter, my take-home income for 2025 was £19,840. A customer who cannot collect a finished door may rearrange the rest of the job, and I cannot simply add another working morning to the week. I would much rather keep trading normally than make a claim for a loss that is difficult to prove afterwards.

Please require a revised traffic management plan before the access arrangements are approved. It should show a holding point away from Sedge Fold, a maximum number of HGV movements per day, the method for checking that every driver has a slot, and a named role with authority to turn an unscheduled vehicle back. It should also show how residents and businesses will be told about exceptional loads, and how deliveries will be managed if the road is blocked for another reason. Those are practical details which can be checked on a drawing. Without them, the assurance that access will be maintained is not much use to someone standing at the workshop gate with a delivery due.

The points above are access requirements, not an objection to the cable in principle. There are also some technical gaps in the current construction assessment which could be closed before the traffic management plan is signed off. I set these out below because the measures need to work together: a revised route drawing is of little use if the programme assumes two work fronts using the same narrow junction at once.

Traffic and access

The transport note for the Dunmarsh Link Cable Project uses an average daily HGV figure. An average conceals the days when excavated material leaves a section and bedding material arrives for the next one. Dunmarsh Gridworks Ltd should provide a day-by-day forecast for the busiest four-week period, split between inbound and outbound movements and between the northern and southern construction compounds. The forecast should state whether a vehicle making two visits is counted twice. It should also reconcile with the material quantities in the construction method statement; at present it is not possible to check that the assumed number of loads could move the stated volume of spoil.

Drawing DMLC-TR-014 Rev C shows the temporary access joining Sedge Fold close to the bend, but its swept-path lines end at the site gate. They should continue through the bend in both directions and show an opposing vehicle, not merely a single articulated lorry on an empty road. A plan should identify the clear width available after barriers, signs and any temporary drainage protection have been installed. If banksmen are proposed, the assessment should explain where they stand and how an approaching driver sees them. The same check is needed for the smaller vehicles expected to arrive outside the main delivery windows. Those movements can obstruct access just as effectively as an HGV if they wait on the carriageway.

The proposed route via Marshgate Road should be tested against a temporary closure of the access, not just ordinary operation. The fallback cannot be an instruction to use local roads without specifying which roads are suitable. A diversion for construction vehicles ought to be shown on a drawing, with the trigger for putting it into effect and the means of notifying drivers already on the way. The construction traffic management plan should record how compliance will be checked, including what happens when a booking is missed. An annual review would come too late for a trenching phase lasting only a few weeks; weekly review while deliveries are at their peak would be more useful.

Drainage and ground conditions

The flood-risk appendix describes temporary drainage as a matter for the contractor. That leaves a gap where the trench, haul road and compound drainage interact. The drawings should show the direction of runoff during each phase, the location and capacity of settlement measures, and the point at which treated water is discharged. A single final layout does not show what happens while topsoil is stripped but the permanent reinstatement is incomplete. The design should include an exceedance route for rainfall greater than the temporary system's design event, so that water is not directed along Sedge Fold or into the open trench.

The ground-level information for the southern compound appears to come from a coarser survey than the level information at the road edge. Before levels are fixed, there should be a consistent survey tied to one datum and a cross-section showing the temporary platform, ditch, road and any proposed bund. This would also make it possible to check whether the platform can be removed without leaving a raised lip that diverts water after construction. The maintenance schedule needs to say who checks silt controls after heavy rain and what condition would require work to stop. Referring generally to good practice is not an inspection regime.

Landscape, ecology and reinstatement

The landscape drawings should distinguish temporary construction screening from permanent planting. Some viewpoints are described as screened even though the relevant hedge is to be removed for the works and replanted afterwards. The visual assessment ought to test the interval between clearance and successful establishment, including a winter view. Where a temporary bund is relied on, its height and footprint need to match the drainage and access drawings. Otherwise the same strip of land is being allocated to several different purposes.

Badger setts have been recorded in East Rill Wood, and the ecology chapter discusses precautionary working methods. That broad description is adequate for the public-facing assessment; a general construction plan does not need to reproduce confidential survey mapping. What it does need is a clear sequence for checking the working corridor immediately before vegetation removal, briefing the workforce and stopping work if protected-species evidence is found. The reinstatement specification should give measurable standards for soil handling, hedge replacement and failed planting, with monitoring long enough to establish whether those standards have been met.

Programme and controls

Finally, the outline programme should be presented as a set of linked activities, rather than a single bar labelled cable installation. It should show when each compound opens, when road works start, the periods of peak deliveries, and when drainage and landscape reinstatement can actually begin. If the northern and southern works overlap, the combined vehicle forecast should be assessed. If they cannot overlap without exceeding the proposed traffic limit, that restriction should be written into the construction requirements rather than left as an assumption in the modelling.

I ask the Examining Authority to require updated, mutually consistent drawings and a secured approval process before these details are treated as resolved. This is about whether the proposed controls can be measured and enforced during construction. It is not necessary to settle the contractor's every working method now, but the limits within which that method must operate should be plain on the face of the approved documents.

Further to my comments on the drawings, I want to explain why the construction traffic limits matter to a small business on this road. I am Tamsin Vale and I run Tamsin Vale Joinery from my home at 14 Sedge Fold, Brindlewick, BN8 4QJ. This is a working workshop, not just an address where post is sent. Timber arrives in lengths that cannot be carried far by hand, and finished cupboards have to leave in a van without being tipped about. There is no yard elsewhere that I can use if access is blocked.

The traffic assessment treats Sedge Fold as though a vehicle either gets through or does not. That misses the ordinary delays caused by two large vehicles meeting at the bend, a reversing movement into the proposed compound entrance, or a delivery driver deciding the safest thing is to stop outside the houses. A ten-minute obstruction at 8 am can make a booked fitting visit impossible. Customers generally cannot wait in all morning while I find out whether the road is open. I have worked in this village for over 20 years and am used to farm and delivery traffic; I am not asking for a road with no lorries on it.

The swept-path drawing for Parcel CT-4 at Salt Mere Road shows the largest vehicle turning in under clear-road conditions. It does not show what happens when a supplier is unloading at my gate, or when a refuse vehicle is coming the other way. The applicant should identify an actual holding point for vehicles that arrive early, with enough room to turn around, rather than assuming drivers will find somewhere. The construction traffic management plan should say who will check the road before a convoy is released. It should also specify whether the banksman can stop a delivery, not merely wave it through once it has reached the bend.

I have been told that deliveries will be booked, but no one has said how I will know which days the heaviest loads are due. Please do not substitute a general newsletter for a useful notice. A weekly list of expected abnormal or multiple HGV movements, updated when it changes, would let me arrange my own deliveries and site visits. A same-day contact must be able to do something about a blocked entrance. Sending a complaint to a mailbox for a response several working days later would not get a kitchen unit out of my workshop that morning. A proposed shared address such as traffic@dunmarshlink.example is fine for the written record, provided there is also a person on duty who can deal with an immediate access problem.

There is a school walking route along the same narrow stretch. My child, Orrin Vale, aged 11, walks to the collection point; Orrin has asthma. I mention the condition because the present plan places an idling and vehicle-checking area beside that route, while describing emissions only at the wider network level. It is quite possible to move the check-in point away from the houses and the waiting children. Even without that change, the requirements should prohibit engines running while drivers wait for permission to enter. I worry about the dust and noise too, but worry by itself is not a substitute for a practical control.

Mr Lyle Renn, who lives at 6 Sedge Fold, Brindlewick, BN8 4QH, is not making a representation as far as I know. I mention the property only because the plan marks the passing place across its entrance, not on spare highway. The applicant needs to show what land it actually has permission to use, and where pedestrians go while a vehicle waits there. My understanding from the exhibition was that the passing place was temporary. The drawing now appears to leave part of it in place after reinstatement. Those two positions cannot both be right, and residents should not have to discover the answer when the kerbs are being laid.

Cllr Sevan Orley raised the lack of a continuous footway at the community meeting. That is a straightforward safety point, not an argument against the cable itself. A banksman stationed at the compound gate cannot see somebody coming round the Sedge Fold bend on foot. Please require a plan showing pedestrian priority, temporary barriers where they will fit, and how a person using a pushchair can pass without stepping into the carriageway. If the available width will not allow that, the plan should say when deliveries must stop so people can get through.

The verge widening also needs checking before it is treated as a quick fix for the swept path. The ecology appendix refers generally to badger setts in Fen Holt Wood, which does not tell residents much about the roadside works. In particular, a badger sett lies at the base of the third ash east of Gate 3 on the north verge of Salt Mere Road, exactly where the revised vehicle-tracking line cuts across the bank. I do not want that detail circulated in a public construction drawing. It does, however, need to be considered by the ecologist and by whoever approves the final highway layout. Widening the verge on paper is not a mitigation measure if it cannot lawfully or safely be built.

I ask the Examining Authority to secure a maximum number of HGV movements for each working day, defined delivery hours, a no-idling rule, advance notice of exceptional loads, and an access procedure that can be used by a home-based business. The limits should apply to the combined works, as I said above, rather than to each contractor separately. A record of arrivals, cancellations and complaints should be kept and made available for checking. Otherwise it will be impossible to tell whether a quiet week is being followed by twice the assumed traffic to catch up.

I can be contacted about access arrangements at tamsin.vale@tamsinvalejoinery.example, or on 07700 900 483, but I do not consent to either being printed in a public schedule. My interested party reference is IP-041826. I am asking for workable conditions, not a promise that building a cable will never be inconvenient. If the contractor knows the limits before pricing and scheduling the job, those conditions should be possible to follow.

Tamsin Vale Joinery
T. Vale
Proprietor

Further note to my written representation
Dunmarsh Link Cable Project — construction traffic
From: Tamsin Vale, Tamsin Vale Joinery

I am adding this note because the proposed traffic management plan does not explain what happens when a booked delivery cannot get through. My workshop is at my home, 7 Sedge Fold, Merrowick, MW4 6QJ. Customers do not normally come to the house, but timber and sheet materials do, and I take finished joinery out in a van. If a cable works vehicle is waiting across the entrance, telling my supplier to try again tomorrow is not a small adjustment. It can put back a fitting appointment as well as the delivery itself.

The drawings show a holding area at the Quarry Exchange works office, 18 Quarry Exchange, Merrowick, MW3 4PT. That is a workplace address, not where I am asking for special treatment. My concern is the last part of the route, where Sedge Fold narrows by the old pump house. Two vehicles cannot pass there without one reversing. The traffic plan counts arrivals at the compound gate but appears not to count vehicles turned round on the lane, vehicles sent back for an incorrect load, or subcontractors coming to look at the works. Those movements still pass our doors.

I have been here for 40+ years and have seen busy harvest weeks. That is not a reason to accept an unmanaged construction timetable. During the September consultation, Cllr Sevan Orley asked whether deliveries could be held outside school travel times. I understood the answer to be that this would be looked at, not that it had been agreed. The latest plan still says only that drivers will be ‘encouraged’ to avoid the busiest periods. I would like an enforceable booking window and an instruction that an early driver waits at the holding area, rather than at the pump house.

My child, Orrin Vale, aged 11, walks to the school bus stop at the end of the lane. Orrin has diagnosed asthma, and dust from vehicles accelerating past the house is a particular concern to me. I am worried about safety as well: the footway ends before the bend and there is no space for a child to step aside if a lorry mounts the verge. Please do not treat the school-run issue as answered by a note saying that all drivers will receive a route map. A map does not tell a driver that children are already on the lane at 8.10 in the morning.

Mr Lyle Renn, who lives at 11 Sedge Fold, Merrowick, MW4 6QJ, helped me measure the usable width beside the pump house. He is not making a representation and I have not asked him to join this examination. The clear width we measured was about 3.2 metres where the verge has broken away. I include that figure to explain why a banksman and a waiting area are needed, not as a substitute for a proper highway survey. A photograph taken from my gateway shows the bend, although the drawing in the application makes it look almost straight.

I spoke to Pella Norwick of Dunmarsh Gridworks Ltd at the public drop-in. I was told to email pella.norwick@dunmarshgridworks.example with any occasions when access was blocked. That may help after an incident, but it is not a traffic management measure. The project mailbox, traffic@dunmarshgridworks.example, would be more useful for publishing a weekly list of delivery slots and changes. I also ask that suppliers are given one number for the traffic marshal, rather than my personal mobile number, 07700 900 483. My own delivery driver should not have to negotiate separately with each works contractor.

For completeness, the hire van VRM VX26 NPL was sent down Sedge Fold during the survey week and reversed from the pump house. I cannot say whether that driver was working for the applicant; that is why the record of vehicle movements matters. The short clip I mentioned at the drop-in is at https://lane-notes.example/sedge-fold-turning. It shows the reversing manoeuvre, not a near miss, and I have no wish to exaggerate it. The applicant’s project page and the general guidance at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects do not answer the practical question of who can stop a vehicle entering the lane when the holding area is full.

There is also an ecology point which needs careful handling if the passing place is moved. The environmental drawings refer generally to badger activity in Brindle Copse; that description alone does not pinpoint anything. In my notes from the site walk, however, the badger sett is beneath the fallen ash at the north-east corner of Plot C17, 9 metres from gate G3. I give that detail to the Examination so that a revised passing place is not drawn over it. It need not appear in a public traffic notice. I am not asking the contractor to use wildlife as an excuse for putting the passing place outside somebody’s front door.

The cost to my business of one cancelled delivery is not the same as the project’s published £4.8 million traffic and access budget. Last month I paid £286 myself for a second delivery after a vehicle could not reach my gate. I am not seeking reimbursement through this representation; the example is why the conditions must deal with access in advance. I felt stressed trying to reorganise that job, but the request I make is a practical one: a daily booking limit covering all contractors, a staffed holding area, no waiting on Sedge Fold, and a published procedure for residents and suppliers when the route is obstructed.

Please add this note to my earlier letter. I would welcome a site visit at the bend before the traffic plan is finalised, with the highway authority present and the turning space measured on the ground. I can explain where my deliveries enter without asking anyone to take my word for the lane width.

Tamsin Vale Joinery
T. Vale
Proprietor

Additional note to my earlier letter – construction traffic on Sedge Fold
20 October 2026

From: Tamsin Vale, Tamsin Vale Joinery
Interested Party reference: IP-408719

I am sending this as an attachment because the proposed Construction Traffic Management Plan still seems to treat Sedge Fold as a line on a route map, rather than a lane people need to use while work is going on. My workshop is at 14 Sedge Fold, Brackenmere, KM7 4PQ. It is also my home. I make fitted cupboards and repair timber windows, and timber arrives on vehicles that cannot simply be parked elsewhere while a project convoy passes. I have worked from here for over 20 years. The problem is not whether a lorry can get through once, with the road empty. It is what happens when two different firms have booked the same narrow stretch at the same time.

The drawings for the Dunmarsh Link Cable Project show access to Works Compound C, Plot 18, Former Tile Field. That is a site address, not a resident's driveway. Between the compound turning and the bend by the old pump house there is no proper passing space. A driver who is told to wait there is effectively blocking deliveries to several properties. The swept-path drawing appears to assume that the verge is available for tyres, although it is soft after rain. I ask that the Examining Authority require a drawing based on a measured carriageway width and show where a timber delivery vehicle can pass a project vehicle without entering private land.

At the drop-in, Pella Norwick of Dunmarsh Gridworks Ltd said contractors would be given arrival slots. I was grateful for the explanation, but I could not find anything saying whether those slots include subcontractors, spoil wagons and vehicles delivering to the temporary compound. If each contractor runs a separate booking list, the limit is not a limit. Please make the limit a total for the lane, with a named person authorised to refuse an early arrival. The holding area should be staffed before the first vehicle is due, not opened when a queue has already formed. A driver should receive the holding-area address in advance and be told plainly that Sedge Fold is not the holding area.

There also needs to be a way for residents to report a blockage that works during the shift. A generic address such as traffic@dunmarshgridworks.example is useful for a written record, but an email answered the following day will not release a van at the bend. I would prefer a project telephone line answered by the traffic marshal, with calls logged and a short report published each month. Please do not publish callers' home numbers in that report. For my own deliveries I can be contacted on 07700 900 462, but that is not permission to circulate my number to every haulage firm. If a direct email contact is needed, it is tamsin.vale@tamsinvalejoinery.example; the project should still provide a shared route for general complaints.

The access arrangement matters for other households too. Mr Lyle Renn, who lives at 9 Sedge Fold, Brackenmere, KM7 4PT, mentioned to me that a delivery had already turned round in the entrance there. I am not speaking for my neighbour and have not asked for that household to be added to the examination. I mention it because asking residents individually to negotiate with drivers will not solve the underlying problem. The plan needs a clear instruction on what drivers do if the lane is occupied, and where they turn round without using a domestic entrance. It should also say who puts right verge damage and how quickly.

I have been trying to explain to Orrin Vale, aged 11, how the road will work during school mornings. Orrin has diagnosed epilepsy, so I am particularly concerned that the lane must remain usable by an ambulance if one is ever needed. I am not asking for a special traffic rule for my family; emergency access ought to be demonstrated for everyone along the route. Please include that test in the traffic plan, using the proposed barriers and signs in their actual positions. Saying that access will be maintained is not the same as showing how it can be maintained when a vehicle breaks down.

There is an ecology point connected with the same stretch. I have seen badger signs in Crowfen Wood, which is a broad area and not a reason by itself to reroute traffic. However, a sett entrance is under the eastern bank of the drainage ditch, 6 metres north of culvert C4 at field gate G12. I have not put a marker on the public route sketch because that detail should go to the ecological clerk of works, not onto signs for drivers. It is another reason not to use the verge as an informal passing place. A driver should not have to decide whether the bank will bear the weight of a loaded wagon.

Cllr Sevan Orley asked at the village meeting whether the traffic figures covered the cable works and the compound set-up at the same time. I did not hear a clear answer. Could the applicant provide a week-by-week table showing the busiest expected day, including both activities, and explain which days would require a marshal at the bend? The information should be understandable without having to add together several appendices. My concern is about the combined movements, not an objection to a particular contractor.

Finally, please make any access protocol an enforceable requirement rather than a promise in a newsletter. It should cover booking limits, the holding area, emergency passage, a contact number, recovery of broken-down vehicles and a way to review the arrangements if they do not work in practice. I do not want compensation or a private exception to the rules. I want to be able to keep working, and for other people to reach their homes, while the project is built.

Yours faithfully,
T. Vale
Proprietor, Tamsin Vale Joinery

Technical addendum — construction access and environmental controls

The access protocol requested above will only be useful if it is based on the busiest realistic construction day, rather than an average across the whole programme. The Construction Traffic Assessment for the Dunmarsh Link Cable Project gives a monthly profile, but its daily figures appear to describe cable delivery, trench excavation and compound servicing separately. Table 6-2 should also state the combined daily total, in both directions, for each phase. A vehicle going out empty after a delivery is still a movement on Sedge Fold. The assessment should say whether its figures count that return trip.

The proposed construction compound at Brackenmere is shown as the point where vehicles will wait before joining the cable route. The drawings do not make clear how many vehicles can be held there without blocking the gate or reversing onto the public road. A swept-path drawing for the largest vehicle expected during ordinary works would help. It should show a queue of at least two vehicles inside the compound, the gate open, and a vehicle passing in the opposite direction. If that cannot be achieved, bookings should be spaced to reflect the actual space available. A booking system is not, by itself, a physical holding area.

The assessment should distinguish between a normal working day and short periods when plant, trench boxes or cable drums arrive. Those deliveries are not frequent, but their effects at the bend could be greater. It would be helpful to have a simple timetable stating the anticipated maximum number of heavy goods vehicle movements in the morning, midday and afternoon periods. Any assumption that deliveries will avoid the school-run period ought to be written into the Construction Traffic Management Plan, with a procedure for refused or late vehicles. Further technical comments on the draft Construction Traffic Management Plan
Dunmarsh Link Cable Project

The traffic assessment should be revised before the Construction Traffic Management Plan is certified. Its weekday peak-hour tables treat the temporary compound at Brackenmere as a single destination, but the programme shows separate flows for cable drums, excavated material, welfare servicing and reinstatement. Combining those movements conceals the likely overlap between inbound deliveries and outbound spoil vehicles. A daily total is not enough to test the operation of the Sedge Fold junction. The assessment should provide hourly profiles for each construction phase, identifying the maximum number of heavy goods vehicle movements in each direction and the assumptions behind the proposed delivery slots.

The drawings also appear to assume that all construction vehicles will approach from the eastern distributor road. That should be an enforceable route, not merely the preferred route stated in a contractor handbook. The route plan needs to mark the point at which drivers receive instructions, the signed turning arrangement and the procedure for a vehicle that misses the turn. A statement that a driver will be directed back to the approved route does not explain where a large vehicle can turn without reversing on the highway. If a holding area is proposed, its capacity and operating hours should be shown on the same plan.

At the western bend on Sedge Fold, the swept-path drawing uses a clear carriageway width throughout. The measured highway width should instead be plotted at regular intervals, together with the usable width after temporary fencing, drainage protection and any parked construction plant are allowed for. The plan should distinguish the legal highway boundary from the surface actually available to traffic. It should also show whether two opposing vehicles can pass at the bend, or whether a marshal-controlled one-way section is required. A passing-place proposal would need its own land plan, visibility assessment and reinstatement specification; it cannot be left to detailed design after the route has been approved.

The assessment’s baseline counts were taken on two weekdays outside the main construction period. Those counts may be adequate for an ordinary junction-capacity exercise, but they do not establish the level of seasonal variation on this route. Before works begin, a seven-day automatic count should record vehicle classes and directions at both ends of Sedge Fold. The results should be compared with the modelled baseline and a threshold specified for reviewing delivery slots if observed traffic materially exceeds it. The review must occur before the busiest cable-installation phase, otherwise it will have little practical value.

The Construction Traffic Management Plan should state how compliance will be checked. Gate records can log arrival time, departure time, vehicle class and route declaration without recording details unrelated to the works. The monthly report should compare those records against the consented daily and hourly limits, identify exceptions and record corrective action. A limit expressed only as an ‘average working day’ would allow a concentrated peak while still appearing compliant over a longer period. The limit should therefore apply both per day and in each defined peak hour. Any departure from the approved route should be reported separately, even if the overall movement cap has not been exceeded.

Drainage is closely linked to the highway proposals. The compound drawing shows a stone-surfaced access, but the drainage note assumes that all runoff from it will infiltrate. No infiltration test result is identified for the access strip or the proposed wheel-wash location. The design should show the fall of the surface, the collection point for silty water and the means of preventing runoff from reaching the road during intense rainfall. Wheel-wash water must be contained and removed or treated under a stated maintenance regime. A line on a plan marked ‘temporary drainage’ is not a sufficient specification for a compound used through the winter earthworks period.

The drainage drawings should also be checked against the construction sequence. Open trenches, temporary stockpiles and haul roads change the direction and speed of surface flows. The present note considers the finished reinstated landform but says little about those interim conditions. Phase-specific plans should identify clean-water diversions, settlement capacity and the inspection arrangements before and after heavy rainfall. They should include a trigger for stopping earthmoving when the control measures are overwhelmed, rather than relying on a general instruction to keep the works tidy. This is a request for a workable construction method, not a change to the permanent drainage design.

On landscape effects, the photomontages use summer views for most receptors. The temporary compound will also be visible when roadside vegetation is not in leaf. A winter baseline photograph and a simple cross-section from the road would make the assessment more transparent. Screening should not be counted as effective at installation if it depends on new planting reaching its predicted height several years later. Temporary fencing colour, lighting orientation and maximum stockpile height are matters that can be fixed now. These details would give the landscape management plan measurable commitments rather than leaving the appearance of the compound to the eventual contractor.

The ecology note refers to badger activity in Crowfen Wood, which is a broad habitat description rather than a mapped location. The relevant construction controls can be set out without putting sensitive survey points into publicly available traffic drawings. In particular, the approved haul route should remain within its defined working width, with no informal passing bays cut into the woodland edge. Ecological checks before vegetation clearance and a clear procedure for unexpected field signs should sit alongside, not replace, the physical limits shown on the construction plans.

Finally, the draft requirements should tie these documents together. A revised traffic plan, phase-specific drainage drawings and the landscape controls ought to be approved before the relevant works start, with changes subject to a recorded approval process. Dunmarsh Gridworks Ltd should not be able to alter delivery hours through an informal site instruction while the certified assessment continues to show the original hours. If the examination concludes that these matters can be secured by requirement, the requirement should name the plans to be submitted, the authority that approves them and the stage at which approval is needed. That would make the commitments capable of being checked on the ground rather than remaining general assurances in separate reports.

Technical appendix – construction traffic, drainage and reinstatement
Dunmarsh Link Cable Project

This appendix sets out the technical points behind the request for a revised traffic management plan. It deals with the proposed construction route, the compound at Brackenmere and the associated trench works. It is not an objection to the principle of a buried cable. The issue is whether the submitted controls are detailed enough to make the construction effects predictable and enforceable.

The traffic assessment for Dunmarsh Gridworks Ltd uses a daily total for heavy goods vehicles, but the road is affected by the number of vehicles arriving within the same short period. A daily total can look modest while two deliveries, a spoil wagon and a water bowser all reach a narrow section together. The assessment should therefore show hourly arrivals and departures for each construction phase, including the peak week of trenching, rather than only an average day. It should distinguish rigid vehicles, articulated vehicles, low loaders and smaller vans. A swept-path drawing for a single design vehicle does not establish that opposing vehicles can pass, or that a vehicle can wait without blocking the carriageway.

The proposed route along Sedge Fold needs a chainage-based schedule of usable widths, bends, entrances and passing places. The drawings should state whether each width includes a soft verge; a verge that can be driven over in a computer model is not necessarily a place where a loaded vehicle can safely stand. Any proposed temporary widening should be drawn in plan and section, with the surface specification, drainage treatment and removal method. This is particularly important at the southern approach to Crowfen Wood, where the road alignment gives a limited view of anything waiting ahead. The final design should show the visibility available at vehicle eye height, not just a line on a plan.

The construction traffic management plan should also specify how deliveries are booked. Saying that movements will be ‘managed’ is not a workable instruction unless the documents identify a holding location, the maximum number of vehicles allowed to approach, and what happens when a booked vehicle is late. The holding location must have space for a vehicle to turn without reversing onto the public highway. A driver should not be sent along Sedge Fold in the hope that the compound gate is free. If escort vehicles are proposed, the plan should explain when they are required and how they will communicate with the compound. These matters should be in a certified plan or a requirement-approved document, not merely in a contractor briefing.

Pedestrian provision requires separate treatment from vehicle tracking. The current drawings indicate the carriageway edge but do not consistently identify a continuous place to walk during the works. A safe arrangement may vary by phase: a marked route beside the road in one section, a short signed diversion in another, and a timed closure where a trench crossing cannot be made safe. Whatever is selected should be shown on a phase plan with dimensions. It should cover access to field gates and the public footpath connection, and state how temporary barriers will be inspected after high winds. A general commitment to maintain access ‘where practicable’ leaves too much to be decided once plant is already on site.

There is a related drainage issue. The compound layout shows a stone surface and perimeter measures, but it is unclear where runoff will go during a prolonged wet period or how sediment will be kept out of the roadside ditch. The drainage note should provide the contributing area, design rainfall event, allowance for climate change, storage volume and proposed discharge rate. It should also show the route taken by water if the normal system is exceeded. The ditch cannot be treated as spare capacity without a survey of its levels and outfall. The pre-construction condition survey should cover existing grips and culverts, with photographs taken before any temporary widening is installed.

The cable trench programme needs to be read alongside that drainage design. Open trench lengths should be limited by a stated maximum, with spoil stored so that it cannot wash back into the ditch. The working drawings should identify where clean water is diverted around an excavation and where water from an excavation is held for treatment before discharge. Simply referring to ‘standard pollution prevention measures’ is not enough to establish which equipment must be available at the workface. The same applies to reinstatement: the method should state how compacted ground is broken up, how topsoil is separated from subsoil, and what inspection is required before a temporarily used verge is handed back.

The landscape material could also be clearer about the difference between temporary and permanent effects. The photomontages for the Brackenmere compound appear to assume screening at the end of the planting establishment period. The examination would benefit from a construction-year view, when fencing, lighting and stacked materials are most apparent and planting has not yet grown. Lighting should be shown by direction and hours of use, with a requirement to turn off non-essential fittings outside active shifts. A planting drawing on its own cannot control temporary light spill.

The ecological survey summary refers to badger activity in Crowfen Wood. That is a broad survey finding, not a basis for identifying any protected feature in this appendix. The relevant technical point is that the construction method should make clear how pre-start checks are recorded and how work is paused if a protected feature is encountered. Any detailed location information should remain in the appropriate confidential ecological material, rather than being added to public traffic drawings.

I ask that these matters be resolved through revised, numbered plans with a clear approval route. The examination does not need to choose a contractor’s equipment, but it does need to establish the limits within which the contractor must work. A table linking each promised measure to a drawing, construction phase and securing requirement would make it much easier to check whether the final scheme delivers what is now being described.

Further to my comments on the ecological appendix, I want to bring the response back to the practical problem for our end of Sedge Fold: the construction traffic. I am submitting this as Tamsin Vale, proprietor of Tamsin Vale Joinery, from my home at 14 Sedge Fold, Brackenmere, BM4 8QX. My Interested Party reference is IP-42861. This is a small joinery business, not a yard with a loading bay or a second entrance. I do not object to the Dunmarsh Link Cable Project simply because it involves building work. I object to the traffic arrangements Dunmarsh Gridworks Ltd has put forward for Brackenmere. Drawing CT-07 marks Sedge Fold as suitable for light construction vehicles, but the distinction between light vehicles and delivery vehicles is not carried through into a delivery schedule. A van with a long roof load, a trailer or a crew cab towing equipment can occupy just as much of the bend as a lorry. Please define the vehicle types by dimensions, not just by what a contractor calls them.

The bend outside my gate is where a supplier normally stops for two or three minutes while I take timber off the van. I cannot move that delivery indoors. If a project vehicle comes down from the compound at the same time, one of us has to reverse towards the Brackenmere junction. I have been trading from here for 40+ years in the area, and I know how often a driver unfamiliar with the lane misjudges that manoeuvre. The swept-path sheet appears to assume that the verge can be driven over. It cannot be treated as spare carriageway without a drawing showing what will be strengthened and who will put it back.

My own business email above is for correspondence about this submission, not a public complaints contact. Please require a staffed number for the traffic manager during delivery hours, and require the number and any exceptional delivery date to be supplied to affected households in advance. I would also like a record of complaints and what happened in response, available to the examining or enforcing authority. That seems more useful than simply counting complaints at the end of the month.

My child Orrin Vale, aged 11, sometimes walks with me to the village stop. Orrin has asthma, so I pay attention to dust as well as to the size of vehicles. I am not asking the examination to decide anyone’s medical needs; the point for the traffic plan is that walking past idling vehicles on this narrow stretch is avoidable. Dust-control measures and a no-idling instruction should apply at the compound gate, not only inside the site. The noise of deliveries already makes me feel anxious about keeping workshop appointments, although that is a concern rather than a medical diagnosis.

I have worked in Brackenmere for over 20 years and do not object to every construction vehicle. Cllr Sevan Orley suggested that residents and businesses be shown the gate layout before works start, and I think that is a sensible way of finding obvious problems early. The applicant’s project page, https://dunmarshlink.example/traffic, contains the general route map but not the detailed turning arrangement. I have also seen comments at https://brackenmere-ledger.example/traffic; I am not relying on that page as evidence and include it only to distinguish it from the applicant’s material.

Lastly, I mentioned Crowfen Wood in my first letter as a place where badgers have been seen. That is a broad observation, not a surveyed sett location. Someone later pointed out a possible sett inside the culvert mouth 6 metres north of the eastern gate of Crowfen Wood, at drawing point CF-17. I cannot verify it and ask that the detail be passed only to the ecologist rather than printed on a public route plan. It does not alter my main request: please fix a morning limit on two-way heavy-vehicle movements, provide holding space inside the compound, and have the turning arrangement inspected before the route is used.

Yours faithfully,
Tamsin Vale Joinery

Technical addendum: construction access and environmental controls
Dunmarsh Link Cable Project

This addendum sets out the technical changes requested in the letter above. It deals with the assessment and the proposed requirements for the Dunmarsh Link Cable Project, rather than repeating the observations about the route. The points below could be resolved through revised drawings and a construction traffic management plan before the compound is brought into use.

The transport assessment gives a daily total of heavy goods vehicle movements, but a daily total does not show whether the access will work during the busiest part of the morning. The assessment should provide an hourly profile for each construction phase, with arrivals and departures shown separately. It should distinguish deliveries to the main compound from vehicles serving the cable trench, spoil movements and any temporary works at the crossing. Otherwise a reader cannot tell whether apparently modest daily totals conceal several vehicles arriving together. The junction capacity calculation should use those phase-specific peaks, not an average spread evenly across the working day.

The swept-path drawings also need to show two-way operation. A drawing of one vehicle entering an empty junction proves very little where another vehicle may be leaving the compound. Please show the design vehicle passing a departing vehicle at the gate, including the effect of any waiting vehicle and the full swept area of the trailer. The drawing should identify where the gate opens, where a driver stops for checks and whether a vehicle can wait wholly within the compound without projecting onto Sedge Fold. The visibility assessment should be based on the actual position from which a driver can see, rather than a point that can be reached only after the cab has entered the carriageway.

For the section of Sedge Fold beside the compound, the applicant should submit a width schedule at regular chainages and at each pinch point. That schedule needs to state whether the width includes usable hardstanding or only the surfaced carriageway. Soft verges cannot be treated as a passing place simply because a vehicle could physically mount them. A plan should mark every proposed passing place, its construction specification, drainage arrangement and the period for which it would remain available. If the assessment assumes that traffic will give way at a particular location, that assumption should be written into the traffic plan and checked against forward visibility in both directions.

A booking system may help, but it is not a substitute for a physical holding area. The plan should give the number of heavy vehicles that can stand inside the compound while a delivery is checked or unloaded. It should prohibit off-site queuing and explain what happens when an early vehicle arrives or the unloading area is occupied. A simple instruction to drivers to avoid peak periods will be difficult to enforce unless the permitted hours, vehicle limits and exception procedure are set out in the approved plan. The monitoring return should record actual arrival and departure times so that compliance can be checked against the modelled figures.

The construction programme should link these measures to phases. The access may have a different level of use while the compound is being established, during cable installation and during reinstatement. A single drawing labelled ‘construction access’ does not establish that the same arrangement is suitable throughout. Before each phase begins, the relevant traffic schedule and swept-path check should be confirmed against the equipment and vehicle types actually proposed. If a different vehicle is required, the drawings should be updated before it uses the route.

Drainage at the gate is a separate practical issue. The submitted layout appears to direct runoff towards the verge, but it does not show levels across the full width of the access or where silt-laden water would go during a heavy rainfall event. A revised plan should include finished levels, the position and capacity of any interception drain, and a maintenance point that can be reached without closing the carriageway. Wheel washing should be shown on the compound side of the gate, with enough surfaced distance for vehicles to drain before reaching Sedge Fold. The construction environmental management plan should specify how deposited mud will be inspected and removed, rather than relying on cleaning only after a complaint.

For landscape assessment, the distinction between temporary disturbance and permanent change needs to be clearer. The drawings should show the maximum extent of temporary vegetation removal, the working width and the areas where soil will be stored. The visualisations should use the same compound boundary as the engineering plans. They should also include a winter view from the publicly accessible route at Crowfen Wood, when screening is least effective. That is a request for a representative public viewpoint, not for any location connected with wildlife. Reinstatement should be tied to a planting specification, aftercare period and replacement trigger for failed planting; the phrase ‘landscaping as necessary’ is not an adequate commitment.

These are matters capable of being secured without changing the principle of the proposal. Dunmarsh Gridworks Ltd could submit a revised traffic plan and access drawing before construction starts, followed by phase-specific updates where the approved assumptions change. Brackenmere Borough Council should have a defined opportunity to review the road-width schedule, drainage detail and monitoring returns. The requirement should say which documents take precedence if the transport assessment, environmental statement and later contractor plan contain different vehicle figures. As drafted, those figures are not easy to compare.

I ask the Examining Authority to seek one consolidated schedule of commitments showing the measure, the drawing or plan that contains it, the point at which it must be approved and who checks it on site. That would make the proposed controls understandable and testable. Without it, the useful detail is scattered across documents and the central question—whether the access can safely accommodate the busiest construction hour—remains unanswered.

I also want to explain what those figures mean for somebody who has to use Sedge Fold as a working access, rather than just a line on the transport drawings. I run Tamsin Vale Joinery from my home at 14 Sedge Fold, Brackenmere, BM4 8QZ. My van goes out with fitted units and comes back with timber, often at times that do not fit a standard commuter peak. I cannot simply leave it in a yard elsewhere: loading and unloading are part of the business I operate from this address.

The proposed compound at Brackenmere would put construction vehicles on the same narrow approach. The swept-path drawing shows a lorry turning at the compound entrance, but it does not show what happens when a van is waiting to turn into Sedge Fold or when an oncoming delivery vehicle has stopped opposite the cottages. In practice, drivers wait where they can see each other. That is sometimes in front of a gate. A drawing that assumes the road is clear for every movement is not an adequate test of the busiest hour.

I have already told Dunmarsh Gridworks Ltd that deliveries to my workshop cannot all be moved outside construction hours. At the public drop-in, Pella Norwick of Dunmarsh Gridworks Ltd suggested that residents could ring the contractor when a delivery was expected. I appreciate that this was meant as a practical suggestion, but it would not give a timber supplier control of its arrival time or tell an approaching lorry driver where to wait. Nor should access to an existing business depend on my being able to reach somebody by phone on the day.

There is a school walk along this stretch as well. My child, Orrin Vale, aged 11, uses the footway by the proposed haul-route junction. The footway ends before the bend and people cross there to carry on towards the village. Orrin has asthma, so I am particularly concerned about idling vehicles close to the crossing point, as well as the obvious issue of a child and a turning HGV occupying the same space. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide how my family makes that journey. I am asking it to ensure the crossing movement is counted and shown on a plan, including where pedestrians would stand if two construction vehicles meet.

Mr Lyle Renn, who lives at 9 Sedge Fold, is not taking part in the examination but has also had delivery vehicles pause across the shared turning area. I mention that only because the turning area is drawn as if it were spare highway width. It is used to reach homes. I do not consent to it being treated as a holding bay, and the contractor should not be instructed to use it as one. Cllr Sevan Orley asked at the Brackenmere meeting whether a marshal would be present at the junction throughout the working day; the answer recorded in my notes was that this was still to be settled. The final traffic plan should settle it before works start, not after complaints.

The applicant's material also needs a workable procedure for changes. If the principal contractor changes its delivery booking system, vehicle size or shift times, residents should not have to discover the change when the first vehicle arrives. Please require a published weekly delivery window for unusually long loads, a named role with authority to turn away unbooked HGVs, and a record of vehicles that arrive outside the approved hours. I would like the monitoring returns sent to Brackenmere Borough Council and placed with the project documents. A generic complaints address, traffic@dunmarshgridworks.example, may be useful, but an acknowledgement is not the same as a remedy when an entrance is blocked.

Drainage is connected to the traffic issue. The verge on the Crowfen Wood side holds water after rain and lorries will need all the usable road width at the bend. If temporary widening is proposed, the plan should say how the ditch will keep working and where the original edge of the carriageway will be reinstated. I have seen badger signs in Crowfen Wood; that is a general observation, not a survey. However, the particular badger sett shown in the applicant's ecology appendix—under the eastern bank of Drain 4, 18 metres north of the Crowfen Wood gate—should not be repeated on a public traffic-management drawing. Any measures needed there can be passed directly to the ecologist and the highway contractor without displaying its position to everyone downloading the road plan.

For clarity, I am not objecting to the cable itself or arguing that no construction vehicle can ever use this road. I am objecting to approving an access arrangement whose operation is left to informal conversations. I have traded here for 40+ years, and a few weeks of unreliable access at the wrong point in an installation programme can mean jobs cannot be finished when promised. I have a business account, but the overdraft of £4,800 is mine personally; I cannot fund repeated cancelled deliveries while the traffic arrangements are being worked out. My concern is about a foreseeable practical effect, not a request for compensation in this examination.

My reference for this representation is IP-628417. I have put a sketch of the gate positions with my earlier submission and can provide a clearer copy if the case team needs one. Please keep my home address and direct contact details off the public version of this letter. I can be contacted at tamsin.vale@tamsinvalejoinery.example or 07700 900 418 for questions about the sketch. I used https://brackenmere-roadwatch.example/lorry-count to note the existing delivery pattern; it is my own working tally, not an official traffic count. The examination timetable at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects-the-examination is helpful, but I could not find a deadline specifically for correcting access drawings.

Yours faithfully,

T. Vale, proprietor, Tamsin Vale Joinery

To the Examining Authority
Merewick Fen Solar and Grid Scheme
21 October 2026

Dear Inspectors,

I am writing about the proposed solar panels and the cable works near Brindle Mere. I am 15 and in Year 10 at Brindle Mere Academy. I know young people can send comments because our geography teacher showed us the examination page, but I wasn't sure if I had to write in a very formal way. These are my own words. I haven't copied what my parents said, although they helped me find the right place to send this.

I don't think solar power is a bad idea. We learn about climate change at school and I would rather have electricity made without burning things. What worries me is how much of the land around here would change all at once, and how long the building work would go on. The application makes it sound tidy when it shows coloured blocks on a map. From our bus, the fields are where you can actually see the sky. I don't know how to explain that as a planning issue, but it matters when it's where you grow up.

I get the bus past the eastern fields most school days. The proposed construction entrance seems very close to the bend where the bus sometimes has to wait for a tractor. Could the Examining Authority ask Fenlight Infrastructure Ltd to show what happens there at school-bus times, not just at an average time of day? The traffic drawings I've seen show vehicles as arrows. An arrow doesn't show what it feels like when a lorry is next to a bus and everyone is trying to get to school. I know the drivers will have rules, but the junction is awkward even without extra traffic.

My friends Lottie Venn and Ishan Pellar walk along the path beside the drainage ditch after school. We use it because the main road has no proper pavement for part of the way. The documents say some paths will stay open, but I couldn't tell whether that means the whole route or only bits of it. If a fence sends us onto the road, even for a few months, that isn't a small change for pupils who walk. Please could there be one simple map showing the route during each stage of construction, with any closed sections clearly marked? It needs to be something people can understand on a phone, not only on a large drawing.

I went to the information event with my mum. A person there said the panels would be screened by planting, which sounded good, but then the picture showed trees already as tall as the fence. New trees don't look like that. Nia Corven pointed this out too. I would like the inspectors to look at what we will see in the first few years, not only at what it might look like when I am grown up. Please don't take this as me saying there should be no planting. Planting along the path could be brilliant if it is cared for and does not block the view at the crossing.

There is wildlife here as well, although I don't know enough to say what species need special protection. We have seen badgers in Brindle Wood, and I heard someone at the event say there were no signs near the paths we use. Last spring I saw a badger sett under the fallen ash 12 metres east of the stile on Footpath BM7. I am mentioning it because the survey should check properly before anyone starts clearing that strip, not because I want people going to look for it. There are also bats over the playing field on warm evenings. I can't tell what kind they are. Would the temporary lights be turned off when nobody is working?

The noise part is hard for me to judge. The report gives numbers, but at home we already hear the grain dryers at certain times and I don't know whether those sounds were included. I have had poor sleep when there is a lot going on, and thinking about months of reversing alarms makes me anxious. My younger brother's asthma means dust is something our family pays attention to as well. I'm not saying the scheme will make anybody ill. I am asking for clear rules about dust, working hours and who residents can tell if the rules aren't followed. A phone number on a board at the gate would help more than a promise hidden in an appendix.

Cllr Merrit Solway said at our school assembly that people should comment on the parts they actually know. That is why I have written mostly about the journey to school and the paths. I've read some of MWFG/EX/12, but I haven't read every document and I hope that doesn't mean my comments count for less. The project mailbox, merewickfen@fenlight.example, sent an automatic reply when I asked where the path plan was, but I couldn't find an answer to that question in it.

If the scheme goes ahead, please make sure pupils can get around safely throughout the works, and that the applicant checks the wildlife and shows realistic views of the new planting. I would also like the construction information to be written so people my age can understand what will happen and when. We will be living with the result for a long time, so it seems fair that we should be able to follow the plans now.

Yours faithfully,
Tamsin Quillan

Email: ada.merrin@post.invalid
Interested Party reference: IP-604182

I object to the proposed increase in flights and the associated changes to road access. I am writing about the health evidence because the figures in the Environmental Statement do not describe what it is like to live here. I have lived in Ternwick for over 20 years. My house is near the route used by cars going to the aerodrome, and I can hear aircraft on many days, although I appreciate that noise is a separate topic in the examination. I am not asking the Examining Authority to assume that every symptom I have is caused by the aerodrome. I am asking for a proper account of what additional pollution at homes, schools and bus stops will mean in practice.

I have been diagnosed with moderate persistent asthma. My GP prescribed a salbutamol inhaler for sudden symptoms and a beclometasone preventer inhaler for regular use. These are not details I would normally put in a public letter, but it seems impossible to explain my concern without them. On days when traffic is queuing past Wrenbank Close, I keep the front windows shut. I cannot prove what proportion of the fumes comes from airport journeys rather than other traffic. The road assessment appears to treat those journeys as if their timing doesn't matter very much, when in the morning they can arrive in a bunch. Please do not read this as a claim that the applicant has caused my diagnosis.

I also have a diagnosis of chronic migraine and take sumatriptan when an attack begins. The noise of reversing vehicles at night and the smell from idling engines can make an already difficult day worse. I know that a personal experience is not a substitute for monitoring. It does, however, explain why the assumption that an annual average tells the whole story worries me. There are days when I can manage an ordinary walk, and days when I have to turn back at the corner because the traffic has built up. The examination should look at short peaks as well as yearly figures, especially at the times children are walking to school.

My daughter, Leni Vale, aged 9, has autism spectrum disorder. Changes to routine and heavy traffic outside the school gate are particularly hard for my daughter to manage. This is not an argument that disabled children can never live near transport infrastructure. It is a request that the applicant consider the route between the estate and Bracken Fold School, including the wait at the crossing, rather than drawing a circle round the school building and calling it assessed. I do not consent to my child's name or medical information being used in promotional material or repeated in an open meeting. I have included it here only so the examination understands why the route matters to our household.

At an appointment, Dr Mara Fenwick of Ternwick Vale Medical Practice advised me to keep a note of when symptoms occur. I have done that intermittently since April 2026, but the notes are not a clinical study and I am not submitting the notebook. I would rather the applicant provide usable monitoring and clear information on the assumptions behind its traffic forecasts. For example, is the assessment based on all staff arriving at evenly spaced times? What happens when a delayed shift overlaps with school drop-off? The documents may answer this somewhere, but I have not found it in the non-technical summary.

I feel anxious when I see a long line of stationary vehicles outside the house, and I sometimes sleep badly after a busy evening. My wellbeing is affected by the uncertainty as much as by the traffic itself. Those statements describe how I feel; I am not offering them as further diagnoses. I understand that cleaner aircraft and electric vehicles may improve things in future. At present, the buses, delivery vans and private cars using the approach road are a real part of the project. Please assess the whole journey to the site, not just activity inside its boundary.

At the community session Cllr Orla Venn asked whether monitoring would continue after opening. I thought that was a sensible question. A public dashboard, with readings shown by time of day and an explanation when equipment is offline, would be more useful to residents than a single annual statement. The applicant could use a shared mailbox such as airquality@skylarkreach.invalid for questions, so that people do not have to send private health details to individual employees. I would also welcome a simple way of reporting a recurring queue without having to photograph drivers or vehicle number plates.

I have read the section about planting near Ternwick Wood. There are reports of badger setts somewhere in the wood, but I do not know where they are and am not making a claim about a particular sett. Planting may be valuable for ecology and screening. It should not be presented as a replacement for reducing emissions at the source. Likewise, telling residents to close windows is not a reasonable long-term mitigation measure for a scheme intended to operate for decades.

I ask the Examining Authority to require clearer peak-hour air quality modelling for the residential road and the school walking route, a monitoring plan that the public can understand, and a commitment to review traffic measures if observed conditions are worse than predicted. I am willing to answer questions about what I have seen, but I do not want my household's clinical information circulated more widely than necessary. My objection is to the adequacy of the assessment and proposed mitigation, not to the people who work at the aerodrome.

Ada Merrin
