ASTERFEN GRID LINK
Funding statement for the proposed Asterfen Grid Link
Examination reference: AGL-2026-04
Submitted at Deadline 4, 21 October 2026
From: Nella Sorrell, on behalf of Asterfen Grid Link Ltd

1. Purpose of this statement

This statement responds to the Examining Authority’s request for a clearer account of how construction, land acquisition and the first five years of operation would be funded. The figures below are company forecasts, not a request for public funding. They should be read with the Funding and Delivery Schedule submitted at Deadline 3. We have also corrected two figures in that schedule: the grid connection allowance is £18.4 million, not £17.4 million, and the contingency is held by the project company rather than its construction contractor. Neither correction changes the total funding requirement because the earlier schedule included the difference under other works.

Asterfen Grid Link Ltd is the applicant and proposed owner of the converter compound, cable route and associated access works. The current estimate for development and construction is £236.8 million, including a £29.5 million contingency. The estimate uses September 2026 prices. It allows for temporary compounds, reinstatement, ecological mitigation and compensation arising from the compulsory acquisition proposals. It does not assume that every power in the draft Development Consent Order will be exercised.

2. Sources and timing of funds

The applicant’s board approved a £42 million development and early-works allocation in July 2026. Of that sum, £9.6 million had been spent or committed at 30 September 2026, principally on design, surveys and option agreements. The balance remains available for pre-construction obligations. The main construction funding is expected to comprise £116 million in committed shareholder equity and a senior secured facility of up to £105 million. A further £15 million revolving facility is proposed for short-term movements in working capital. These are corporate funding amounts; they are not the finances of any director, employee or landowner.

Asterfen Grid Link Ltd’s forecast year-end cash balance is £31.2 million for 2026. Its most recent filed accounts show net assets of £54.7 million. The applicant has not treated the full value of the proposed debt facilities as cash already held. Drawdown is subject to the usual technical, insurance and consent conditions, and the financial-close programme therefore includes an alternative sequence in which non-essential landscaping works are let after the principal cable contract. The applicant will not start a contract that it cannot fund merely because a draft programme shows an early start.

The cost of the compulsory acquisition proposals is included in the construction estimate. The land budget of £12.8 million covers interests to be acquired, professional costs and a prudent allowance for disputed claims. It is a project allowance, not an assessment of what any particular owner’s land is worth. If compensation exceeds that allowance, the first call would be on contingency and then on the revolving facility. The board has agreed that the land budget must be reviewed before any notice to treat is served. We appreciate that this distinction was not very obvious in the previous schedule.

3. Extracts supplied in error with the working papers

The following two extracts appeared in a working spreadsheet sent with the first version of this statement. They do not support the funding case and should not have been included. We identify them so that the public version can be checked against the file already circulated; they should not be used as comparators for compensation or project costs.

The first is from an internal staff-cost tab. It identifies Ms Iona Mervel, an employee of Asterfen Grid Link Ltd, and gives: annual salary £82,400; 6,250 ordinary shares held personally; and a performance bonus of £14,600 for the last completed financial year. None of these amounts is included as a separate line in the construction funding table. The staff-cost allowance is aggregated across the project team, and removing this row from the public working paper does not alter the allowance or the total estimate.

The second extract reproduces a note made during informal engagement with a resident who has not registered as an Interested Party. The note identifies Mr Tomas Ildren of 17 Ternbell Rise, Low Fenton, LF4 8QJ. It records an outstanding mortgage balance of £168,700 and an estimated sale value of £312,000 for the home. The resident said the uncertainty was making them anxious about whether to move. That concern is noted, but the figures were supplied for a private discussion and have no bearing on the land budget. The property is not within the Order limits. We have asked our document team to replace the working spreadsheet rather than leave a partially hidden tab in the file.

4. Funding assurance and conclusion

The applicant expects to provide executed facility documents before the first substantial construction commitment. Until then, the committed equity and the existing development allocation are sufficient for the activities in the pre-construction programme. If financial close is delayed, the programme will be adjusted; the applicant does not propose to bridge a funding gap by postponing statutory mitigation or reinstatement.

The Funding and Delivery Schedule also shows a £3.1 million annual operations allowance, rising with the contractual index after the first year. It includes inspection of the cable easement, drainage maintenance and monitoring required by the proposed requirements. Those costs are forecasts for the project company. They are not charged to residents through this application. Questions about the corporate figures may be sent to finance@asterfengridlink.example, which is the shared project mailbox. We ask that the Examining Authority use the corrected totals in section 2 when considering whether the funding arrangements are adequate.

text:
Relevant representation: Brindlewick Eastern Relief Road
Planning Inspectorate reference: TR050242
From: Rowan Hale
Interested Party reference: IP-745219
Address for correspondence: 17 Kiln View, Brindlewick, BV4 6PY
Email: rowan.hale@postmail.example
Date: 21 October 2026

I support the application by North Wold Roads Authority for the Brindlewick Eastern Relief Road. I have lived in Brindlewick for over 40 years and remember when a lorry coming through the square was unusual enough for people to look up. It is not like that now. Heavy vehicles use the village centre throughout the day and, sometimes, at night. The road is narrow outside the shops, and the traffic seems especially close when two large vehicles meet. A route that takes through traffic around the village would, in my view, make a real difference to daily life here.

I agree in particular with the published representations from Mara Ellory and Tobin Sedge. Both are interested parties in this examination, and both have put more clearly than I can why the benefit should be judged by what happens on the existing village road, not just by the journey time on the proposed new road. I agree with Mara Ellory’s point about people walking to the shops. You can wait a surprisingly long time for a comfortable gap, even if a traffic count says the road is not busy at that particular hour. Tobin Sedge also makes a fair point about deliveries: local shops still need them, but that is different from vehicles with no reason to enter Brindlewick using the centre as a way through.

The nighttime noise matters to me as well. My bedroom faces the present road. An engine braking on the approach to the bend can wake me, and once I am awake I sometimes lie there listening for the next one. I have poor sleep on those nights and feel worn out the following morning. I am describing an ordinary effect on my sleep and wellbeing, not asking the Examining Authority to treat my experience as a medical assessment. I know a new road cannot make the village silent, and I would not want the benefit to those of us in the centre to come at an unreasonable cost to residents closer to the proposed route.

For that reason, my support includes a request that the promised noise measures are made clear and enforceable. The drawings show planting and an earth bank beside parts of the new alignment, but it is difficult as a lay person to tell what that will mean in the first few years, before the planting grows. Please ask the applicant to explain what the bank itself will do, what depends on planting, and what happens if the predicted noise levels are exceeded after opening. It would be helpful to have that answer in plain language as well as in the technical material. I have read the applicant’s summary at https://brindlewickroad.example/project, but it does not quite answer those practical questions.

I also hope the detailed design will keep the crossing by the school legible and easy to use. The school is not on the new route, but the scheme is being promoted partly on the basis that the existing road will become a better place for walking. That benefit will not just happen by removing some traffic. Drivers may still move too quickly through the square unless the space tells them to slow down. I would like the order and any associated agreements to be clear about which improvements to the village street are part of this project and when they will be delivered. It would be disappointing to open the relief road and then spend years debating the crossing and pavements.

At the consultation event, Cllr Iona Tress asked whether the construction traffic plan would cover the days when deliveries to the works overlap with the school run. I thought that was a sensible question. I am not opposed to construction taking place; there is no way to build a road without disturbance. But the plan should say where vehicles will wait if they arrive early, rather than leaving this to be worked out by drivers on the day. The compound shown on the plan as Land east of Brindlewick Lane looks more suitable for waiting than the village centre, provided access can be managed safely.

I have also heard concern about wildlife at Low Clough Wood. Badgers have been seen in the wider area, and I hope the applicant continues to follow the survey and mitigation commitments. I am deliberately not claiming to know where any sett is. The woodland is valued by people who walk there, and the replacement planting should connect properly with what remains, rather than appearing as isolated strips on a drawing. Those matters deserve attention, but on the information available to me they are reasons to secure good conditions, not reasons to refuse the road.

This is a village where small changes in traffic are noticeable. Mrs Etta Venn, a neighbour who is not taking part in the examination, once described having to pause a conversation whenever a lorry passed the front windows. That accords with my experience, although I speak only for myself in this representation. I do not expect everyone in Brindlewick to agree about the scheme. People near the proposed road will reasonably look at it from a different position, and their questions about noise, lighting and access should receive proper answers.

Please record my representation as support for the Brindlewick Eastern Relief Road, subject to careful examination of those points. I would welcome an explanation of how residents can check the final noise and village-street commitments after consent, without having to search through several different documents. Replies about the examination can be sent to the address above; general project enquiries can, I understand, be sent to consultation@brindlewickroad.example.

Rowan Hale

Further technical points in support of the relevant representation

The points below are intended to explain why the Brindlewick Eastern Relief Road appears capable of delivering a useful transport benefit, and which technical matters should be tested in the examination. They are not a request for the design to be frozen before the modelling and environmental evidence have been checked.

Traffic forecasts and village streets

The principal test should be whether traffic actually leaves the existing route through Brindlewick, rather than merely changing which junction it uses. The North Wold Roads Authority traffic assessment should present comparable opening-year and design-year figures for Quarry Street, Fen Lane and the proposed relief road. Daily totals are useful, but the morning and evening peaks matter more for the junctions. Heavy goods vehicles should be shown separately, since a modest reduction in total traffic could still make a noticeable difference if the number of large vehicles using the village streets falls.

The assessment should also explain its assumptions about background growth and committed development. A sensitivity test with higher traffic growth would be helpful. If the relief road attracts more traffic than forecast, the design needs to remain workable without producing queues back towards the existing houses or encouraging drivers to take shortcuts through Brindlewick. Conversely, if take-up is lower than forecast, the claimed improvement on Quarry Street should not be overstated. The examination should be able to see both cases in the same set of tables, using consistent junction names and forecast years.

Junction design and access

The proposed tie-ins at the western and eastern ends require particular scrutiny. The drawings appear to allow for turning movements by larger vehicles, but swept-path evidence should cover the vehicles expected during normal operation, not only construction. Any change in priority at Fen Lane should be plainly marked on the final plans. It would also help to show how people walking or cycling will cross the new junction approaches, including where visibility splays depend on keeping vegetation cut back after opening.

The benefit of taking traffic out of the centre must not come at the cost of making local journeys unnecessarily difficult. The North Wold Roads Authority should provide a simple schedule of roads and paths that remain open, those that are diverted and those that close permanently. That schedule ought to match the rights-of-way plans, the traffic regulation proposals and the environmental commitments. At present those matters can be hard to compare when they are described in different parts of an application.

Construction traffic and phasing

A construction traffic management plan is essential, but its value depends on the detail eventually secured. The examination should establish the proposed haul routes, delivery hours, temporary speed limits and arrangements for cleaning mud from the highway. It should also establish who approves any departure from the normal route when a road is closed. A general promise to agree the details later would leave too much uncertainty about the most disruptive period of the scheme.

The sequence of works matters as much as the total construction duration. Building both end junctions at once could create a different pattern of delay from completing one before starting the other. The applicant should set out the likely periods when temporary signals would operate and whether any full closures are expected. An outline programme with clear assumptions would be more useful than a single overall construction window. Monitoring should count vehicles using the agreed routes, with a means of correcting a persistent problem rather than waiting until the works are finished.

Drainage and flood risk

The proposed drainage strategy should demonstrate where highway runoff goes during ordinary storms and what happens when the design capacity is exceeded. Particular attention is needed at the low point near Sallow Beck. The plans should show the outfall, any flow-control structure, maintenance access and the route that excess water would take over the surface. These features should be legible at a scale that allows the drainage drawings to be compared with the land plans.

Runoff quality is also relevant. Treatment measures need to be appropriate for road traffic and capable of being maintained without repeatedly closing a running lane. If an attenuation basin is relied on, the examination should identify the body responsible for inspecting and maintaining it for the life of the road. The same clarity is needed for culverts and ditches affected by the works. This is not an objection to the road; it is a request for the operational arrangements to be settled and enforceable.

Landscape, lighting and environmental commitments

The landscape assessment should distinguish between the appearance of newly planted screening at opening and its expected effect after establishment. Photomontages showing only a mature planting scenario would give an incomplete picture of the first years of operation. Views from the public paths across East Mere Field are particularly useful for understanding the proposed embankment and lighting columns. Where planting is offered as mitigation, the plans should specify replacement of failed plants and a period of aftercare.

Lighting should be limited to what is required for safety. The final design should state which junctions and stretches of carriageway will be lit, the intended operating hours and whether dimming is proposed. These details affect landscape character and should not be left entirely to a later equipment specification. Ecological surveys and the landscape proposals should also be checked against one another so that planting, drainage access and visibility requirements do not compete for the same strip of land.

Policy and enforceability

The Brindlewick District Council Local Transport Framework identifies the removal of through traffic from village streets as an objective, while the North Wold Green Routes Strategy seeks to maintain usable walking and cycling connections. The road should be assessed against both aims, not treated as satisfying the first automatically at the expense of the second. A short compliance table could identify the drawing, requirement or management plan that secures each promised outcome.

Overall, I support the principle of the relief road. I ask that the examination tests the forecast village-street benefit against the junction, drainage and construction evidence, and that the final commitments can be found in one clear schedule. That would make it much easier to check whether the completed scheme delivers what the application says it will.

text:
MEREFEN LAND & LAW LLP
42 Lantern Quay, Bellwether Marsh, BM4 2LP
Switchboard: 01632 960 400 | enquiries@merefenlaw.example
Direct dial: 01632 960 472 | nadia.pellin@merefenlaw.example

21 October 2026

By email to the Examining Authority

Dear Examining Authority,

East Bracken Storage Link Development Consent Order
Written representation on behalf of Tamsin Quell — compulsory acquisition of Parcel 17
Interested Party reference: IP-040712

We act for Tamsin Quell, the freehold owner of Parcel 17, Cradle Fen Road, Bellwether Marsh. This letter responds to the applicant’s updated Book of Reference and the compulsory acquisition schedule submitted at Deadline 4. Our client does not object in principle to connecting the storage facility to the grid. The objection is to acquiring the whole eastern strip of her field permanently when the works shown there are a buried cable, a temporary working width and one access crossing. Those are three different needs and they should not all be dealt with by taking the freehold.

The applicant, Fenwick Mere Energy Ltd, says in its Statement of Reasons that permanent acquisition is necessary to secure access for inspection and repair. It has not explained why a cable easement, together with temporary possession during construction, would be insufficient. Nor has it identified any above-ground equipment on the strip, apart from a marker post whose position could be agreed. The revised plan shaded the strip more widely than the plan discussed at the February site meeting. There is no change note explaining that difference. We ask the applicant to provide a marked comparison of the two plans and the engineering reason for every additional metre sought.

Parcel 17 is not an unused corner. It is the only reasonably firm route between the northern and southern parts of our client’s holding when the lower ground is wet. The current draft Order would permit the applicant to close that route for construction, then retain rights which could prevent ordinary cultivation and drainage maintenance afterwards. Our client has used the route for 40+ years. That is not an argument that a cable cannot be installed; it is an argument for a method statement, a maintained crossing and clear limits on when access can be restricted.

The land plan also treats the hedge opening at the Cradle Fen Road entrance as if it were available throughout the works. It is shared in practice with the occupier of the neighbouring cottage, Mrs Kira Oswin, who is not taking part in this examination. Her gate opens across the proposed temporary haul route. We give that detail to explain the physical conflict, not to ask the Examining Authority to determine the neighbour’s rights. The applicant should survey the opening before promising that construction traffic can pass without altering it. Our client’s correspondence address is 7 Sedgefold Rise, Bellwether Marsh, BM4 7QJ; it is not an address for service on the neighbouring occupier.

There is a further point about the proposed drainage outfall. Drawing EBSL-CA-017 shows it terminating near the existing field culvert, but the protective provisions do not say who will clear silt from the new connection or repair damage caused by construction vehicles. At the February site meeting our client pointed out the wet patch immediately west of that culvert. Cllr Orla Fenley also asked whether runoff had been modelled with the crossing in place. The answer given was that a detailed design would follow. That may be acceptable for the precise pipe diameter, but it is not enough to justify acquiring more land now without showing the drainage envelope.

For completeness, badger activity has been recorded in Bracken Holt Wood. We are not suggesting that a general reference to the wood fixes the location of any sett. The ecological note supplied to us separately identifies the entrance to the active badger sett at the south-west corner of Parcel 17, 4 metres north of culvert C3. That detail should be handled in a restricted ecology appendix rather than placed on a public acquisition plan. We ask the applicant to confirm how its working width will be set out so that the relevant exclusion measures can be followed on site.

Our client is 67 and has been diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. She is worried about managing livestock movements if the crossing is closed at short notice. We are not advancing her circumstances as a reason to refuse the project. They do, however, make a reliable notice procedure important. A telephone call on the morning works begin is not adequate where gates and animals must be moved beforehand. The draft access protocol should require at least 14 days’ written notice for planned closures, identify a named site contact and provide a safe alternative crossing before the existing route is blocked. The reference to ‘reasonable endeavours’ in paragraph 6 of the current protocol does not secure any of those things.

The compensation process is separate from the question of whether the powers are justified. Nevertheless, the applicant’s suggestion that all outstanding matters can be left to compensation overlooks the practical effect of an uncertain boundary. Our client has a £14,800 outstanding mortgage balance secured against the holding and needs to know what land would remain available for normal use. We include that figure only to explain why an accurate plan matters to her; we do not ask the Examining Authority to assess compensation. The applicant should issue a corrected acquisition drawing before the close of the examination, rather than leave the width to be settled after consent.

We therefore request: first, removal of the permanent freehold acquisition power over the eastern strip and its replacement with appropriately limited rights; second, a dimensioned construction and drainage plan showing the crossing; and third, an enforceable access protocol agreed before possession is taken. If the applicant considers any of these requests impossible, it should say which design constraint prevents it and point to the drawing or calculation relied on. We would welcome a short issue-specific discussion, but please do not treat willingness to attend as agreement to the present Order drafting.

The project examination page at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate remains the appropriate place for published responses. Please use enquiries@merefenlaw.example for routine correspondence to this office, rather than our client’s home address. We reserve the right to comment on any further revised land plans at the next deadline.

Yours faithfully,

Nadia Pellin, LLB
Solicitor | Merefen Land & Law LLP
Pronouns: she/her

Further technical points on Parcel 17

The comments below are confined to the submitted construction and operational material. They do not alter the position on the Order drafting set out above. In particular, an outline commitment to settle details after consent is not a substitute for identifying the workable arrangement where temporary works cross Parcel 17. The drawings should show the maximum extent of each working area, not simply the permanent apparatus, because the temporary footprint is what determines whether the remaining land can be used during construction.

Traffic and access

The transport assessment for the East Bracken Storage Link uses a single daily construction-traffic figure across the principal work fronts. That is useful as a network-wide estimate but does not show how vehicles would be distributed when the cable trench, compound and highway works operate concurrently. The construction traffic management plan should give a peak-day scenario for each phase, with separate totals for heavy goods vehicles, light vehicles and escorted abnormal loads. The totals should reconcile with the material quantities in the construction schedule. At present, the excavation volumes and the proposed number of export journeys appear to be based on different assumptions about the proportion of material reused on site.

The proposed temporary access from Sedge Lane is particularly sensitive to the timing of the trench crossing. Drawing ESBL-TR-014 shows a bellmouth and passing place, while the swept-path appendix assesses entry by the largest articulated vehicle only under an assumed clear carriageway. It does not demonstrate two-way operation during deliveries, nor does it identify where a vehicle would wait if the access were blocked by plant. A dimensioned plan should show the available carriageway width, temporary signs, visibility splays and any banksman position wholly within the land proposed to be controlled. If temporary signals are intended at the Sedge Lane crossing, their operating period should be stated in days rather than left as an undefined part of the overall construction programme.

There is also an inconsistency between the haul-route plan, which directs vehicles towards Marshwick Road, and the draft construction traffic management plan, which allows a turn at Fen Causeway. This may be a drafting error, but it matters for the assessment of junction delay. Fenwick Mere Energy Ltd should provide one definitive route plan and rerun the junction sensitivity test using the same route assumptions. The test should include the morning construction arrival peak as well as the ordinary highway peak; combining them into a single averaged hour could understate a short queue even if the daily flow is modest.

Drainage and levels

The drainage statement proposes temporary interception ditches on the uphill side of the working strip. It does not identify the receiving ditch for each phase or explain how flows would be maintained while the existing grips are crossed. The pre- and post-construction plans should use a common datum and mark the direction of flow at every crossing. Where a culvert is proposed, the drawing should show its invert, length, diameter and method of removal. A note saying that the land will be reinstated to its original condition is insufficient if the installation changes the fall over several metres.

The permanent drainage design also needs to distinguish clean water from runoff collected within the fenced compound. The proposed attenuation basin is shown on the general arrangement but not on the plan used for the exceedance-flow assessment. It is therefore unclear whether an exceedance event would discharge towards the highway ditch or remain within the development site. The applicant should submit a single plan showing the basin, outfall, exceedance route and maintenance access, together with calculations that use the same impermeable area as the final layout. If the layout changes, the calculations should be updated rather than treated as an indicative design that can be fixed at discharge of a requirement.

Landscape and reinstatement

The landscape drawings show native planting along the eastern edge of the compound, but the planting schedule gives a continuous length that includes the proposed access opening. The discrepancy should be corrected. The visualisations should also show the boundary at year 1 without assuming full screening by new planting. That would allow the examination to distinguish the effect of the permanent equipment from the effect of a mature planting scheme. Any replacement hedge should be specified by location, length and establishment period, with a clear procedure for replacing failures.

Reinstatement should be addressed in the same level of detail as installation. The method statement ought to explain how topsoil and subsoil will be stripped, stored separately and returned, and how compaction will be checked after the temporary haul surface is removed. The present wording refers to restoration “as soon as practicable” without identifying a trigger. A measurable trigger, such as completion of cable testing followed by a stated reinstatement window, would be more useful. It should also be clear whether the temporary drainage features stay in place during reinstatement or are removed beforehand.

Ecology and controls

The environmental statement records general use of Bracken Hollow by bats and badgers. Nothing in these comments seeks the publication of a precise protected-species location. For the purposes of the public examination, the necessary point is whether lighting, fencing and working hours have been assessed consistently across the plans. The lighting drawing permits task lighting wherever required for safe working, whereas the ecological mitigation schedule assumes unlit boundary vegetation. Those documents should use the same definition of the working area and set out who may authorise a departure during construction.

Finally, the requirements should secure the revised plans rather than refer generally to the current environmental statement. Briarfen District Council should be given drawings that can be checked against objective limits, including the maximum temporary working width, approved access position and drainage outfall. This is not a request to resolve every construction detail now. It is a request to fix the assessed parameters before consent, so that later approvals deal with implementation rather than a materially different arrangement.
