Relevant representation: Fallowmere Grid Link Project
From: Mara Fenwick
Interested Party reference: IP-483726

I object to the proposed cable corridor and construction compound beside Alder Fen Lane. I am not against connecting renewable electricity to the grid. My objection is to putting the compound, its access and a long period of heavy vehicle movements so close to homes when the applicant has not properly explained why the more distant route was ruled out. I ask to be registered as an interested party and to speak at a hearing if one is held locally.

I live at 14 Wrenfold Cottages, Alder Fen Lane, Mereholt, MH4 8QP. From our upstairs window you can see the proposed compound field, marked C3 on the applicant’s plans. This is not just a line on a map to us. It is where the lane bends and drivers already come round too fast. The transport chapter says traffic will be managed, but I cannot find a drawing showing how two construction lorries would pass there without mounting the verge. The verge is used by people walking to the bus stop, including school children. A traffic marshal at the compound gate will not help at the bend.

My son, Toby Fenwick, is 11-year-old and walks that way with friends. Toby Fenwick has asthma and uses an inhaler, so dust matters to our household in a way that a promise to ‘monitor’ it does not answer. I have rheumatoid arthritis, and on some mornings walking further to avoid a blocked footway is not a realistic option for me. I am 47 and have lived around Mereholt for over 20 years; I know the lane is narrow because I use it, not because I have measured it from a desktop map. I mention these things because the assessment treats pedestrians as an average number of trips rather than people who need a safe, continuous route.

The construction timetable is also hard to understand. One table suggests the compound would be used for 18 months, another says works along this section may overlap with testing and reinstatement. If the applicant needs the field for longer, it should say so plainly now. I am worried about the noise and poor sleep, especially if reversing alarms start before the morning bus. Feeling anxious about that is not the same thing as being assured that the noise will be within a calculated limit. Please require a binding start time, not a statement that contractors will be ‘encouraged’ to be considerate.

Mrs Etta Venn, who lives at 16 Wrenfold Cottages, Alder Fen Lane, Mereholt, MH4 8QP, asked me whether the hedge along the lane would be left in place. Mrs Etta Venn is not taking part in the examination, so I am only repeating the question, not claiming to speak for my neighbour. The drawings colour the hedge green in one document and show a temporary haul road over it in another. Could the applicant publish one plan showing exactly what would be removed, when it would be replanted and who would maintain it after construction? My neighbour has lived here for 40+ years, but length of residence should not be the test for whether a question gets answered.

At our house, Niall Fenwick is recovering from a knee operation. Access arrangements matter when someone cannot easily climb in and out of a car parked several streets away. We have received no clear explanation of whether the lane would be closed completely or whether residents would be escorted through. I am not asking for an exemption from necessary works. I am asking for an actual access plan, with notice periods and a number answered by a person when a vehicle needs to get through. The leaflet tells us to write to fallowmere-link@inquiries.example, which is fine for general questions but no use during an unexpected closure.

There are wildlife issues as well. Badger activity has been recorded in Brackenholt Wood, and I realise that alone does not identify a particular sett. However, the badger sett is inside the western bank of the drainage ditch, 18 metres south of gate G4 in Field 12. Please do not put that precise detail on a publicly accessible construction drawing. I raised it because the ditch appears to fall within the proposed temporary working area. I have also seen bats flying over the lane; that is an observation, not a claim to have located a roost. The applicant should have a competent ecologist check the ditch and the trees before any clearance, with the results supplied to the examining authority in an appropriately restricted form if necessary.

Cllr Briony Tallow said at the Mereholt Parish Council drop-in that residents ought to be able to see the final traffic route before the examination closes. I agree. I have read the applicant’s project page at https://www.fallowmere-grid.example/documents, but the drawings there do not make the daily route obvious to a non-specialist. Nor does a consultation summary tell us which suggestion was accepted and which was rejected. Please ask for a short, readable response to the alternative route along Old Kiln Track, including the land and drainage reasons, rather than another statement that it was ‘not preferred’.

Finally, the proposed planting is welcome but cannot compensate for an unsafe walking route while construction is happening. Please examine a smaller compound, a different access point and enforceable pedestrian arrangements before recommending consent. My preference is for the application to be refused unless those matters are resolved. I am happy to receive updates by email at mara.fenwick@example.invalid or on 07700 900123, but I do not consent to my contact details being put on the public website.

Mara Fenwick

Postscript to my relevant representation – additional points on construction access
From: Mara Fenwick

I apologise for sending another sheet after signing my original comments. I found the construction traffic drawing in document REP2-031 only after I had finished writing. It seems important because the drawing shows vehicles turning across the same bit of Old Kiln Track that I asked the Examining Authority to consider as an alternative access. I still object to the Fallowmere Grid Link Project as submitted.

The drawing marks the track as a construction vehicle route but does not show where people on foot are supposed to stand when a lorry meets them. There is no continuous footway, and the ditch makes it difficult to step aside. I am not asking for a guarantee that no vehicle will ever use the lane. I am asking for a drawing at a scale where residents can see the passing places, any temporary barriers and the actual point where the banksman will stand. Saying that traffic will be managed does not answer those questions. The school walking period is especially awkward, but people use the track at other times as well, including to reach the bus stop.

My child, Toby Fenwick, is 11 years old and sometimes walks that way with me. Toby has asthma and uses a prescribed preventer inhaler. I am concerned about dust from the stripped ground and from vehicles pulling out of the compound, as well as the risk of a collision. I do not suggest that every child will have the same difficulty. I am explaining why a condition requiring a dust management plan, without a clear trigger for stopping work when dust crosses the path, would not give my family much confidence. The noise has already made me anxious when I imagine what the construction months might be like. That is a feeling, not an argument that every sound must be removed.

My brother Niall Fenwick visits to help with the garden and pointed out that the drainage drawing appears to put a temporary pipe under the narrowest part of the track. Please check whether the pipe can take surface water during a heavy storm while the compound is in place. I have lived locally for over 40 years and I have seen water stand on the bend, although I cannot give a measured flood depth. This is not a request to make a decision on the basis of my memory alone; it is a request for the applicant to provide a section through the bank and ditch, showing where overflow would go if that pipe blocked.

Mrs Etta Venn lives at 6 Darnel Lane, Mereholt, FM4 2AB, immediately opposite the proposed gate. This neighbour is not making a representation, as far as I know, and I have not asked for anyone's views to be treated as evidence. I mention the position of the dwelling because the gate drawing stops just before the front gardens. My own home is 8 Darnel Lane, Mereholt, FM4 2AD. Please withhold these home details from the public copy; a plan showing the affected frontage would be enough to understand the objection.

At the drop-in session, Lenna Vale of Fallowmere Grid Connections Ltd said the access arrangement could still change. I did not understand whether that meant a minor alteration to the gate or an entirely different route. The later consultation table says only that the concern was ‘noted’. Could the applicant state which version of the access drawing it now relies on and whether a revised drawing will be available before the examination closes? A response sent to my personal email, mara.fenwick@post.example.invalid, is fine for correspondence, but the address should not appear in published material. The generic project mailbox, access@fallowmeregrid.example.invalid, could be printed instead.

I have also checked the ecology appendix. It says badgers use the wider Mereholt Common area, which by itself does not tell a reader where any sett is. Separately, the badger sett is in the bank 12 metres north of the culvert at the eastern end of Old Kiln Track. That detail should be kept out of a public version of this note and passed to the ecological officer through a suitable confidential route. Bats have been seen over Mereholt Common too, but I do not know of a particular roost and would not want an unverified sighting to be treated as one. The ecological question for me is whether the temporary lights at the gate can be directed away from the ditch without leaving the walking route unlit.

Cllr Briony Tallow suggested at a public meeting that residents could send in photographs after rain. I think that is sensible, though it should supplement rather than replace the applicant's drainage calculations. Mereholt Parish Council may have records of previous ditch clearance, but I do not speak for the council. I have included the reference to the meeting to explain why I looked again at the drainage information, not to attribute my objection to an elected member.

I also want to be frank about why I keep returning to the access point. I still have an outstanding mortgage balance of £92,400, and I cannot simply move house for the construction period. That is not a valuation of the project land or a claim for compensation. It is why an unenforceable promise about considerate working offers little comfort. A condition should identify who receives complaints, how quickly a blocked walking route must be cleared and who can require a vehicle movement to stop. If those details are left to a contractor's later plan, residents will have no meaningful chance to comment on the solution.

I looked at the project website rather than relying on the page at https://lane-notes.example.invalid/track-report, which is somebody else's account of local traffic. The application's own plans are the proper starting point. They still leave the key question open: can construction deliveries be made without placing pedestrians in the carriageway at the gate? Please require a revised access and drainage plan, with pedestrian arrangements shown on the same drawing, before deciding what weight to give the proposed mitigation. My objection remains in place.

Supplementary points on the Fallowmere Grid Link Project
Relevant representation by Mara Fenwick

I am sending these further points because the application drawings do not answer the question I raised about the construction gate. I live at 14 Bracken Fold, Mereholt, MV4 7QP. This is my home, not a business address. The nearest gate shown on the construction plan is the one I use as a landmark when walking to the village shop. A line on a plan saying that pedestrians will be managed does not tell residents where to stand when a delivery vehicle is turning.

The problem is not only the number of lorries. The lane has no continuous pavement, and the ditch beside the gate fills after ordinary rain. On those days people walk on the firmer part of the carriageway. My neighbour, Mrs Etta Venn, is not making a representation, but the same lane is the only reasonable walking route from that end of Bracken Fold. I am mentioning the route, not asking the Examining Authority to treat my neighbour as someone who has agreed with this objection.

My child, Toby Fenwick, is aged 11 and sometimes walks with me to the bus stop. Toby Fenwick has epilepsy, so a vague promise that a marshal will be available is not reassuring. I need to know whether a vehicle would be held before it reaches the bend, and whether pedestrians would have somewhere safe to wait without stepping into the ditch. I have diagnosed asthma and the prospect of dust from an unsealed access track is a separate concern. I am not saying that every dusty day would cause an attack; I am asking for an enforceable dust-control measure, with a named person responsible for responding to complaints. The uncertainty is causing me stress and poor sleep as well, though those feelings are not the basis of my request for the dust measure.

The applicant's drawing FGCL-TRA-017 shows a passing place but not the space needed for a person on foot when that place is occupied. Its note refers to a traffic management plan to be produced later. A later plan could choose a different arrangement from the one residents have been shown. Please require the applicant to show, now, a pedestrian waiting area, the position of any banksman, a trigger for stopping deliveries and a way of keeping the drainage ditch clear. This ought to be one drawing rather than four assurances in different documents.

At the drop-in I asked Lenna Vale of Fallowmere Grid Connections Ltd about the bend. The answer given was that the contractor would work out the practical details. I appreciate that the exact working method may change, but the limits of a safe method should be examined before consent. Fallowmere Grid Connections Ltd could, for example, commit to no deliveries at school-bus times and demonstrate where a stopped vehicle would wait without blocking the junction. That is a suggestion for assessment, not a claim that those times have already been agreed.

Niall Fenwick, a family member who stays at my home from time to time, has also found the lane difficult to use after heavy rain. I have included that observation because drainage and walking space are connected here. I do not want a general statement that mud will be swept up: I want to see where runoff from the temporary track would go, and how frequently the ditch would be checked. If a blocked ditch is discovered on a Friday evening, the documents should say who can arrange clearance before the next scheduled delivery.

There is an ecology point which I have not seen dealt with carefully in the public material. Badger activity has been recorded in Brindle Shaw; that description is deliberately broad and does not identify a sett. The particular sett I saw is beneath the exposed roots of the leaning ash, 6 metres south of the stile at the north-east corner of field P14. I am providing that detail so it can be passed to the relevant ecological adviser, not put on a public plan. A route or compound change made to solve the traffic problem must not accidentally put plant beside the sett. An ecological clerk of works should check any revised layout before vehicles start using it.

I have lived in this area for over 40 years and understand that construction cannot happen without some disruption. The objection is to leaving the difficult choices until afterwards. Cllr Briony Tallow said at the Mereholt Parish Council meeting that the parish wanted a clear complaints route; I understood that as a request for clarity, not as an endorsement of my suggested traffic restrictions. The council's planning@mereholtparish.example mailbox could receive notices, but it should not be expected to manage an applicant's contractors. For completeness, the scheme page at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate is not a substitute for a drawing that residents can read.

There is a personal practical consequence if access is routinely delayed. My monthly mortgage payment is £1,420, and I cannot simply move away for the construction period. I include that to explain why an answer along the lines of ‘use another route’ is not realistic for my household, not to invite an assessment of my finances. I would rather see a workable gate arrangement than argue about compensation later.

Please keep my objection recorded and ask for the revised access, pedestrian and drainage drawing before the examination closes. If a site visit is arranged, the bend, ditch and bus-stop approach should be viewed together, preferably after rain. I can be contacted at mara.fenwick@homepost.example about my representation, but I do not consent to my home contact details being published with it.

Mara Fenwick

Further technical points on the Fallowmere Grid Link Project

I remain concerned that the access drawing, transport assessment and drainage strategy describe the same works in slightly different ways. This is not just a matter of presentation. The examination needs one consistent account of what will be built, which route construction vehicles will use, and what happens to surface water during each stage. The points below are intended to help identify the drawings and controls that would make the proposal capable of proper assessment.

1. Construction traffic and access

The transport assessment assigns construction vehicles to the southern approach along Fallowmere Lane, but the indicative construction programme also refers to deliveries from Wychfen Road. The applicant should provide a single route plan showing the direction of travel for abnormal loads, aggregate deliveries, concrete wagons and ordinary staff traffic. If Wychfen Road is retained as a contingency route, the circumstances in which it may be used should be specified rather than left to a contractor's judgement.

The swept-path drawings should show the proposed temporary access in its actual construction condition. In particular, the assessment should include the width available when fencing, wheel-wash equipment, temporary signs and waiting vehicles are in place. A swept path drawn across an unobstructed plan does not establish that two vehicles can pass safely while the compound is operating. The drawings should also mark the position at which an arriving vehicle can wait without obstructing the bend or the footway.

The current traffic figures appear to use daily totals. Those totals do not show whether several heavy goods vehicles would arrive in a short period, which is the practical issue at this access. Please provide an hourly profile for the busiest construction week, including assumptions about concrete pours and the removal of excavated material. The construction traffic management plan should set an enforceable booking system, a maximum number of vehicle movements per hour and a procedure for dealing with an early or late delivery. The plan should say where a vehicle would be held if its allocated slot is unavailable; holding on Fallowmere Lane should not be the default solution.

The pedestrian survey should be updated to cover the bus-stop approach on Wychfen Road. Its present counts appear to have been taken outside the likely busiest construction period and do not explain how pedestrians would get past the access when a large vehicle is turning. A drawing showing the temporary walking route, the point of crossing and the proposed sight lines would be more useful than a general commitment to banksmen. Banksmen may assist an individual manoeuvre, but they do not replace a safe layout.

2. Surface water and temporary works

The drainage strategy concentrates on the completed development. It gives much less detail about the period after topsoil stripping and before permanent drainage is connected. That is likely to be the period when exposed ground, stockpiles and vehicle movements create the greatest risk of sediment reaching the roadside ditch. A construction-phase drainage drawing is needed, with the boundaries of each disturbed area, the direction of temporary runoff and the proposed location and capacity of settlement measures. The drawing should distinguish clean water that can remain in its existing catchment from water that requires treatment.

The assessment should test a blocked or partially silted ditch as well as the assumed clear-channel condition. The ditch already carries water from land beyond the application boundary, so its performance cannot be considered solely as a means of draining the new works. Please show the levels at the access, the ditch invert and the proposed culvert connections on one long section. Without that information it is difficult to tell whether the access would interrupt the existing flow path or push water towards the carriageway during a heavy storm.

It would also help to identify who is responsible for inspecting temporary controls after rainfall and for removing accumulated silt. This should be a requirement in the construction environmental management plan, with an inspection frequency and a record that can be checked. A statement that measures will be maintained is too open-ended if no inspection trigger or corrective action is defined.

3. Landscape, lighting and ecology

The landscape drawings show planting at the end of construction but not the visual effect while the temporary compound is in use. The viewpoints should be supplemented by a simple construction-stage section showing the maximum height of stockpiles, fencing, lighting columns and any temporary cabins. For the permanent scheme, the photomontages should state the assumed planting height and the year represented. The screening shown at establishment must not be confused with screening that might exist much later.

The lighting assessment should specify the hours and direction of task lighting during winter construction. A condition limiting light spill would be more effective if it identified the areas to be measured and the maximum permitted level. Bat activity recorded around Fallowmere Wood warrants sensible controls on upward and sideways light spill, but the broad reference to that wood is not a reason to omit the measurements or the proposed lantern specification.

4. Documents and examination controls

The application documents should use the same drawing revision wherever they refer to the temporary access. At present, the access schedule refers to Drawing FG-AC-014 Rev B, while the drainage appendix discusses a culvert arrangement labelled Rev C. A short reconciliation table, identifying which drawing supersedes which and what changed, would avoid uncertainty. The same table should list the relevant commitments in the draft development consent order and the construction plans, so that a measure described as mitigation is secured in a document that will actually govern the works.

Mereholt Local Plan Policy TR4 calls for safe movement through development sites, and Policy DW2 addresses runoff at the point where new works meet existing drainage. Those are useful tests here, notwithstanding the national significance of the application. Mereholt Parish Council's published highway comments also raise the need for a workable temporary layout. The applicant could respond to all three points through coordinated drawings rather than separate assurances in different reports.

I am not suggesting that every construction detail must be fixed now. The route, access envelope, drainage outfall and minimum pedestrian provision do need to be fixed sufficiently for the impacts to be assessed. Later contractor plans can then explain how those defined requirements will be delivered. I ask that the examining authority request the coordinated drawings, hourly traffic profile and construction-phase drainage plan before relying on the proposed mitigation.

The coordinated drawings should be treated as a means of testing the assessment, not simply as a condition to be discharged after consent. In the Fallowmere Grid Link Project application, the construction traffic, landscape and drainage chapters appear to use different assumptions about the width and duration of the working corridor. This matters at the Cinderbank Road crossing, where the highway plan shows a temporary access, the landscape plan shows retained planting and the drainage plan shows a swale in approximately the same strip of land. All three may be achievable, but the submitted plans do not yet demonstrate how.

On traffic, the daily totals in the Transport Assessment are not a substitute for an hourly profile. A total of 84 two-way heavy goods vehicle movements on a peak day could have very different effects depending on whether arrivals are spread across ten hours or concentrated around the start of a shift. The junction assessment uses a peak-hour input, but it is not clear how that input relates to the delivery programme for cable drums, aggregate and compound materials. The assessment should state the number of vehicles entering and leaving in each hour, identify any assumptions about holding areas, and test a reasonable overlap between deliveries to the converter site and works along Mereholt Lane.

The same point applies to the proposed construction phases. The programme shows sequential sections of cable installation, while the description allows more than one workfront to operate when ground conditions permit. If that flexibility is retained, the traffic assessment should test the busiest credible combination of workfronts. If it is not intended, the restriction should appear in the construction requirements. Merely describing the sequence as 'indicative' leaves it difficult to know which scenario has actually been assessed. The temporary access drawings should also show the swept path of the largest expected vehicle without relying on the verge beyond the proposed highway works.

At the Cinderbank Road junction, visibility has been measured to a point on the carriageway, but the drawing does not show the effect of temporary fencing, stored materials or the proposed wheel-wash enclosure. These features can be moved; that is precisely why an integrated construction layout is needed. The plan should distinguish space required at all times from space that can be used only when particular deliveries occur. It should also show a continuous walking route past the junction, with its minimum usable width and the points at which users would need to cross an access. A note promising traffic management does not show whether that arrangement fits within the land shown on the works plans.

For drainage, the construction-phase plan needs a clearer relationship with the permanent design. The Flood Risk Assessment describes the permanent attenuation basin and the final outfall to East Mere Drain, but the early earthworks would take place before either feature is fully operational. The Outline Construction Environmental Management Plan refers to settlement measures without locating them or stating the contributing catchments. A phasing drawing should show where runoff from exposed ground would be directed during each principal stage, including the stage when the permanent basin is excavated but cannot yet be brought into use.

This is not a request for the make and model of every temporary tank or pump. It is a request for the design parameters against which later measures can be checked: the area draining to each control, the discharge point, the maximum proposed rate and the treatment route for sediment-laden water. The cross-sections should confirm that there is room for those measures alongside the haul route and the retained vegetation. If the construction swale is to be placed in the same strip as the landscape planting, the plans should say when it will be removed, how the ground will be restored and whether the planting can still be established in the first available season.

The landscape assessment similarly needs to reflect the construction envelope actually sought. Viewpoint 7 from Bracken Hollow is assessed using a photomontage with the permanent fence and planting in place. The written assessment acknowledges that the construction compound would be visible, but gives little indication of the height of stockpiles, temporary lighting columns or acoustic screening. A separate construction-phase visualisation, or a clearly dimensioned maximum-parameters drawing, would allow the worst realistic change to be understood. The proposed planting should not be credited with screening during the period before it has grown sufficiently to do so.

There is also an apparent discrepancy between the tree retention drawing and the cable installation method. One drawing indicates a retained hedgerow at the eastern edge of the corridor; another allows an open trench through that edge. If a trenchless crossing is required to retain the hedgerow, that method should be secured rather than offered as one possible option. If removal is possible, the landscape assessment should assess that outcome. The distinction affects the conclusions about both construction views and the time needed for the boundary to recover.

These points go to the adequacy of the evidence under National Policy Statement EN-5, rather than to a preference for any one construction contractor's method. The examination does not need a final site handbook. It does need a consistent set of maximum parameters from which the traffic, water and visual effects can be reproduced. Mereholt Parish Council has separately asked for a workable temporary highway arrangement; a single set of phased plans would help establish whether that arrangement is compatible with the drainage and landscape measures relied upon elsewhere in the application.

I therefore ask for a consolidated drawing schedule identifying the controlling plan for each phase, together with revised assessment text wherever the plans change an assumed impact. Any matter left to a later management plan should have a stated limit or performance requirement in the consent documents. Without that link, there is a risk that each topic is judged on a layout which is individually plausible but cannot be built alongside the others.

Further relevant representation: Fallowmere Grid Link Project

This representation concerns whether the transport, drainage and landscape assessments use a consistent construction layout. The points below follow my request for a consolidated drawing schedule and are intended to help identify what should be secured in the development consent order, rather than left entirely to later approval.

1. Construction traffic and highway capacity

The Transport Assessment presents a peak daily total for construction vehicles, but the route diagrams appear to show different access arrangements for the cable works and the substation compound. The junction capacity results should be checked against the busiest period in which those activities overlap, not simply against the busiest week for each activity considered separately. Fallowmere Grid Connections Ltd should provide a table showing, for each construction phase, the active work fronts, daily heavy goods vehicle movements, staff vehicle assumptions and proposed access points. The table should reconcile with the programme used in the environmental assessment.

The proposed temporary access from Mereholt Road needs particular attention. Its swept-path drawing assumes an unobstructed verge, while the general arrangement drawing places a drainage swale along part of the same frontage. It is not clear whether the swept-path analysis allows for the swale, its edge treatment and any temporary traffic signs. A single dimensioned plan would make this testable. If the access can operate only after a particular section of drainage has been built, that sequence should be stated. The same applies if the drainage is to be installed after access works are removed.

The traffic chapter should also explain how vehicles would be held when a delivery cannot enter the compound immediately. A statement that deliveries will be booked does not establish where an early vehicle would wait or how a missed booking would be handled. The Construction Traffic Management Plan should specify a maximum number of vehicles permitted to arrive within each booking period, a procedure for turning vehicles away without using the local road network for informal circulation, and a means of recording compliance. These are practical controls which could be secured without prescribing every journey in advance.

2. Drainage and flood risk

The drainage strategy relies on infiltration for parts of the temporary compound, but the infiltration results are presented for the permanent works area. Ground conditions may vary across the corridor. The applicant should identify which test locations support each proposed drainage feature and whether the design includes an alternative if the temporary compound does not achieve the assumed infiltration rate. Any alternative should be assessed now if it would move an outfall, enlarge a basin or occupy land currently shown as landscape mitigation.

The Flood Risk Assessment identifies runoff rates for the operational site but does not clearly state the allowable discharge rate during the earthworks phase. Exposed ground and temporary haul roads will have different runoff characteristics from the finished site. The assessment should provide a phase-by-phase drainage plan showing clean-water diversions, treatment for sediment-laden water, emergency exceedance routes and the point at which permanent controls take over. A commitment to prepare a later method statement is useful, but it should sit beneath defined discharge and storage limits in the consent documentation.

The cable trench crossings are also relevant. The drawings should show how field drainage will remain connected while trenches are open and how it will be reinstated. This is not a request for every construction detail at examination stage; it is a request for a clear design basis so that the assessed effects do not depend on an untested solution being found later.

3. Landscape and visual assessment

The Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment assesses screening at opening year and after establishment. Several of the illustrated viewpoints assume the proposed planting is in place, whereas the construction programme appears to retain a haul road through the same strip until late in the works. The assessment should distinguish between planting that can be completed before the substation becomes operational and planting that must wait for temporary infrastructure to be removed. It should then assess the intervening period using a realistic height and density of vegetation.

The proposed bund north of the compound is shown with different footprints on the landscape drawing and the drainage drawing. Its final width matters because the visual assessment depends on its crest level and planting area. A coordinated cross-section should show the bund, drainage feature, maintenance access and boundary treatment together. The drawings should also confirm whether the material balance assumes all excavated material is suitable for bund construction. If imported material is required, the associated vehicle movements should be reflected in the transport figures.

I am not asking the Examining Authority to prefer a particular planting species or fence finish. The important point is that the physical space needed for the proposed mitigation is reserved and that a measurable outcome is secured. The landscape requirement could specify minimum planting widths, replacement of failed planting and the latest phase by which each area must be completed, subject to the approved detailed scheme.

4. Documents and controls

Mereholt Parish Council has requested a workable temporary highway arrangement. That request cannot be resolved by a highway drawing alone if the same land is required for drainage or visual mitigation. An updated drawing register should identify the revision relied on for each assessment, with superseded layouts clearly marked. Where a change affects a traffic total, runoff calculation or viewpoint illustration, the corresponding chapter should be updated rather than leaving the reader to infer which assumption prevails.

I ask that the examination clarify these matters before detailed management plans are approved after consent. A requirement should identify the relevant approved parameter plan, the quantitative limit it protects and the process for demonstrating compliance. This would allow flexibility in construction methods while keeping the assessed envelope understandable and enforceable.

The following points concern the assessments that would have to support those limits. They are not objections to a particular contractor's method; they are about whether the worst reasonably foreseeable effects have been assessed consistently across the application.

Traffic and construction access

The transport assessment for the Fallowmere Grid Link Project gives a daily total for heavy goods vehicles, but the construction programme divides the works into phases without showing how those daily movements would be distributed between them. A daily maximum is of limited use if it is not clear whether deliveries to the converter site, cable corridor and temporary compounds could all occur on the same day. The assessment should provide a phase-by-phase table showing the assumed and maximum two-way movements at each access, including abnormal loads, spoil removal and deliveries for reinstatement. It should also say whether the figures include subcontractor vehicles. I am not asking for a prediction of every delivery, only a test of the busiest combination that the draft requirements would permit.

The junction assessment at Mereholt Crossroads appears to use the existing give-way layout, while the access drawing shows a widened bellmouth on the eastern arm. The drawing may well improve turning space, but the assessment and drawing should describe the same arrangement. Similarly, the swept-path plan for Mill Drove assumes that vehicles can wait clear of the carriageway at the north compound. The compound plan shows storage close to that waiting area. If the waiting space is essential to avoid vehicles standing on Mill Drove, it needs to remain available throughout the relevant phase, not merely appear on an illustrative plan. A construction traffic management plan submitted later cannot resolve a conflict between the assessed traffic arrangement and the land shown for other uses.

The proposed routing restriction is also difficult to check as drafted. It refers to the designated construction route, whereas the route plan distinguishes a primary route and a contingency route. The contingency route passes through Lower Mereholt and crosses the narrow bridge on Fen Bank Lane. The application should state the circumstances in which that route could be used, its maximum daily movements and whether those movements are already included in the transport assessment. Otherwise a route described as exceptional could operate without a clear assessed limit. Consultation with Mereholt Borough Council on traffic management would be useful, but consultation is not a substitute for stating the limit in the Order documents.

Landscape and visual assessment

The landscape chapter describes a maximum equipment height, but some photomontages appear to depict a lower arrangement with mature planting in place. I cannot tell from the viewpoint schedule which images represent the opening year and which represent a later year. This matters at the southern edge of Mereholt, where the land rises towards the proposed converter buildings. The visual assessment should identify the building and gantry heights used for each verified view, the age of planting shown, and the season represented. A view with screening after establishment may be helpful, but it should not be used as the sole illustration of effects at completion.

The proposed earth bund beside Rookshaw Field is labelled as both landscape mitigation and a place for retained excavated material. Its indicative crest varies between the landscape plan and the materials management drawing. If its height is necessary to screen the compound, that height should be secured and assessed for landscape and drainage effects. If its shape may change to accommodate a different volume of spoil, the assessment should test that range instead. The same applies to the proposed hedgerow on the eastern boundary: the commitment should distinguish retained hedgerow from new planting, because their screening value at the start of construction is not equivalent.

Drainage and ground conditions

The drainage strategy says surface water will be managed within the application boundary, yet its basin schedule assigns storage to a basin shown on the temporary works plan beneath the later cable laydown area. The documents need to explain whether that basin operates during the period when the laydown area is occupied, and what temporary storage replaces it if not. The relevant test is the construction condition as well as the final operational layout. A statement that detailed drainage will be agreed later does not demonstrate that sufficient space has been reserved now.

The strategy also uses different impermeable-area figures in the runoff summary and the converter-site layout. Please reconcile these figures and show the allowance made for tracks, hardstandings and any surfaces that will be compacted during construction but restored afterwards. The proposed discharge point at Old Mere Drain should be identified consistently across the outfall drawing and flood-risk assessment. This is an infrastructure location, not a request to publish ecological survey details. If an outfall must move within a defined corridor, the corridor and its hydraulic assumptions should be assessed.

Parameters and policy

Mereholt Local Plan Policy INF4 asks major infrastructure proposals to demonstrate that construction effects have been considered alongside the completed development. The current application separates the two quite neatly on paper, but the land uses overlap in practice. The final schedule of mitigation should therefore cross-reference traffic, drainage, materials storage and landscape measures for each phase. It should make clear which measure is needed before an access opens, before earthworks begin, and before temporary land is released for reinstatement.

I would welcome a single updated assumptions table, tied to the drawing register, before the close of the examination. That would make it possible to check whether the proposed requirements secure the same development that the environmental statement assesses. Without that reconciliation, approval of later plans could choose between conflicting drawings rather than provide the detail of an already assessed proposal.

That reconciliation also matters for the traffic assessment. The construction traffic tables give totals by phase, but the access drawings show more than one route into the working area. A daily total is not enough to establish the effect at each junction if deliveries can be moved between routes after consent. The applicant should provide an access-by-access schedule showing the maximum two-way HGV movements, the hours of use, the vehicle types assumed and the phase in which each access would operate. The figures should match both the transport assessment and the construction programme. If flexibility is sought, the assessment should test the busiest credible combination rather than treating every access as though it will be used only lightly.

The Fallowmere Grid Link Project would place temporary construction movements on the Mereholt Road and the Belling Lane junction during the same period as cable works further east. The submitted junction assessment appears to use an average day, whereas deliveries of aggregate, ducts and large plant are unlikely to arrive evenly across a week. An average may be useful for reporting total traffic, but it does not demonstrate that the junction can accommodate a concentrated delivery period. A sensitivity test for the peak construction week, including the proposed workforce vehicles, would be more informative. It should also state whether the assumed delivery booking system is a binding control or simply good practice described in the construction management plan.

The proposed routing restriction needs similar precision. The drawings mark the eastern section of Belling Lane as unsuitable for HGVs, yet the outline management plan allows alternative routes where a road closure or incident occurs. There is no map of those alternatives and no stated approval process. A temporary diversion might be unavoidable, but the route should first be checked for width, turning space and conflicts with the proposed pedestrian diversion. This could be secured through a requirement for a route-specific method statement before the relevant works start. Merely asking a contractor to consider local conditions would not give a clear basis for enforcement.

The drainage information should then be checked against that same programme. Drawing DR-07 shows a temporary settlement basin at the northern compound. The construction phasing plan, however, indicates stripping and stockpiling within its proposed catchment before the basin is marked as operational. Fallowmere Grid Connections Ltd should explain where runoff will go during that interval. A statement that controls will be installed progressively is not a substitute for a sequence showing temporary bunds, clean-water cut-offs, settlement capacity and a defined discharge point for each phase. The sequence should also cover the period when the basin is removed but reinstatement is not yet established.

In particular, the calculations appear to address the permanent drainage arrangement and the final compound layout rather than the largest exposed area during construction. Temporary stone surfaces, excavated trenches and soil heaps could drain differently from either of those end states. The assessment should identify the design rainfall event and the area used to size each temporary control. It should say how capacity will be maintained if sediment accumulates, who will inspect the measures and what happens when a discharge point cannot be used. These are practical matters, not an invitation to redesign the scheme after consent.

The landscape drawings raise a related issue about timing. Planting along the southern edge of the converter site is presented as mitigation for views from the Brackenfold track, but the schedule does not distinguish advance planting from planting after the heavy works. If it is installed only at the end, it cannot reduce construction effects described as mitigated in the environmental statement. The landscape and ecological management plan should identify the earliest feasible planting season, any areas that must remain clear for construction and the interim screening proposed in those areas. It should also give a measurable replacement standard for failed plants. A general promise to maintain planting for five years does not establish what density will remain at the end of that period.

I am not suggesting that every hedge has to be fixed to the centimetre at this stage. The concern is that the limit of deviation, compound footprint and planting belt are each shown on separate plans, with no combined drawing demonstrating that they fit at the narrowest point. The applicant should provide one coordinated plan at a readable scale, including the security fence, maintenance strip, drainage features and the land available for planting. If there is insufficient room for the planting assumed in the visual assessment, that should be identified now and the residual effect reassessed, rather than left for a later approval of details.

Mereholt Parish Council has also asked for clearer reinstatement criteria for temporary land. That is a planning point rather than simply a matter of presentation. The proposed requirement refers to reinstatement in accordance with an approved scheme but does not say when the scheme must be submitted, which construction areas it must cover, or what evidence would demonstrate completion. Separate triggers may be needed for the cable corridor, temporary accesses and the northern compound. Otherwise land could remain in an interim condition while a later phase continues elsewhere, with no clear date by which drainage and landscape functions are restored.

Finally, the draft requirements should be checked against the updated assumptions table requested above. Each requirement should identify the relevant approved plan and the point at which its details are needed. A pre-commencement requirement may be appropriate for measures that must exist before stripping starts; it is less helpful if the approval can be deferred until a general construction plan is produced, after the physical sequence has effectively been decided. I ask the Examining Authority to seek those clarifications during examination and to test the revised documents as a set, not as isolated replies to separate questions.

Further technical observations on the combined effects

I have set out above why the assumptions and requirements need to be read together. The following points are intended to help identify the drawings and calculations that should be put in the examination library before any conclusion is reached on whether the effects are acceptable. They do not depend on a particular choice of contractor or a final detailed design.

Traffic and construction access

The Transport Assessment for the Fallowmere Grid Link Project treats construction traffic as a daily total. That is not enough to test the junctions shown on Construction Access Plan CA-04. Deliveries for the cable trench, temporary haul road and compound may overlap on the same day, and the assessment should show the busiest hour in each construction stage, not just an average across the programme. The assessment should also state whether the figures include empty return trips, staff vehicles and movements between compounds. Otherwise there is no reliable basis for comparing its forecasts with the capacity tables.

At Mereholt South Junction, the turning diagrams show a long vehicle entering from Cinderbank Road, but not the opposing movement when another vehicle is waiting to leave the site. The swept-path drawing also appears to assume that the whole bellmouth is available, although the proposed temporary drainage channel runs along its eastern edge. Fallowmere Grid Connections Ltd should submit a drawing that includes both features and identifies the actual usable carriageway width. If temporary traffic signals are proposed, the assessment needs to account for the queue they would create on Mereholt Lane during the same peak hour used in the traffic model.

I cannot tell from the current programme whether the southern compound would close before deliveries to the northern workfront start. If both accesses can operate at once, the cumulative assignment should show that; if they cannot, the programme and construction traffic management measures should secure the restriction. A statement that routes will be agreed later does not resolve the capacity question being examined now.

Landscape and visual assessment

The landscape drawings use planting at its proposed mature height in several illustrative views, while the assessment discusses effects during the first years of operation. Those are different tests. A set of matching viewpoints at installation, after five growing seasons and at the design year would make the comparison intelligible. The drawings should distinguish retained hedgerow from new planting, including the lengths removed for access and the gaps that would remain until replacement planting establishes.

The view from the public route along the West Fen Drain is particularly difficult to check because the photomontage viewpoint is shown on the western bank, while the route on the access plan is on the eastern bank. This may be a drawing error, but it matters: the fence, drainage works and nearest equipment would sit between the two positions. The viewpoint schedule and plan should use the same coordinates, and the corrected image should include the temporary works as well as the permanent development. This is a request for a consistent assessment, not an objection to planting in principle.

Drainage and ground conditions

The outline drainage strategy assumes infiltration for the northern compound but its testing plan places most trial pits outside the proposed hardstanding. It should explain how those results have been applied to the area that will actually receive runoff. The calculations also use an undeveloped runoff rate without clearly distinguishing existing field drains from overland flow. A plan of known drains, outfalls and proposed diversions would allow the receiving catchments to be checked against the calculations.

The temporary works are important here. Stripped ground, stockpiles and haul-road surfacing will change both the speed and direction of runoff before the permanent drainage is built. For each construction stage the applicant should identify the available storage volume, the discharge point and who checks that the controls are functioning. The current drawing labels a settlement area but gives neither its dimensions nor the stage at which it becomes operational. A generic commitment to good construction practice cannot demonstrate that capacity exists during the first stripping operation.

The crossing of Lower Harth Beck is another point where documents need to agree. The construction section shows a temporary pipe crossing, while the drainage narrative refers to an open-span arrangement. The difference affects the obstruction to flow, the method of installation and the land needed for the works. One option should be assessed consistently, or both should be assessed with a clear mechanism for selecting between them before works at the crossing begin.

Plans, parameters and requirements

Document 8.14 describes the limits of deviation as allowing minor design refinement. On the works plans, however, the limits appear wide enough to move the northern compound toward the drainage corridor and to alter the length of hedgerow affected. The environmental assessments should either test the worst case within those limits or the limits should be narrowed. It is not sufficient to assess the preferred layout and then consent a wider one without explaining the consequences.

The draft requirement for a Construction Environmental Management Plan should identify which traffic, landscape and drainage drawings it must conform to. It should also specify the approvals needed before each relevant activity, rather than rely on one approval before construction generally. For example, the drainage measures serving a compound must be approved and installed before that compound is stripped; replacement planting details can follow a different timetable, provided the land required for them is secured on the approved plans.

I ask the Examining Authority to request a single cross-reference table setting out each changed assumption, the corresponding model or drawing, the affected assessment conclusion and the securing requirement. This would make it possible to check whether an amendment in one discipline has been carried through into the others. Without that table, separate technical replies may look complete while relying on different construction sequences or different versions of the layout.
