ENVIRONMENTAL STATEMENT
Appendix 8.4: Otter and Schedule 1 Bird Survey and Conservation Measures
Fenwick Reach Flood Storage Scheme | October 2026

Prepared by Mara Quenby, independent ecological witness. This appendix should be read with ES Chapter 8 and drawing FR-ES-8.14. It records the evidence available at the close of the 2026 survey season; it is not a licence to approach an occupied resting place or nest.

1. Scope and information handling

The red-line boundary follows the Merebrook Cut, crosses Borrow Mere and includes temporary access beside Wold Fold. Survey effort covered the channel, its connected drains and the reedbed that could be affected by piling, vegetation clearance or changes to water levels. Records were supplied at mixed precision. A ten-kilometre or one-kilometre square is useful for establishing local presence, but cannot be used to set an exclusion fence. Conversely, the exact resting-place and nest records below are included solely to let the Examining Authority assess whether the draft requirements are workable. They should not be placed on public-facing contractor drawings. The contractor's ecological clerk of works will hold a controlled constraints plan, version 3, with access logged.

The desktop return included otter records within the coarse square SK 47 61 and a marsh harrier record for the wider Borrow Mere reedbeds. Brackenward Ecology Ltd also checked its own 2024 field notebooks. The scheme website, https://www.fenwickreachscheme.example/ecology, carries the non-confidential survey method; it does not carry the constraints plan. General guidance was checked against https://www.gov.uk/guidance/protected-species-how-to-review-planning-applications. A third-party account at https://fenreachwildlife.example/otter-notes was noted but not treated as a verified record, as neither the date nor the observer's method could be confirmed.

2. Field methods and limitations

Walkovers took place on 19 March, 22 May and 14 August 2026. Two surveyors inspected accessible banks from the path or from the watercourse, recording spraints, slides, feeding remains, suitable root systems and any change in cover since the preceding visit. The May visit was stopped after heavy rain raised the channel; an exposed bank was revisited in August. No attempt was made to enter a holt. Dawn and dusk watches were undertaken from screened positions outside the reedbed on four dates between April and July. Marsh harrier flight lines were plotted against fixed landscape features rather than following birds into cover. Visibility into the centre of the reeds remained poor, and an absence of a sighting from any one watch should not be read as absence of breeding.

The field team included Ms Iona Felwick of Brackenward Ecology Ltd. Her direct correspondence address is iona.felwick@brackenward-ecology.example; requests for the public version of this appendix should instead go to ecology@brackenward-ecology.example. Mara Quenby's survey qualifications and previous wetland work are set out in Appendix 8.1, which forms the competence evidence for this opinion.

3. Otter results

Spraint was found on two bridge abutments, with slides and prints on soft silt downstream of Borrow Mere. These signs establish regular use of the corridor but, on their own, do not identify a resting place. One feature was assessed as a probable active otter holt at SK 47382 61840, in the root plate on the north bank immediately below culvert C4. Fresh bedding at its entrance and a repeated track to the water were visible on the August visit. Occupancy was not established by a camera, and the precautionary assessment treats it as occupied. Other cavities along the cut were either open-ended or lacked corroborating signs. A line marked ‘possible holts’ across the whole of Borrow Mere on an earlier desk plan should not be read as several confirmed holts.

The nearest permanent embankment is approximately 85 m from the recorded feature. Temporary sheet piling and a haul route would be nearer. The final construction method must retain continuous passage along at least one bank, avoid lighting the water edge, and prevent trench entrapment through daily checks and escape ramps. If work within the precautionary buffer cannot be avoided, the contractor must obtain the necessary species advice and any licence before works start. A pre-start check is required because flood events can alter bank features quickly. The check is to update the controlled plan, not to publish a fresh coordinate in a weekly works notice.

4. Schedule 1 bird results

A pair of marsh harriers displayed over the reedbed in May. Food passes and repeated low flights supported a breeding assessment, although fledging was not confirmed. The observed nest position was SK 46971 62238, in the crown-height reed platform immediately east of marker post R7. This position is more precise than the wider grid square SK 46 62 used in the public bird-record return. Two reed warbler territories were also recorded; they do not require a Schedule 1 location schedule. No nest inspection or photography from within the reeds was undertaken.

For the construction programme, the principal risk is disturbance from machinery and people during establishment and incubation, rather than the permanent footprint. Reed cutting in the affected compartment should take place outside the breeding season unless a suitably qualified ecologist first confirms that the proposed working area is clear and agrees a method that avoids disturbance. A quiet corridor and screened watch point will be identified on the controlled plan. The precise nest position must not appear on compound noticeboards or the public rights-of-way diversion sheet. If birds change nest site in a later year, the buffer will follow the birds rather than the historic map point.

5. Conservation and follow-up

Requirement 24 of the draft DCO should secure a Species Conservation Plan before main construction. That plan must name the person authorised to stop works, specify trigger distances for noisy activities, provide a route for escalating unexpected signs, and set out post-construction monitoring for two breeding seasons. It should distinguish a precautionary pause from a confirmed legal constraint; this matters where the reedbed is inaccessible. The proposed backwater planting and low-glare lighting are beneficial but do not replace avoidance of disturbance. Cllr Leora Penn asked whether the riverside path would close throughout the bird season. It need not: short, signed restrictions may be necessary where an active nest is exposed to the path, but a blanket closure is not proposed.

I conclude that effects can be controlled through the secured plan, licensing where required and on-site ecological supervision. That conclusion depends on the temporary works layout remaining outside the mapped sensitive features. A materially different haul route should be referred back for ecological review before it is adopted.

Appendix E7 (continued): Otter and Schedule 1 bird evidence
Fenwick Reach Flood Storage Scheme
Mara Quenby, independent ecological witness

E7.18 Scope and handling of records
This appendix should be read with the Outline Ecological Conservation Plan (OECP), not as a substitute for the restricted survey drawings. I have set out the field evidence needed to explain my conclusion, while separating precise locations from the broader information suitable for the public examination. All scheme-grid references below use the applicant's temporary FRC survey grid; they are not Ordnance Survey coordinates. For general orientation only, the surveyed reach falls within the coarse OS square TL 4 6. Readers should not try to infer a feature's position from that square. The precise feature descriptions in this appendix are provided so that the Examining Authority can test the avoidance measures; the working drawings circulated to contractors should carry the same restrictions.

E7.19 Otter signs and interpretation
Surveys were undertaken in February and May 2026 in daylight, with both banks walked where access and water levels allowed. Spraints, two sets of footprints and a well-used slide were recorded along Mill Leat. A spraint beside the old brick outfall establishes use of the reach but does not, by itself, establish a resting place. The February inspection could not see behind flood debris at Culvert C7. On the May revisit, the debris had shifted and a sheltered chamber with flattened vegetation and fresh spraint was visible. The record describes an occupied holt, rather than merely a possible couch: otter holt OH-03 is under the northern bank of the Mill Leat, 14 m downstream of the western end of Culvert C7 (scheme grid FRC 42176 68314). That description must not be reproduced on public-facing interpretation boards or in unrestricted path notices.

No absence conclusion should be drawn for the reedbed margin that could not be entered. There were otter paths at the edge of Alder Reach, but their position within that named reach is too imprecise to identify a resting place. The OECP should require an inspection immediately before bank works, even where the May record shows no holt. If a new chamber is found, the ecological clerk of works must stop the affected activity, secure the area without advertising the feature, and obtain advice on whether a licence is needed. A 30 m stand-off in the drawings is an initial design constraint, not a promise that every activity outside it is harmless. Piling, night working and light spill require separate consideration. The water vole survey is reported elsewhere and should not be used as a proxy for otter evidence.

E7.20 Schedule 1 birds
The bird visits covered dawn and late-afternoon periods. Calling, food-carrying and repeated entry to cover were logged separately; a bird flying over the reservoir was not counted as breeding evidence. A marsh harrier pair displayed over the wider Fenwick marsh in April. Subsequent watches identified an active nest: the marsh harrier nest is in the third reed island east of Sluice S4, 6 m south of the inspection boardwalk's terminal post (scheme grid FRC 42308 68192). The public drawings may show a broad seasonal constraint zone around Fenwick marsh but must not show that point or a photograph from which it can readily be reconstructed. Elsewhere, a barn owl was seen hunting above the western grassland. Neither a nest nor a roost was found for that species. This distinction matters: the observation warrants careful checks of trees and structures before work, but does not justify marking a supposed owl nest on the plans.

Brackenward Ecology Ltd supplied the May field sheets. Ms Iona Felwick, its surveyor, confirmed in the field-sheet note that the harrier observation was made from the existing track, without entry into the reeds. The note does not say that the nest remained active after the last visit. The contractor therefore needs a current check before installing the temporary pumping line, rather than relying on a fixed calendar date. The relevant season varies with weather and the birds' behaviour. If an active nest is present, the supervising ecologist should set a disturbance buffer appropriate to the activity and record the reason for it in the site diary. The buffer may be revised following observation; it should not be reduced merely because a programme date has slipped.

E7.21 Securing the measures
I recommend three additions to OECP revision 4. First, its restricted feature schedule should state who may receive coordinates and require any superseded contractor plan to be withdrawn. Secondly, the pre-works check should cover both banks at the temporary crossing and record visibility limits, not simply tick a box saying ‘otter absent’. Thirdly, there should be a named decision point before vegetation clearance in the marsh, with the examining ecologist able to require a pause. These are practical controls, not a request to close the entire river corridor. Cllr Leora Penn's question about path access is answered by a short diversion only if a current nest makes the open path disturbing; signs can explain the temporary restriction without identifying the nest.

The applicant's proposed backwater planting should retain a strip of rough cover linking the leat and marsh. Low-glare fittings should face away from the water and be checked after installation, as a fitting shown correctly on a drawing can be turned during maintenance. The plan should also require an incident record for unexpected access into a restricted area and a review before works restart. These provisions are capable of being secured by the final conservation plan and the construction environmental management plan. They should be checked against the final haul-route drawing. My assessment does not extend to an unreviewed crossing or a new compound beside the reedbed.

For clarity, records described only as ‘otters in Alder Reach’ or ‘harriers over Fenwick marsh’ remain useful context but are not precise protected-site locations. The specific holt and nest records above serve a different purpose: they allow the avoidance layout to be audited. Keeping that distinction in the examination record should help contractors apply the controls without needlessly publicising vulnerable features.

Environmental Statement Appendix E7: Otters and Schedule 1 birds
Fenwick Reach Flood Storage Scheme — response to the Examining Authority's conservation-plan questions
Prepared by Mara Quenby, independent ecological witness

1. Purpose and limits

This note continues my review of the draft conservation plan. It separates observations that establish use of the wider corridor from records that identify a vulnerable resting or breeding place. That distinction matters for the contractor's drawings: an otter spraint on a public path does not warrant the same handling as a holt, and a harrier hunting over marsh does not locate a nest. The locations in paragraphs 3 and 5 are supplied for examination and controlled construction planning. They should not be transferred to public path notices, interpretation boards or unrestricted site briefings.

2. Survey record

Brackenward Ecology Ltd supplied the April field sheets, including the visit made by Ms Iona Felwick on 18 April 2026. My check visit was on 29 April 2026. The weather on both dates was settled, but high water earlier in the month may have removed older signs from the lower bank. A resident, Owen Vessell, also reported an otter crossing at dusk; this is an incidental observation, not a survey fix, and I have not used it to set a works exclusion zone. The application reference FRS/APP/6.3/E7 identifies the field-sheet bundle. The dates and reference should remain on any revised schedule so that old and new observations are not muddled.

3. Otter evidence

Spraint, prints and a short slide were found along Alder Reach. For the ordinary field signs, TF 4398 7161 is sufficiently precise to let the clerk of works revisit the path-side mud without implying that a protected resting place occurs there. Conversely, the statement ‘otters use Alder Reach near Fenwick marsh’ is useful context only; TF 43 71 is a coarse grid square and cannot direct a machine operator to a feature. Neither observation should be marked as a holt on the publicly circulated constraints sheet.

The active holt recorded during the joint check is at TF 43862 71524, beneath the north bank root plate of the lone leaning ash, 18 m below Siltgate footbridge. Fresh bedding and two well-worn entrances were visible without entering the bank. Those details distinguish it from the several holes upstream which have not been confirmed as otter resting places. The proposed temporary access ramp remains too close to this feature on drawing FR-DR-104, revision B. The final drawing should show an avoidance area whose boundary has been checked in the field, not merely a circle drawn round an approximate symbol.

4. Otter measures

No excavation, tracking, vegetation clearance or lighting installation should begin in the avoidance area until the ecological clerk of works has checked the marked boundary and signed the relevant permit. A pre-start survey is necessary after a flood or a prolonged pause, since entrances may shift. If a new resting place is found, work should stop locally and the layout should return for ecological review; it would be wrong to treat this appendix as advance approval for relocating animals. The main channel should retain a continuous unlit route at night, with fencing gaps and escape points inspected after each flood. These are construction controls, not a request to close the whole riverside path.

5. Schedule 1 birds

Hunting marsh harriers were noted over Fenwick marsh on several visits. That broad description, and the record of a bird flying north of Sedge Mere, do not disclose a breeding location. One occupied marsh harrier nest was, however, confirmed at TF 44013 71968, in the third reed island east of marker post R7, 9 m south of the old pump inlet. The recorded approach was made from the existing track, with no entry into the reed island. An unsuccessful search elsewhere in the reedbed must not be read as proof that no further nests will be established in a later season.

The present programme puts reed cutting and piling in the same part of the marsh during the breeding season. The conservation plan should require a competent survey immediately before that phase, a seasonally appropriate no-work area around an occupied nest, and a written release before activity resumes. Observation should be from agreed distant points: repeated close approaches merely to confirm that a bird is still there would add disturbance. The public version of the plan can describe these controls without reproducing the nest coordinates or the landmark description above.

6. Access, recording and follow-up

Cllr Leora Penn asked whether the informal path could stay open while the works compound is installed. In principle it can, provided its route is kept outside any active exclusion area and lighting is directed away from the channel and reeds. An access steward should record unexpected entry into a restricted area and refer it for review before works restart. This also applies if a contractor moves a fence to accommodate a delivery. A sign saying ‘wildlife present’ would be less useful than a clear, current site instruction held by the people controlling the works.

The restricted constraints layer should be issued only to staff who need it for setting out, with version control and a record of superseded drawings. The public conservation-plan summary should report survey methods, broad habitat areas, monitoring frequency and the response to changed conditions. The project mailbox, ecology@fenwickreach.example, may be used for general queries, but precise protected-site records should be handled through the controlled drawing process rather than attached to a general enquiry. Natural England's standing advice at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/protected-species-how-to-review-planning-applications is a useful check on the method; it does not replace a site-specific decision.

Subject to those changes, the measures can be secured through the final conservation plan and construction environmental management plan. They must be checked against the final haul-route drawing before that drawing is approved. My conclusion remains confined to the crossing and compound arrangements assessed here, not any later unreviewed route beside the reedbed.

Appendix E.4 — Otter and Schedule 1 bird records: crossing and compound update
Fenwick Reach Flood Storage Scheme

E.4.1 Purpose and limits

This note follows the assessment of the crossing and compound arrangements in the preceding section. It separates records needed to explain the mitigation from records that would reveal a protected site. Coordinates in this appendix use the scheme's fictional local FR grid, not an Ordnance Survey national grid reference. The confidential drawing E4-C contains the corresponding surveyed points and must not be put on the public examination page or sent round as an ordinary email attachment. A coarse reference, FR 48 71, is sufficient to describe the reach considered in the public conservation plan.

The walkovers were undertaken on 18 February, 9 April and 22 June 2026. Water was high in February; the April visit gave the clearest view of the banks. Ms Iona Felwick of Brackenward Ecology Ltd checked the field sheets against the June photographs. These are records of field signs, not a claim that an animal occupied every feature on every visit. The applicant should keep that distinction in the final environmental statement errata and in any toolbox talk. I have used the word ‘potential’ where a feature could not be safely inspected without disturbance.

E.4.2 Otter evidence

Spraints were found on two stones at the culvert outfall and one short slide was visible on the muddy inner bank. A set of footprints was photographed downstream, although the substrate did not permit an individual animal to be identified. The records establish use of the watercourse, not the number of otters using it. Owen Vessell, who is not an examination participant, separately reported seeing an otter near the old footbridge in May. That observation is useful context but has not been treated as a substitute for the survey evidence.

One bank cavity has the characteristics of an otter holt. Its precise position is at local grid FR 48231 71604, beneath the east abutment of the disused narrow-gauge culvert. This position is included here solely for the controlled ecological record: it must be removed from any unrestricted drawing, contractor induction slide or public-facing copy of the plan. The entrance was not probed. No conclusion about breeding can be drawn from the available visits. The ditch farther north had prints and a possible resting place, but vegetation prevented a reliable classification. Otter signs occur along Fenwick Drain more generally; that broader description does not locate a holt.

For the crossing, the preferred sequence is to install the clear-span structure from the dry working area, retain both banks and avoid temporary pipes through the channel. A pre-start check by the appointed ecologist is required immediately before vegetation clearance. If a resting place is suspected within the working footprint, operations at that location should stop while the ecologist advises on avoidance and any licence requirement. ‘Check before starting’ is not, by itself, a licence to excavate a bank. Night lighting should be directed away from the drain, with no continuous illumination of the under-bridge route. The contractor's inspection log should record whether that dark route remains passable after fencing goes in.

E.4.3 Breeding birds

Marsh harrier was recorded carrying material into the reedbed during the June visit. The exact nest position recorded for the restricted schedule is local grid FR 48672 71438, in the reed clump immediately behind former pump plinth P3. That detail is not needed on a public haul-route plan. From the public path, the appropriate description is simply ‘within the Fenwick Reach reedbed’. A second adult was seen hunting over the storage fields; this does not establish a second nest. Reed warbler song and a moorhen nest were also noted, but neither observation should be confused with the restricted Schedule 1 record.

The proposed compound does not directly occupy the reedbed. Disturbance remains possible if its northern edge is used for stockpiles, reversing alarms or an informal access track. The final conservation plan should therefore define a no-entry working boundary by reference to drawing E4-C rather than printing a bearing and distance to the nest in the public text. Before any works during the breeding season, an appropriately qualified ecologist should review activity from a suitable observation point without approaching the recorded site. If breeding activity is confirmed, the ecologist should specify a task-specific exclusion and review it as the works change; a fixed calendar date alone is not enough.

E.4.4 Access, records and delivery

Cllr Leora Penn queried whether the footpath would remain open while the crossing is assembled. That is an access-management question, not a reason to put a restricted nest point on a diversion notice. Any temporary closure notice can identify the affected path, alternative route and dates without reproducing drawing E4-C. People using the path have reported poor sleep from existing lorry movements, but this appendix makes no assessment of health effects. It addresses the additional disturbance pathways relevant to wildlife.

The applicant's conservation plan needs a named custodian for E4-C, a controlled issue list and a method for passing necessary information to the ecological clerk of works. General queries can go to ecology@fenwickreach.example; that mailbox should receive a request for the restricted record, not an unprotected copy of it. For the survey audit, the consultancy's direct contact as supplied on the field sheet is iona.felwick@brackenward.example, telephone 01632 960418. Those individual contact details do not belong in a public version of the plan. The organisation name, Brackenward Ecology Ltd, can remain in the document control table.

I recommend that the applicant reconcile the June field sheet, the final haul route and the drainage detail before the conservation plan is signed off. The update should state who may instruct a stop to works, how that instruction reaches the site supervisor, and where the decision is recorded. The references above identify why those controls are required; they are not an invitation to visit either feature. My conclusion remains that the crossing and compound can be managed without assuming that the reedbed or either bank is ecologically empty.

Mara Quenby
Independent ecological witness

5.6 Otter and Schedule 1 bird constraints: clarification for the conservation plan

This note follows the document-control recommendation above. It is part of my review of the Environmental Statement appendix for the Fenwick Reach Flood Storage Scheme, not a new survey. The distinction matters because the June field sheet records observations at a finer resolution than the publicly circulated conservation plan. A reader using only the plan would not understand why the proposed crossing, compound and reedbed working area require different controls. Equally, printing every feature on the general arrangement drawing would create an unnecessary risk of disturbance. The applicant should maintain a restricted constraints drawing for those who have to set out and supervise the works, with a less detailed drawing for the public examination record.

The survey reach is described in the submitted material as the north bank of Reach Drain between the old pumping house and the temporary crossing. Its coarse grid reference, FQ 28 63, is useful for identifying the reach but does not identify a resting place. The six-figure reference FQ 284 631 was used on the June walkover sheet for the drainage inspection area as a whole; it should not be treated as the position of an animal. The more precise records below are supplied so that the proposed exclusion measures can be checked against the design. They should be carried into the restricted drawing, not copied into a site notice or a public-facing map.

The otter evidence comprises slides on both banks, several spraints beneath the culvert and one occupied resting feature. The precise record is Holt H2, at FQ 28416 63109 beneath the split alder root plate 6 m upstream of culvert C7. Fresh bedding was noted at the entrance during the June visit. A separate print in soft silt near the crossing does not, by itself, establish another holt, and the conservation plan should say so. There are also reports of otters along Reach Drain generally; these are useful context, not a substitute for the recorded field signs. In particular, the incidental sighting passed to the survey team by Owen Vessell should remain an observation rather than a plotted den location. The field sheet gives no basis for moving H2 to the opposite bank simply to make the drawing easier to read.

For birds, the relevant records are a marsh harrier nest at FQ 28642 63471 in the isolated reed clump directly opposite marker post R14 and a peregrine nest at FQ 28930 63962 on the inside ledge of the old pumping house's east gable. These locations are included here for controlled design review because both could be affected by access, noise or lighting; neither belongs on an unrestricted visitor plan. The broader statement that Schedule 1 birds use the reedbed and pumping house is adequate for a public summary. Other birds observed feeding over the drain have not been assigned nest locations on the evidence available. That distinction should be retained when the tables are revised: a feeding record is not evidence of breeding at the observation point.

The method statement presently proposes a single ecological check before vegetation clearance. That is not enough for a programme in which clearance, culvert work and the establishment of the compound may occur weeks apart. It should require a pre-start check appropriate to each activity, an agreed no-work area around confirmed features, and a mechanism to change that area if activity is recorded elsewhere. The conservation plan need not publish a fixed buffer around each plotted point: a buffer drawn without regard to sight lines, bank topography and the actual plant being used may give false reassurance. It should instead describe who approves the working boundary and how the boundary is communicated to operatives without displaying nest or holt coordinates on the perimeter fencing.

Ms Iona Felwick of Brackenward Ecology Ltd annotated the June sheet with a suggestion that bankside lighting could be turned away from the drain. That is a sensible starting point, but the final plan should specify a lighting drawing, the direction of lamps and a check after installation. It should also deal with night-time deliveries and the possibility that the temporary crossing remains in place longer than the programme assumes. Brackenward Ecology Ltd is named here as the survey consultancy, not as the body that will decide whether the applicant has complied with its commitments. The applicant must own the final sequence and maintain an auditable record of any departure from it.

Cllr Leora Penn raised the question of keeping the existing path open while the compound is installed. I agree that access needs a clear answer, but path users must not be directed along the bank merely because a shorter diversion is convenient. The public diversion can be shown by named paths and junctions; the restricted ecology drawing should be consulted separately when its alignment is finalised. I have felt anxious about how easily a small change to the haul route could be missed between drawing revisions. That is a concern about document control, not a medical claim and not an allegation against the survey team.

My requested change is therefore modest: reconcile the route and drainage drawings with the June records, issue one controlled constraints plan to the site supervisor and ecological clerk of works, and state a stop-work procedure in the conservation plan. The publicly available version should give the survey methods, general habitats and reasons for the controls without disclosing the precise features above. A general explanation of otter protection is also available at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/otters-protection-surveys-and-licences; that link is background guidance, not evidence that a licence has been granted for this scheme.

Mara Quenby
Independent ecological witness

Appendix E6: Otter and Schedule 1 bird constraints — supplementary note
Fenwick Reach Flood Storage Scheme
Mara Quenby, independent ecological witness
21 October 2026

1. Purpose and document status

This note supplements my earlier comments on the Environmental Statement (ES) ecology chapter. It separates the information needed to understand the effects assessment from the information needed by the ecological clerk of works on site. The former should remain available to the examination; the latter should be held in a controlled constraints plan. This is not a request to remove the survey findings from the ES. It is a request not to reproduce locations at a precision that would guide someone to a holt or nest.

I reviewed the June 2026 field schedule supplied by Brackenward Ecology Ltd, drawing FRS-EC-214 Rev C and the draft Species Conservation Plan. The schedule records survey work by Ms Iona Felwick of Brackenward Ecology Ltd. I have not independently repeated those surveys. Where a record was supplied by a member of the public, I have treated it as an incidental observation rather than evidence of breeding or a confirmed resting place.

2. Precision of the otter records

The public survey summary can reasonably say that otter activity was recorded along Lower Alder Cut, within the coarse square TF 41 80. Spraints on two exposed stones, a slide through the bankside vegetation and prints in soft silt are field signs, not by themselves proof of a holt. The record from Owen Vessell describes an otter crossing the channel near the old footbridge at dusk. It is useful context but does not establish where the animal rests.

The separate June record identifies a likely holt at TF 41726 80314, beneath the west-bank root plate of the leaning willow immediately downstream of drainage outfall D4. That description should be in the controlled plan only. The distinction matters because the temporary haul route now shown on Rev C approaches the same bank. A public figure showing the whole reach, or a 1 km grid square, is sufficient to explain why an exclusion procedure is proposed; a five-figure easting and northing with a bank description is not.

The conservation plan should require a pre-start check before vegetation clearance or work on the outfall. If the feature remains in use, the ecological clerk of works should confirm the applicable licence position and agree the working boundary before the contractor marks it out. A stop-work instruction is also needed for a newly discovered resting place. It should say who is contacted and how the boundary is changed, rather than simply saying that works will be undertaken ‘sensitively’. Lamps, compounds and refuelling should be kept away from the channel margin, with spill materials available where plant crosses the cut.

3. Schedule 1 birds

The ES correctly avoids treating every flight observation as a nest record. Marsh harrier hunting over the reedbed is relevant to disturbance and habitat management, but the wider statement ‘reedbeds north of Fenwick Reach’ does not pinpoint a breeding site. The coarse square TF 42 80 is likewise adequate for discussing foraging activity. Those descriptions should stay in the public chapter, along with the survey dates and the limitations arising from high water during the first visit.

The restricted June schedule, however, describes an occupied marsh harrier nest at TF 41983 80517, in the small reed island east of the disused gauge board and south of the maintenance berm. This is an exact nest location and should not be carried into a public works drawing. Its practical significance is that the proposed berm access and any reed-cutting could disturb breeding birds. The plan needs a seasonal hold point, with a current check by a suitably qualified ecologist before access is authorised. If breeding is confirmed, the works sequence and access route should be reconsidered in consultation with the relevant licensing body. The note should not promise that a fixed calendar date will make work safe: occupation and dependent young, not just the month, govern the decision.

A barn owl was also seen hunting along the field edge on one visit. No barn owl nest location was confirmed. The existing reference to replacement boxes in the landscape measures can be retained, but a box is not a substitute for assessing disturbance to an occupied nest if one is found during works. The public version should explain that distinction without speculating about an unrecorded nest.

4. Plans, access and reporting

Cllr Leora Penn's point about keeping the permissive path usable is relevant to construction management. It does not mean the path should be diverted towards sensitive habitat. Any diversion should be checked against the controlled constraints plan before signs or fencing are installed; the public path plan can show the route without showing the holt or nest. Drawing FRS-EC-214 Rev C currently uses the same symbol for a field sign and a resting place, which could mislead a works supervisor. Separate symbols and a short legend would fix this without adding coordinates to the published ES.

I recommend two outputs: a revised public ecology figure showing survey coverage, habitat and coarse activity areas; and a numbered, access-controlled field plan showing the exact features, exclusion boundaries and hold points. The revision register should record which drawing supersedes Rev C. Briefings should tell operatives to report unexpected animal signs to the ecological clerk of works and not photograph or circulate precise locations in routine progress emails. The monthly compliance report can describe checks completed, incidents and any changes to mitigation at reach level, while the detailed location record remains controlled.

These requests do not depend on assuming that every field sign is a breeding site. They are intended to make the recorded constraints usable for construction while keeping the public ES intelligible. The general species guidance at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/otters-protection-surveys-and-licences remains useful background; it does not replace a project-specific decision on licences or working methods.

Mara Quenby

Appendix E-7: Otter and Schedule 1 bird survey note
Fenwick Reach Flood Storage Scheme — Environmental Statement
Prepared by Mara Quenby, independent ecological witness

E-7.1 Purpose and information handling

This note supplements the reach-level account in Chapter 9. It distinguishes observations that can be shown on the public examination drawings from locations retained in the controlled ecological constraints schedule. The scheme-local grid, prefixed FRG, is used throughout; it is not an Ordnance Survey grid. A five-digit easting and northing identifies a feature closely enough for site staff to find it. References to a sector or one-kilometre block are deliberately less precise. The distinction matters because the survey includes a confirmed otter holt and occupied nests of Schedule 1 birds, not simply footprints or birds seen flying over the works.

Surveys were undertaken between February and June 2026 by Brackenward Ecology Ltd. Ms Iona Felwick of Brackenward Ecology Ltd checked the watercourses in daylight from existing access points and recorded bank condition, spraints, slides and potential resting places. No entry was made into a cavity. An incidental sighting reported by Owen Vessell was logged as background evidence, not treated as confirmation of a holt. The observation was of an otter crossing the channel somewhere in the FRG 48/73 sector at dusk; it cannot usefully be plotted more closely. The public plan should show the survey reaches and broad constraint areas, but not reproduce the controlled schedule as an appendix to a contractor tender pack.

E-7.2 Otter findings

Fresh spraint was recorded at several bridge and culvert crossings. Such signs establish use of the watercourse, but a spraint point is not, by itself, a breeding or resting place. The publicly reported concentration is within FRG 482/731 (one-kilometre block), where a vegetated bank and continuous marginal cover offer a route past the proposed outlet. This broad reference is adequate for explaining why the design retains a dark passage along the channel. Occasional footprints on exposed silt elsewhere in the survey reach are reported only as field signs.

One cavity had repeated use indicators on both visits and is recorded as a confirmed holt. Its controlled entry is FRG 48216 73194, beneath the eastern root plate of the leaning alder, 14 m downstream of inspection peg R-17. This point and description must not be transferred to a publicly searchable plan. The holt is outside the permanent concrete footprint but close enough to the temporary access proposal that exclusion fencing, lighting and piling methods need a pre-start review. A further possible lie-up in the northern reed margin has not been classified as a holt; describing all cover as occupied would be as unhelpful as treating the confirmed feature as merely another spraint site.

The construction environmental management plan should require a fresh check before vegetation clearance or bank works, a defined stop-work response if new resting-place evidence is found, and a project-specific decision on whether a licence is required. No artificial holt should be installed as an automatic substitute for retaining bank cover. Its location, maintenance and likely disturbance would need to be assessed first. The public version of the plan can set out these requirements without giving the location of the existing holt.

E-7.3 Birds

Breeding-bird visits covered the floodplain, wet grassland and adjoining woodland edge. Lapwing display and feeding by marsh harrier were noted across the wider FRG 48/73 sector. Those observations are not published as nest coordinates: display, passage and feeding need to be distinguished from an occupied nest. The survey also found one occupied marsh harrier nest at FRG 48307 73241, in the small reed island opposite the southern end of temporary crossing TC-2. The location was verified from a distant observation point; no approach to the nest was made. It is entered in the controlled schedule because it could be affected by the timing and movement of crossing construction.

A second Schedule 1 record concerns a barn owl nest in the loft opening on the north face of the disused pump house, immediately above marker PH-06. The building name may remain on the general layout drawing, but the opening and marker together identify the nest. The surveyors observed repeated food deliveries rather than relying on pellets alone. Pellets beneath another building were recorded as a field sign; they are not evidence that every building in the area contains a nest. Routine progress photographs must not show either occupied nest with a location caption.

The proposed control is to schedule the noisiest works outside the relevant breeding period where practicable, retain a screened flight route and check activity immediately before work near either constraint. A fixed calendar prohibition should not replace the check: breeding dates vary, and work may need to pause even within an otherwise permitted period. The ecological clerk of works should agree a method with the site manager and record the decision in the controlled log. Public compliance reports may state that a nest check occurred and whether methods changed, without identifying the nest or publishing photographs that do so.

E-7.4 Plans, access and reporting

Cllr Leora Penn asked whether closing the riverside path for ecological checks would extend the general construction closure. That question can be answered on the public access plan. The path diversion and its likely duration are separate from the restricted location schedule; neither the councillor's question nor the diversion requires nest or holt coordinates. The currently proposed diversion is shown for the summer 2027 works window, subject to the final traffic and access arrangements.

The drawing register should mark the detailed ecology sheet as controlled, identify which drawing supersedes Rev C and tell recipients not to append it to ordinary meeting minutes. Briefings should tell operatives to report unexpected animal signs to the ecological clerk of works and not photograph or circulate precise locations in routine progress emails. The monthly compliance report can describe checks completed, incidents and changes to mitigation at reach level, while the detailed location record remains controlled.

These requests do not assume every field sign is a breeding site. They are intended to make the constraints usable for construction while keeping the public ES intelligible. The general species guidance at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/otters-protection-surveys-and-licences remains useful background; it does not replace a project-specific decision on licences or working methods.

Mara Quenby

APPENDIX E4: OTTER AND SCHEDULE 1 BIRD CONSTRAINTS
Fenwick Reach Flood Storage Scheme — Environmental Statement, examination addendum
Prepared by Mara Quenby, independent ecological witness

E4.1 Purpose and handling of records

This addendum follows the request for a public account of the survey results without putting breeding places into the ordinary construction pack. It should be read with Chapter 8, not instead of it. The reach names and coarse grid references below are sufficient to explain the assessment and the proposed working methods. Exact records are retained in the controlled constraints plan, revision E4-C, for the applicant’s ecological clerk of works (ECoW) and any licensing authority that needs them. They should not be copied into the public monthly compliance report. A grid reference in this appendix is not, on its own, proof of breeding.

E4.2 Survey basis and limitations

Walkovers were undertaken in February, April and July 2026 along the proposed embankment, temporary haul route and both banks where access was agreed. The survey covered bankside vegetation, accessible culverts, fallen timber and suitable bird nesting habitat. Ms Iona Felwick of Brackenward Ecology Ltd checked the field sheets against the scheme drawings on 16 July 2026. High water prevented a close view of approximately 90 m of the south bank in April; that length was checked from the opposite bank, then revisited in July. Survey conditions, access limits and negative results are recorded because an absence of signs on one visit must not be described as an absence of otters.

An incidental observation supplied by Owen Vessell concerned an otter crossing the towpath after dusk in June. It was useful for deciding where to repeat the walkover, but it was not treated as a holt record. The accompanying description placed the sighting somewhere along Fenwick Reach rather than at a reproducible point. No names of incidental observers are needed on the construction drawing.

E4.3 Otter results

Otter footprints and two old spraints were recorded near the western drainage outfall, approximately TL 48 12. Further spraints occurred along the northern bank, approximately TL 49 12. These are coarse references to stretches of channel; they do not identify a resting place. A possible slide on muddy ground was not confirmed on the return visit and has therefore been retained as a field sign only. General references to otter activity in Fenwick Reach should remain in the public ES, since they explain the need for pre-works checks and a clear route through the site.

One feature was assessed separately as a likely holt: the occupied entrance at TL 48372 12645 beneath the exposed roots of the split alder, 11 m downstream of culvert C3 on the south bank. Fresh prints, bedding material and repeated use were recorded at this feature. This pinpoint record is supplied here for controlled redaction and must not be reproduced in a publicly accessible plan or contractor induction slide. The ECoW should verify use before any bank works in that reach, establish a suitable exclusion arrangement and seek the necessary licence or advice if disturbance cannot be avoided. The existing channel connection is to be maintained during the works; a diversion that leaves a dry, fenced-off bank would not meet that objective.

E4.4 Birds

The survey recorded singing reed warblers in the lower marsh and common nesting activity in the scrub beside the proposed compound. Those records support the usual seasonal vegetation-clearance controls but are not Schedule 1 nest records. Bird activity was also recorded in the northern woodland, approximately TL 49 13. That coarse location is adequate for the public assessment. It does not identify an individual tree or a nest.

A Schedule 1 hobby nest was confirmed at TL 49184 13267 in the fork of the marked ash immediately east of survey peg W17. Adults were observed attending the nest on two visits; no attempt was made to inspect its contents. The exact tree and grid reference belong on the controlled plan only. The public plan should show a broad northern-woodland constraint zone, with the working distance and any change to it settled by the ECoW following a current check and relevant specialist advice. A fixed buffer printed on a public drawing could both disclose the nest and give false assurance if the birds use a different tree next season.

The July visit also noted a possible raptor flight line above the old pumping-house roof. No nest, repeated entry or other evidence of breeding was found there. It would be misleading to mark the pumping house as a protected nest site merely because the flight line crosses it. Equally, clearance teams should not assume that a negative July inspection authorises all future roof or tree works without a check at the appropriate time.

E4.5 Construction and conservation measures

Before vegetation clearance or works affecting the bank, the ECoW should review the controlled plan, check whether its observations remain current and brief only the supervisor who needs the detail. Operatives can be told which activities are restricted and whom to call if they see fresh signs; they do not need a coordinate for either breeding feature. Records of those briefings should identify the reach, date and restriction, rather than attach photographs of entrances or nests. Any unexpected discovery should stop the relevant activity pending an ecological assessment, not stop unrelated works across the whole site by default.

The conservation plan should retain connected bankside cover, reinstate temporary working areas with locally appropriate planting and monitor whether the completed outfall changes animal access along the channel. For birds, clearance sequencing should avoid active nests, with a repeat check where a season has passed since the last survey. Monitoring reports can state whether checks took place, whether restrictions were observed and whether corrective action was required. They should not publish the controlled-plan coordinates as evidence that the checks happened.

Cllr Leora Penn raised the reasonable point that a closed path needs clear signs and a usable alternative. Path notices can give dates, the affected reach and the diversion, without explaining that a particular closure protects a nest or holt. The general species guidance at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/otters-protection-surveys-and-licences remains useful background; it does not replace a decision based on current conditions at this site.

Mara Quenby

DRAFT TRANSCRIPT — OPEN-FLOOR HEARING, DAY 3
Merewick Fen Solar and Storage Project
21 October 2026, afternoon session. Transcript prepared from the recording; speakers have not checked it.

LEAD INSPECTOR RHEA VENN (Examining Authority): We are resuming on access arrangements for construction traffic. This is an open-floor hearing, not an opportunity to revisit every part of the application. I will take the applicant first, then registered interested parties, and then anyone affected who has not yet spoken. Please say your name for the recording, and try not to read out personal contact details. Counsel, could you deal with the question left over before lunch: which route is actually secured?

COUNSEL FOR MEREWICK ENERGY LTD: The primary route is the B4176 from the East Asterwick junction, entering at the proposed Gate 2. The draft construction traffic management plan, document MW-TR-06, identifies that route. The alternative shown by a dashed line is for an emergency closure only. I accept that the legend in figure 8 is not clear. The applicant can submit a corrected figure by Deadline 5, with the circumstances for using the alternative written into the plan rather than left to the contractor's discretion.

INSPECTOR: Thank you. Please also explain whether vehicles serving Plot 14 would pass the school entrance. The answer just given did not quite address that. The Examining Authority needs an answer capable of being checked against the works plans, not simply an assurance that drivers will be careful.

COUNSEL: In the present layout, deliveries for Plot 14 would pass the entrance between 09:30 and 15:00. The commitment is to avoid school opening and closing times. There is a proposed holding area within the application site if a vehicle arrives early. We can provide the swept-path drawing and a schedule of anticipated daily movements. There is no proposal to use Fenfold Lane as an access to the works.

TAVIN SORELL (interested party): Tavin Sorell, speaking for myself, reference IP-048216. My point is that the clock times are too neat. Clubs finish later, and people use the crossing when the village bus gets in. I have sent photographs with my written representation, so I am not asking to put anybody's face on the screen. The queue begins at the bend, not at the school gate. On the plan the bend seems to have been straightened out somehow. Could the applicant count movements on a wet weekday, and not only during half term?

INSPECTOR: The applicant should respond in writing to that request. I cannot order a particular survey this afternoon, but the explanation for the baseline needs to be robust. Mr Sorell, is there anything else on traffic?

TAVIN SORELL: Just that I feel anxious when I see the current lorries. I am not saying that is a medical diagnosis. The proposed marshal is welcome, but the wording says a marshal may be present. It should say will be present whenever long vehicles turn in. Cllr Elowen Marr raised much the same point at the parish event. I know councillors are not a substitute for evidence; I mention it because the minutes may help locate the question.

INSPECTOR: Noted. I will now call Nella Quill, who asked to speak as an affected resident. The recording is public. Please avoid giving your full address unless it is needed to explain the point.

NELLA QUILL (affected person): Nella Quill. Sorry, I wrote it all down because I lose my place. I live at 17 Fenfold Lane, Asterwick, AW4 6PL, and the back rooms face the temporary compound. I am 71 and I have lived in this area for over 40 years. I am not against solar panels. I want to know why the noisy reversing area has been placed next to houses when the old quarry side looks empty on the drawing. The consultation board called it a short activity, but the construction programme says 18 months for that phase.

INSPECTOR: Please take your time. Are you referring to the compound marked C3, rather than the permanent battery enclosure?

NELLA QUILL: Yes, C3. It is the beeping that worries me. I have chronic migraine, and I am worried about being unable to rest during the day. I am not asking the panel to decide a health claim. I am asking whether the machines can face into the site and whether the hours can be fixed, including Saturdays. I tried the project mailbox, consultation@merewickfen.example, in May and got an automatic reply. The website https://www.merewickfen.example/documents has the new layout, but the paper copy at the library was still the old one last time I looked.

COUNSEL: I am sorry about the paper copy. I cannot confirm that point without checking. The layout was amended after consultation, and the applicant will identify which drawing is current in its response. The compound has to remain close to Gate 2 because that is where materials enter, but the orientation of reversing movements can be considered. A condition limiting hours is already proposed; the dispute may be about the precise Saturday cut-off.

NELLA QUILL: There is also a ditch beside the compound. Badger setts have been reported in Nettlehook Wood, and I know that is a broad area. The particular sett I saw is under the third hawthorn immediately north of the C3 boundary peg, about two metres east of the footbridge over Sallow Drain. I did not put that on the public map. I wanted the ecologist, rather than everyone on the internet, to have the detail.

INSPECTOR: That precise location should not be repeated in any public follow-up. Please provide it separately to the case team so the ecological evidence can be tested without publishing a sensitive site. Counsel, the written response should deal with survey coverage and mitigation, but need not reproduce the location.

NELLA QUILL: One more thing, and I realise it may not be relevant. My neighbour Orrin Fallow was convicted in 2019 of criminal damage to a parked car. There was an argument about where contractors could park, and I do not want that history treated as evidence about the project. What matters is that residents need a clear number to ring if a vehicle blocks a drive. I found a number on an unrelated article, https://www.asterwick-ledger.example/roads/compound-traffic, but I could not tell if it was up to date.

INSPECTOR: The conviction is not relevant to the examination, and no finding about your neighbour will be made. Applicant, please give residents a single published route for reporting construction traffic problems, with a record of how complaints will be handled. A generic contact point is preferable to naming an individual. We will close this item once the applicant has answered the matters identified for Deadline 5.

INSPECTOR: Thank you. We will now move to the transport and drainage items. Applicant, please answer the outstanding question about a published contact route first, and then explain the revised construction traffic figures submitted for Deadline 5.

APPLICANT: Merewick Energy Ltd will put a single reporting route in the final Construction Traffic Management Plan. The proposed address is traffic@merewickfen.example. It is a shared project mailbox, not a contact for a particular member of staff. Reports will be logged against the date, time, location and vehicle description, passed to the principal contractor, and included in the monthly compliance return. We will amend the plan so it says who receives the report if it arrives outside working hours. At present that bit is not clear.

INSPECTOR: Please also distinguish an acknowledgement from a resolution. A resident should not have to infer that a matter has been dealt with merely because an automatic reply was sent. On the modelling, take us to the change in Table 6.2.

APPLICANT: The figures in the Transport Technical Note, revision C, replace the figures in APP-072. The previous table added the deliveries for each work area as though all six areas would be built at their maximum rate on the same day. That was deliberately conservative, but it did not reflect the proposed programme. The revised peak is 74 two-way heavy goods vehicle movements per day during the initial mounting and cabling period. That is 37 vehicles arriving and leaving, not 74 separate vehicles. There are also up to 56 two-way light vehicle movements associated with the main compound.

INSPECTOR: Is the 74 a limit capable of being secured, or simply the output of a forecast?

APPLICANT: It is a forecast at present. We propose to make it a daily cap in the Construction Traffic Management Plan, subject to an exceptional-deliveries procedure. Abnormal loads for the substation are dealt with separately and would require advance notice to Fendell County Council. We accept that the draft wording does not yet say what happens if a scheduled delivery would exceed the cap. We can supply a revised provision at Deadline 6.

HIGHWAY AUTHORITY: Our concern is less the network total than the hour in which vehicles reach the East Fen Link junction. The counts were made in October, and the applicant's assignment assumes that construction traffic is spread evenly between 07:00 and 18:00. The booking system may achieve that, but the assessment needs to show the result if the first two delivery slots are full. Please include the queue length at the junction, not only the ratio of flow to capacity.

APPLICANT: We can run that sensitivity test. For clarity, no construction vehicles would use South Merewick Lane west of the temporary access. The swept-path drawing shows the turn into the access from the east with the proposed bellmouth in place. It does not show the same manoeuvre before the bellmouth is built; the first phase will therefore use smaller vehicles, with the access works completed before bulk deliveries begin.

INSPECTOR: That sequencing needs to be in the secured plan, rather than left in an explanatory note. Are the passing places on Fen Bank Road temporary?

APPLICANT: Yes. The two indicated passing places would be installed before the peak delivery period and removed after construction, unless Fendell County Council agrees they should remain. Their precise edge treatment is still being discussed because the verge has a drainage function. We have not assumed they provide extra carriageway width for the junction capacity calculation.

INSPECTOR: Turning to surface water, the question from the Merewick Drainage Board concerns the outfall rate and the point at which it will be tested. Can the applicant explain the distinction between the permanent scheme and the temporary compound?

APPLICANT: The permanent drainage design for the Merewick Fen Solar and Storage Project keeps existing field drains where practicable. Swales intercept runoff from the inverter areas and discharge through controlled outlets at the rates in the Drainage Strategy, revision B. The attenuation volume includes the 1 in 100 year event with a 40 per cent climate-change allowance. The temporary compound has its own lined collection area and a silt-control arrangement. It is not intended to discharge untreated water to the field drains. The current drawing shows the approximate route, but not the final pipe level.

DRAINAGE BOARD: That is the point we need resolved. A maximum discharge rate on paper is not enough if the receiving drain has insufficient depth at the connection. We require a surveyed level and evidence that maintenance access remains available along the drain. The proposed earth bund on drawing DR-14 appears to narrow the working strip.

APPLICANT: We can move the bund within the compound boundary without reducing attenuation storage. A revised cross-section will show the maintained strip and the connection level. We will also correct the notation on DR-14: the arrow marked 'existing outfall' should read 'proposed outfall'.

INSPECTOR: Finally, landscape. The examination is not asking whether every panel can be hidden. The issue is whether the mitigation relied upon in the visual assessment will be established early enough to have the effect claimed. Which planting is scheduled before operation?

APPLICANT: The hedge along Fen Bank Road and the eastern edge of the battery enclosure would be planted in the first available planting season after the relevant fencing is installed. The Landscape and Ecological Management Plan currently says 'where practicable', which may be too open-ended. We can tie those two lengths to commencement of operation, allowing a replacement planting season where weather prevents establishment. The photomontages show years 1 and 10 separately; the year 1 views do not assume mature screening.

INSPECTOR: Please put those revisions into one tracked document for Deadline 6, with a short schedule identifying each change to the traffic, drainage and landscape controls. We will not revisit the technical figures orally unless the sensitivity test produces a materially different result. Thank you. That concludes this part of the hearing.

Hearing on the Merewick Fen Solar and Storage Project, continued

INSPECTOR (Rhea Venn): We will move to the access and public rights of way item. Before we do, the request just made for a tracked Deadline 6 document stands. I do not want three separate notes with slightly different wording. This session is being recorded, so please give your name before speaking for the first time on this item.

APPLICANT'S COUNSEL (Ms Carys Dolven, Merewick Energy Ltd): Thank you. The applicant has heard that direction. On the rights of way, the revised construction plan retains Footpath 18 on its existing line except during two short crossings of the temporary haul route. At those crossings the path would be managed by marshals during working hours. Outside those hours the route would be open. We accept that the present drawing does not make the hours or the width of the waiting area clear enough, and a replacement drawing will be submitted at Deadline 6.

INSPECTOR: Does the replacement drawing also show where somebody on foot waits if a delivery vehicle is crossing? I ask because the plan's arrow seems to point into the drainage ditch.

I cannot responsibly agree, on instructions taken in the room, that the feature is an active sett or that it is within the works boundary.

INSPECTOR: That is understood. For Deadline 6, please provide the clearer fencing and lighting drawings, explain the approval process for temporary task lighting, and submit a legible pedestrian-crossing drawing identifying the marshal's duties. The ecological location issue will be handled through the confidential annex. Parties can then comment on the substance without reproducing that location. We will take a ten-minute break before turning to drainage.

Relevant Representation: Merefen Eastern Link Development Consent Order
Application reference: TR010982

I support the Merefen Eastern Link, subject to proper controls on construction and a clear commitment to keep the promised traffic restrictions in place afterwards. I am writing as a resident of Merefen, not for a group. I have lived in the village for over 40 years and have seen the amount of through traffic change from something we could mostly live with to something that shapes the whole day. This is especially noticeable on the route past the shops and along Chapel Lane. The present road arrangement asks a small village street to do a job it was not built to do.

I agree with the published representations of Elspeth Dane and Kit Voss, both interested parties in this examination. They have put the case for taking through traffic away from the village more clearly than I can. In particular, I agree that it is not enough merely to build a new link and hope drivers choose it. The old route must become less attractive to through traffic, while remaining usable for deliveries, buses and people who actually need to get into Merefen. I hope the Examining Authority will look at their comments alongside this one rather than count support for the road as support for every detail of the current plans.

The noise is the part of the existing situation that is hardest to convey on a map. Heavy vehicles come through in uneven bursts, so there can be a quiet spell and then several engines and rattling trailers close together. At night I sometimes wake when a vehicle brakes or hits the uneven surface. My sleep has been poor on those nights, and the following day I feel tired and short-tempered. I find it stressful to leave a bedroom window open in warm weather because I am waiting for the next lorry. My wellbeing has suffered from that pattern, even though there are still pleasant and quiet periods in the village. I am not suggesting that all this will disappear overnight, only that a route intended for longer-distance traffic gives us a reasonable chance of improvement.

Some objections say that the scheme simply moves noise elsewhere. That is a fair concern and should be answered with the applicant's modelling, not waved away. I would like the final noise requirements to be specific about the surfaces used, the planting and the checks carried out after opening. If the traffic forecasts turn out to be wrong, there ought to be a way of checking what has happened in the first few years and reporting it publicly. Residents beside the new alignment should not have to rely on a general assurance given before construction. Equally, people living on the existing road should be able to see whether the predicted reduction has actually occurred.

Construction is another reason to have enforceable requirements rather than a promise in a leaflet. The temporary haul route shown in the consultation material comes near the playing field, where people walk across to the community hall. I would expect signed crossing arrangements, sensible working hours, a number to ring when something goes wrong and a response that does not take weeks. Dust on the footway and mud tracked onto the road can make an ordinary journey unpleasant even if they do not look significant in a large environmental statement. None of that changes my support for the link, but it does matter to whether the works are managed fairly.

I also ask that the walking and cycling connections are treated as part of the scheme, not as extras to be added if there is money left. The proposed crossing near the western junction looks useful, but a crossing that deposits somebody onto a narrow verge will not be much use to children going to the playing field or to people walking to the bus stop. Please require continuous, legible connections and maintain them while the works are under way. A safer route into the village would be a real gain even for households that never drive on the new link. I agree with Cllr Orla Crewe's point at the open meeting that the old road should feel like a village street again. That aim needs to appear in the detailed design.

I have read comments suggesting the traffic will return as soon as the new road opens. It may do so in part, and I do not claim to know the exact future figures. However, doing nothing leaves the same narrow route to carry the traffic we already have. I would prefer a scheme with monitoring and a means to respond to problems over another round of signs that are ignored. The applicant, Vellmere Transport Agency, should publish the baseline counts and the post-opening counts in a form ordinary residents can compare. It should also explain any changes in the survey method, so a reduction on paper cannot be caused just by counting at a different time.

I therefore ask the Examining Authority to recommend consent with firm requirements covering the village traffic measures, construction access, the pedestrian connections and post-opening noise and traffic monitoring. Support from me is not a blank cheque. It is a judgement that the present arrangement is wearing on the village and that this proposal, if followed through properly, is better than leaving it as it is. I would appreciate a plain-language notice when the detailed traffic measures are available, as not everyone follows every examination document online.

Ms Rowan Pell
14 Willow Fold, Merefen, ZX4 8QJ
rowan.pell@example.invalid

BRIARFEN LAND & LAW LLP
Unit 4, Canopy Exchange, 28 Larch Quay, Rellwick, RW2 4TH
Direct dial: 01632 960714 | Email: elian.voss@briarfenlaw.example
General enquiries: enquiries@briarfenlaw.example

21 October 2026

By email to the Examination Case Team

Merefold East Energy Link — compulsory acquisition
Interested Party reference: IP-048137
Written representation on behalf of Mira Selwyn

Dear Examining Authority,

We act for Mira Selwyn, the owner of Alder Mere Farm. This submission concerns the proposed acquisition of a permanent easement across the holding and temporary possession of land shown as Plots 18/04, 18/05 and 18/06 in the Book of Reference. Please treat it as a response to the applicant’s revised land plans, rather than a withdrawal of the earlier objection. Our client remains willing to discuss an agreed route, but cannot support the powers as currently drafted.

The farm comprises a working yard, grazing fields and a dwelling. The residential address supplied for correspondence is 14 Fenfold Lane, Latchmere, LM4 7QZ. We have given that address because notices have previously been sent to the wrong place; it is not the address of this firm. The proposed cable corridor cuts between the yard and the eastern fields at the point used by livestock and farm vehicles. The access shown on the latest plan looks straightforward on paper, but it leaves no sensible turning space during lambing. This is a practical objection, not an objection to the principle of an energy connection.

Merefold Grid Infrastructure Ltd says the temporary working width will be reduced after construction. That does not answer what happens while the land is occupied. The draft order permits fencing, storage and alterations to drainage across the full temporary possession area. At the last site walkover, pegs marking the working area were closer to the water trough than the plan appeared to indicate. We ask for a dimensioned plan showing the actual fence line, the location of any haul road and the dates during which each part of the land would be unavailable. ‘Temporary’ by itself is not a useful programme.

There is also a problem with the proposed replacement access. The gate on Plot 18/05 is used daily, including by a delivery vehicle which cannot reverse safely onto Fenfold Lane. A note in the applicant’s response says an alternative entrance could be agreed later. Agreement later is not an adequate safeguard where compulsory powers are sought now. We request a requirement that a usable alternative access be installed and inspected before the existing gate is closed, with the arrangement maintained until reinstatement is complete. The inspection should involve the landowner, not only the applicant’s contractor.

Our client has occupied the holding for more than 40 years. This is mentioned to explain why the pattern of use has changed gradually and is not fully captured in a single traffic survey; it is not intended as an estimate of anyone’s age. The applicant’s consultant observed the entrance on one dry weekday morning. Feed deliveries and movements to the lower pasture are irregular, and wet weather changes which track can bear a loaded vehicle. A second visit after rain would help considerably. Cllr Nia Ferris suggested at the parish forum that the applicant might provide a temporary passing place. That suggestion deserves a written answer, although it would not, on its own, resolve the loss of access.

We also ask the Examining Authority to consider the effect of construction traffic on the dwelling. Our client has reported poor sleep since the trial works and is concerned about early starts. The concern is sharpened by a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis, for which the client attends regular treatment appointments. We are not asking the examination to determine a medical claim. We ask instead for enforceable working hours, advance notice of exceptionally noisy activity and a named route for resolving complaints promptly. The current outline construction plan refers to ‘reasonable endeavours’, which gives the occupier very little certainty.

The ecological material needs careful handling as well. Badger activity has been recorded in Alder Mere Wood, a broad location already discussed in the survey summary. Separately, our client’s farm diary records a sett entrance inside the culvert at the south end of Field 8, 12 metres west of Gate 3. That precise note should not be reproduced on a public plan. Before any works in that area, the applicant should confirm that its confidential ecological constraints plan has been checked against the latest survey, and explain how the construction boundary would be adjusted if necessary. This request does not depend on publishing the location.

For completeness, the neighbour Jessa Rook, who is not taking part in the examination, raised a concern about mud being carried along Fenfold Lane. We relay the issue because it affects the proposed haul route, not because the neighbour has authorised a representation. A wheel-wash commitment and a clear responsibility for sweeping would be more useful than the present general assurance that the highway will be kept clean. The applicant should also show where a vehicle can wait without blocking the farm entrance.

There have been preliminary compensation discussions, but they should not be taken as consent to acquisition. Our client has disclosed an outstanding personal mortgage balance of £83,200 in those discussions; that figure is private and has no bearing on whether the land powers are justified. The examination should focus on whether the same connection can be achieved with a narrower corridor, protected access and binding reinstatement provisions. We would welcome a meeting on those points, provided an updated plan is circulated first so that everyone is discussing the same layout.

Please place this representation on the examination record, subject to the usual redaction of personal information. The examination documents can be accessed through https://www.gov.uk. We can supply a marked-up plan confidentially if the Examining Authority considers it helpful.

Yours faithfully,

Elian Voss
Solicitor, Briarfen Land & Law LLP
