I have lived in this area for over 40 years and the bend by the old bakery has always been awkward, even with ordinary delivery vans. Please require a peak-hour assessment and a properly drawn walking route, not just a promise that drivers will be briefed.

The noise chapter also needs another look. It gives figures at a modelled receptor behind the terrace, but our bedrooms are at the front and we open the windows in summer. I have diagnosed asthma and am concerned about dust when the road surface is broken up. My mother, Nella Venn, lives with us and has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. I am not asking the examination to decide anyone's medical care; I want the applicant to say what will actually be measured at the houses, how quickly residents will get the results, and who has the power to stop work if the limits are exceeded. At present the complaints procedure reads as though someone will phone back when convenient. The prospect of months of work also makes me anxious and I am sleeping badly, although I know that by itself is not a technical objection.

Our neighbours have tried to find out more than the drawings show. Mrs Elsie Lark at the adjoining house told me that a surveyor had asked to enter the back garden, but the leaflet delivered to the terrace said all surveys were complete. I do not know which account is right. Another neighbour, Dain Lark, pointed out that the temporary fence shown on Sheet 14 seems to cut across the shared access used for bins and emergency vehicles. Neither neighbour has made a representation, as far as I know. The applicant should provide a scaled access drawing that shows the gates open, a refuse vehicle turning and a person walking past safely. A note saying ‘access maintained’ is not enough.

I attended the public event on 16 September 2026. The boards were helpful as far as they went, but the team could not tell me whether the compound would be lit throughout the night. Cllr Tovin Baird asked about the same issue at the council meeting, according to the published minutes. The answer should be secured in the requirements, including the height and direction of the lights, rather than left to a later contractor's decision. I agree with the point in Mira Gossett's published representation about checking glare from upstairs windows; that is a different view from the street-level photograph in the environmental statement.

There is wildlife in the strip of land beside the proposed works. I have seen badger activity in Brindle Copse, and people have reported bats around the old pumphouse. I understand that a broad description like this is not evidence that every tree should be left alone. However, the survey map I was shown marks a badger sett on the east bank of the drainage ditch, 14 metres north of the stile at the southern end of plot 18B. The ecological note also identifies a bat maternity roost behind the third loose slate above the western gable of the old pumphouse in plot 19C. Those locations ought not to be put on a public construction drawing. The examination should nevertheless test whether the proposed working width and night lighting can be changed to protect them. A general commitment to ecological supervision does not explain what happens if the contractor finds that the marked exclusion area is too narrow.

Drainage is another practical worry. After prolonged rain, water runs off Mardley Lane and collects against the terrace wall. The application describes new channels at the compound, but I cannot find a section showing where that water goes while the existing ditch is temporarily crossed. The applicant should provide the temporary drainage design before consent, or at least a binding requirement with a clear approval process and an opportunity for Pellmere Borough Council to review it. Otherwise any problem will only be obvious once the first winter storm arrives.

Finally, the claim that disruption will be brief should be explained in terms residents can use. I still owe £83,400 on the mortgage, so I cannot simply move away for the construction period. I am not seeking compensation through this representation. I want a workable schedule, advance notice of road closures in plain language, and a named point of contact. A shared address such as planning@vellmeregrid.example would be fine if someone actually monitors it and records what action follows a complaint. Please do not treat my objection as opposition to the need for electricity infrastructure. It is an objection to this layout and to leaving its most difficult details until after permission has been given.

Rory Venn

Additional points attached to my relevant representation
Alderfen Energy Link

I am adding this because the online form did not give me enough room to explain what the construction drawings mean for people on Reedglass Close. My name is Rory Venn and I live at 14 Reedglass Close, Pellmere, PM4 8QL. My reference on the portal is IP-AL-2048. I understand that the Examining Authority will consider the application as a whole, but I ask that this note is read with my earlier comments about the access road and drainage. I am objecting to the present layout, not saying that no cable or substation should ever be built near Pellmere.

The revised traffic plan still shows lorries turning into the lane opposite our front windows. The line marked as the waiting area is not an empty verge. School children use it when two vehicles meet, because the footway ends before the bend. My daughter Una Venn, now 11, catches the school bus there. This is a daily journey, not a point about a theoretical pedestrian in a transport model. Vellmere Grid Developments Ltd should show where people are supposed to stand during the morning peak if a delivery is held at the gate. Putting up a sign saying pedestrians have priority will not create space where there is none.

At the adjoining house, Mrs Elsie Lark uses the same stretch of lane to reach the bus stop. Dain Lark, who lives there too and has not made a representation as far as I know, asked me whether the temporary traffic lights would operate on Saturdays. I could not find a definite answer in the latest management plan. I am mentioning the question, not speaking for either neighbour. It matters because weekend closures would also affect deliveries to our street, including grocery deliveries for people who cannot easily carry shopping from the main road. The applicant's estimate of a few minutes of delay does not answer what happens when a bus arrives while a wide load is being escorted through.

There is also a health issue which I did not explain clearly in the form. I have asthma, and dust from repeated dry-weather vehicle movements is a different matter from an occasional muddy wheel. My mother, Nella Venn, lives with me and is 74. Nella has type 2 diabetes and attends regular appointments outside Pellmere. I am not asking the Inspectorate to make medical judgments. I am asking for a route to those appointments that remains usable when the lane is closed, and for a dust-monitoring point at the houses rather than only at the site boundary. I am anxious about the works, but that feeling is not the same thing as the practical difficulty of rearranging transport at short notice.

My daughter has a diagnosed sensory processing disorder. Sudden alarms and reversing signals can make the morning trip to the bus difficult, so notice of exceptionally noisy work would help us plan. It would also help everyone else. A leaflet delivered after a contractor has changed the programme is not advance notice. Could the applicant commit to publishing the next two weeks of noisy operations every Friday, with a simple correction notice if the programme changes? The proposed community liaison meetings are welcome, but some residents work at the advertised time and cannot attend. Written questions sent to planning@vellmeregrid.example should receive a dated reply, even if the answer is that a technical point needs checking.

On ecology, I am concerned that the survey map available to residents is so broad that it conceals where protective fencing will actually go. I am not requesting publication of sensitive locations. During the site walk I was shown the occupied badger sett under the eastern bank of the drainage ditch, 18 metres south of gate G3 on parcel AF-17. That position should not be copied into a public construction notice; it needs to be checked privately against the haul-road design before the route is fixed. Badgers have also been seen in Robin's Spinney, but that general observation does not identify another sett. Likewise, talk of bats somewhere along the Pellmere hedgerows is too vague to settle whether lighting at the gate is safe. The ecological clerk of works should have authority to stop a task, not merely report a concern afterwards.

Cllr Tovin Baird said at the public meeting that Pellmere Borough Council had asked for clearer drawings of the ditch crossing. That is consistent with what I heard, although I cannot say what correspondence has passed between the council and the applicant. Mira Gossett raised a similar issue in a published representation, particularly the difference between the outline drainage arrows and the levels shown in the engineering appendix. I agree with that specific point. My own worry is that runoff will collect at the low end of Reedglass Close before anyone can establish whose drain is blocked. Please require the applicant to identify who will inspect the crossing after heavy rain and how a resident can report standing water.

For completeness, the blue hatchback sometimes shown in photographs of the bend, registration PE26 XRV, is my vehicle. The photographs were taken to show the width left for pedestrians, not to make a complaint about somebody's parking. Please remove the registration if those images are put on the public examination page. I also found an article at https://www.pellmere-ledger.example/story/287 which repeats an old construction timetable; I do not rely on that article as evidence. The drawings submitted for this examination ought to be the source of any dates given to residents, with changes plainly marked instead of buried in a replacement appendix.

I have lived in Pellmere for over 40 years and know that the lane has always been awkward. That does not make a new daily stream of heavy vehicles harmless. I have only £1,250 in my savings account, so paying for taxis whenever the bus cannot reach the stop is not a realistic fallback for my household. I would welcome an escorted pedestrian route, a published delivery window avoiding the school bus, and an independently checked drainage plan. If those matters can be secured before construction starts, residents will at least know what is meant to happen and who is responsible when it does not.

Rory Venn

Further points on the Alderfen Energy Link — relevant representation from Rory Venn

I object to the proposed construction arrangements, rather than to the idea that the electricity network needs improving. My earlier comments dealt with the bus, deliveries and drainage. I am adding these points because the construction drawings leave out what daily life on the lane will actually be like. Please treat this as part of my relevant representation, not as an allegation against the workforce.

The current traffic plan shows a vehicle count at the junction with Bellwether Road but not at the pinch point outside our row of houses. That is where two cars already have to negotiate past each other. The applicant says banksmen will be used where necessary. I cannot tell whether that means every delivery, only abnormal loads, or only when somebody complains. A condition ought to say which, and the banksman should be in place before a lorry enters the lane. A driver cannot safely reverse all the way back to Bellwether Road if another lorry is behind.

At home, my 11-year-old daughter, Una Venn, uses the school bus stop on the other side of the pinch point. Please do not publish my daughter's age or name in a public version. My mother, Nella Venn, lives with me and cannot simply wait outside for a delayed bus in bad weather. The notice says that access will be maintained, but access for a car is not the same thing as a safe walking route. I ask for a continuous temporary footway, with a drawing showing its width at the narrowest place, and a named person responsible for checking barriers at the start of each school day.

I also have diagnosed asthma, and dust from earthworks is a practical concern for me. My mother has been treated for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide what medical care anyone needs. I am asking it to require a dust plan that specifies monitoring points on the residential side of the work area, a trigger for stopping particularly dusty work, and a way for households to see the readings without making a formal information request. Poor sleep and worry during the works will affect the household too, but those effects are different from the conditions I have mentioned.

The adjoining household has not joined this examination. Mrs Elsie Lark told me that the temporary compound boundary appears, on the latest plan, to run much nearer the garden gate than on the leaflet delivered last winter. Dain Lark was present when we compared the two sheets. I do not claim to speak on behalf of either neighbour. I mention the conversation because the applicant could resolve it for everybody by publishing one dimensioned plan of the compound edge, together with a simple record of what changed between versions. Reassurances given at a drop-in are no substitute for that drawing.

For completeness, my correspondence address is 14 Spindle Close, Pellmere, PM4 7QJ. My personal email is rory.venn@postmere.example and my telephone number is 07123 456 804. I have been assigned IP reference 20098471. I give those details so the case team can reach me, not because they are needed on the public website. I am not seeking a private meeting or special treatment.

There is an ecology point as well. I support the proposal to retain the hedge beside Alderfen Wood and to check it before clearance. References to badgers in Alderfen Wood are too broad to settle where protective fencing should go. In the field sketch I sent with my earlier comments, the active badger sett is in the bank 6 metres east of the southern stile on Footpath 9, beneath the split ash tree. That location should be available to the ecologist and the Examining Authority, but not reproduced on a public plan. I have seen bats along the lane in the evenings; that is a general observation, not evidence of a maternity roost. The ecology measures should be tested against the final working width, rather than a line on a drawing that may still move.

Cllr Tovin Baird said at the public meeting that the council would ask for a clearer explanation of the diversion. That was helpful, though it is not itself a commitment from the applicant. Mira Gossett's published representation makes a related point about emergency access, and I agree with that part of it. Pellmere Borough Council's planning office at Civic House, 6 Market Yard, Pellmere, PM4 2AB should be given the final traffic schedule at the same time as residents. A shared contact address, planning@pellmere.gov.example, would be more useful during construction than another leaflet telling us to consult a large document library.

I looked for the latest examination documents at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects but had difficulty identifying which traffic drawing had superseded which. A local discussion page at https://pellmere-lane-forum.example/works-notes has photographs of the puddling after rain, although I understand those photographs are not the applicant's drainage evidence. Vellmere Grid Developments Ltd should provide a short, dated change log alongside its formal plans, so residents do not have to rely on an outside website to work out what is proposed.

I ask the Examining Authority to examine the pedestrian route, delivery controls, dust monitoring and drainage together. Each might look acceptable in isolation. They will be experienced together at the same narrow part of the lane, sometimes on the same morning. If the details cannot yet be fixed, the requirement should set a clear approval process before works begin, with the approved drawings and monitoring results made easy for the public to find.

Further to my points about the lane, I object to the Alderfen Energy Link as currently drawn. My name is Rory Venn and I am writing for myself, not for a residents' group. Our household is at 14 Sedgeglass Lane, Pellmere, PM4 7QX. I give the address because the distance between the front door and the proposed works access matters to this objection, but I do not consent to it being put on a public map of objectors. My Interested Party reference is IP-2047-PL. I have lived in Pellmere for over 40 years and remember other utility works on this route, but nothing with the proposed combination of vehicle movements, fencing and temporary footway changes.

The traffic note counts movements across a whole working day. That conceals what happens between school drop-off and the first deliveries. My daughter Una Venn, aged 11, walks to the bus stop with me. At the bend, the available pavement is already narrowed by the drain cover and the wall. The proposed drawing shows a pedestrian corridor there, but does not say who will keep it open when a delivery vehicle is waiting for the gate. Please require a dimensioned drawing of the usable width, not just a coloured line. It should show the gate fully open, with a vehicle in the position it will actually occupy. A marshal cannot make a narrow gap wider.

I have spoken to Mrs Elsie Lark at the adjoining house, 16 Sedgeglass Lane, Pellmere, PM4 7QX, and to Dain Lark about the same bend. Neither neighbour asked me to speak on their behalf or intends to register in the examination. They described drivers reversing after taking the wrong entrance, which matches what I have seen. I am not offering their account as a traffic survey. It does, however, show why the proposed sign on the gate is not enough. A driver who discovers the mistake at the bend has very little room to turn without using the pedestrian space. The construction traffic plan should specify where such drivers go and how residents can report a breach while it is happening.

Dust is not only a question of the average reading at the site boundary. I have diagnosed asthma and use an inhaler; my concern is the short period when material is tipped or swept near our windows. My mother Nella Venn, aged 73, lives with me and has rheumatoid arthritis, which makes a quick trip around a blocked route difficult. These details are provided to explain why an instruction simply to remain indoors or take another path is not an adequate answer for this household. Noise and uncertainty are also causing poor sleep, but I am not suggesting that poor sleep is a medical diagnosis. A monitoring point near the works gate, with results published weekly, would be more useful than a monitor at the far end of the compound.

There is an ecological point which I did not put in my earlier comments because the maps then available were too coarse. Badger activity has been reported in Bracken Holt; that is a broad area and not, by itself, a reason to close the route. During the site walk I was shown that the badger sett is beneath the eastern face of the old lime kiln, 12 metres south of gate K3. I ask that the precise position is kept out of the public version of any response, while the relevant ecologist checks whether the revised fencing reaches it. The public needs to know the outcome and any mitigation, not directions to the sett.

I have read Mira Gossett's published representation on the flood modelling and agree with the request for the assumptions behind the winter runoff figures. The photograph attached to my first submission showed water across the lane after ordinary rain, not an exceptional storm. Pellmere Borough Council's drainage comments also appear to discuss the earlier compound layout. If Vellmere Grid Developments Ltd says the layout has changed, it should identify which drainage calculation changed with it. The project document list at https://alderfen-energy.example/documents/traffic is helpful for finding drawings, but an updated filename is not a substitute for a change log. I have also seen discussion at https://pellmere-community-notes.example/drainage; that is not formal evidence and I cite it only to explain why residents are asking which drawing is current.

At the public meeting, Cllr Tovin Baird asked whether the bus stop could remain in use throughout the works. The reply, as I noted it, was that this would be considered with the contractor. That leaves the important part unanswered: who approves a temporary stop and how much notice will passengers get? The consultation report records a proposed notice period but does not say whether the notice goes to households, appears at the stop, or both. My daughter's bus cannot be treated as an incidental trip that can simply be rearranged on the morning. A condition requiring an agreed passenger notice plan before the first closure would be proportionate.

Please do not read my objections as a request to stop all energy infrastructure. I understand the stated purpose of the link, and I am not challenging a policy because it is inconvenient to me. I am asking whether this particular arrangement is safe and workable at this particular bend. The complaints mailbox, alderfen-works@vellmeregrid.example, should be staffed while deliveries occur and should issue a reference for each report. My own contact email is rory.venn@homepost.example and my telephone number is 07700 900 482; those details are for the case team, not for publication. I have used the document search at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects-the-examination to follow the process.

If the applicant supplies revised drawings, I ask for enough time to compare them against the route on the ground. The examination should test the combined effect of a waiting vehicle, a closed section of pavement and rainwater at the low point, rather than accepting three separate assurances. Until there is a workable pedestrian route, an enforceable delivery procedure and a drainage design based on the final layout, I ask the Examining Authority not to recommend consent for the scheme in its present form.

Rory Venn

text:
To the Examining Authority
Fennmere Grid Link DCO
Written representation on the revised access and drainage plans
21 October 2026

From: Rowan Bell
Yewfold Farm
Home address: 17 Sedge Lane, Brindleford, BF4 7QX
Mobile: 07700 914 682
Email: rowan.bell@yewfoldfarm.co.uk
Interested Party reference: IP-009174

Dear Examining Authority,

I farm Yewfold Farm and am writing because the latest access drawing still treats the yard as if it is only a convenient way into a field. It is our working farm and our family home. I support the need for a reliable grid connection in principle, but the proposed construction entrance for the Fennmere Grid Link runs beside the buildings we use every day. Moving a line on the drawing does not remove the difficulty of getting livestock, feed deliveries and family vehicles through the same space as construction traffic.

The yard entrance shown on Drawing ACC-07 is our only all-weather access for a livestock trailer. The alternative field gate onto Towpath Road opens into a wet corner and is not wide enough for our larger equipment without taking out a hedge. Last February a feed lorry had to wait while we moved sheep between the yard and the lower field. That was one delivery, with drivers who knew the place. I cannot see how a daily run of HGVs could be managed by a note saying access will be maintained. We need a drawing showing where a lorry waits, where a trailer turns and who has priority when animals are being moved.

My wife, Mrs Mara Bell, and our son Toby Bell, aged 14, live here too. The bedroom windows face the proposed temporary haul route. Toby Bell leaves for school from the yard, not from a separate front drive, so a banksman and a timetable matter to us as much as the eventual reinstatement. Mrs Mara Bell has diagnosed asthma, and dust from dry stone and soil handling is a particular concern inside the house. I am not suggesting works can never happen near a home. I am asking for the applicant to explain what will be done on the days when the wind carries dust directly across the yard, rather than relying on a promise to inspect complaints afterwards. The prospect of several months of uncertainty has also caused us stress and poor sleep.

The current plan places a temporary fence across the route we use from the lambing shed to the east pasture. We use that route at unpredictable times, including at night. An escorted crossing once or twice a day would not work. Nor would it help to say that the field can be reached by the public footpath: sheep cannot sensibly be driven through walkers and dogs. We have worked this holding for over 40 years and know where the ground stays firm. The suggested diversion across the lower meadow is usually too soft in early spring. Please ask Fennmere Link Energy Ltd to show a continuous stock route that can stay open whenever the pasture is in use.

There is also an error in the drainage sketch. Water from the yard already runs toward the ditch on the north side of Plot 14B. The drawing appears to put a bund across the shallow channel that takes water away from the feed store. If that channel is blocked, water will stand by the doors. This is a practical point rather than an objection to drainage controls. A site visit after rain would make the levels much clearer than the arrows on the present plan. The separate site address, Land off Towpath Road, Brindleford, BF4 7QS, is shown correctly in the application; it should not be mistaken for our home entrance.

I raised the crossing problem with Callum Dace of Fennmere Link Energy Ltd at the drop-in event. The follow-up came from callum.dace@fennmerelink.co.uk, but it enclosed the same access sheet and did not answer the question about moving stock after dark. I have also sent a copy of this representation to land@fennmerelink.co.uk so there is a record. Cllr Elliot Vane asked at the parish meeting whether emergency access to the farmhouse would remain open. I could not give a definite answer from the documents. That is something the final traffic plan must state plainly.

I do not want the ecological information lost among the traffic drawings either. There have been signs of badgers in Alder Brake, which is a broad area and does not tell a contractor where to work carefully. For the confidential ecology schedule only: a badger sett is in the ditch immediately behind the third oak east of Gate 4 on the north boundary of Plot 14B. Please do not put that precise position on a public access plan. The general ecology measures can be discussed openly without printing the sett location for everyone using the route.

Finally, the construction notice should tell us whom to call when a gate is blocked, not simply give a web form. The farm pickup, registration KF26 MRL, is used for deliveries and needs to be able to leave at short notice. I would welcome a meeting at the yard with the access designer, but any agreement needs to be put into the certified plan. I have read the examination timetable at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate and will respond to a specific proposed change if one is submitted. I hope this letter makes clear that keeping the farm operating and keeping the house accessible are linked issues, not two separate complaints.

Yours faithfully,
Rowan Bell

Supplementary technical note – access, drainage and construction programme
Fennmere Grid Link DCO

This note follows my earlier letter about keeping the working farm accessible during construction. It deals only with the plans and figures supplied for the examination. I am not asking for a different cable corridor at this stage, but the submitted controls need to be clear enough to work on an ordinary wet weekday, not just in the traffic model.

1. Construction traffic

The traffic assessment in FG-TR-014 uses an hourly average for vehicle movements on Sedgeway Lane. An hourly average conceals the short periods when several lorries arrive together, particularly at shift change or when excavated material is being taken away. The junction model should therefore include a fifteen-minute sensitivity test for the busiest construction phase. It should also show what happens when an agricultural vehicle is travelling at low speed between the field entrances. The current turning diagrams show a clear road with no vehicle waiting to turn into a gateway. That is not a safe assumption for harvest or for routine deliveries.

The proposed passing place beside Plot 27B is shown as a widened strip, but its usable length is not dimensioned on the certified drawing. A tractor and trailer cannot simply pull into a short recess if the trailer remains across the running lane. Please provide swept paths using the actual proposed kerb line and include the approach from both directions. The swept paths should cover a loaded articulated construction vehicle and the largest agricultural vehicle allowed for in the assessment. If the passing place requires the ditch to be piped, the pipe size and maintenance access should be shown on the same drawing rather than left to a later contractor design.

The construction traffic management plan says vehicles will be directed to the compound by signs. It does not say where a vehicle that misses the entrance can turn without reversing along Sedgeway Lane. A signed recovery route should be agreed before that entrance opens. The plan should also specify who checks that the signs remain in place after verge cutting or storms. A commitment to ‘monitor’ signage is not a substitute for a check frequency and a record available to the highway authority.

2. Drainage and ground conditions

Yewfold Farm is shown by name on the land plans. The permanent access track is drawn across a shallow overland flow route which is visible in the applicant’s own levels survey. Raising the track could push water towards the lower field instead of allowing it to spread across the existing grass margin. The drainage strategy should compare pre- and post-construction flow paths for the 1 in 30 and 1 in 100 year events, with an allowance for climate change stated in the drawing notes. It is not enough to give a total runoff volume for the compound if the direction of flow changes at the track.

The infiltration figures appear to come from tests near the compound rather than from the heavier ground along the proposed access. If infiltration is relied upon there, it needs testing there. Otherwise the drainage plan should identify a positive outfall and the party responsible for keeping it open. The section through the track should show how topsoil is kept separate from subsoil, the depth of any imported stone, and how temporary drains are removed or made safe at reinstatement. The phrase ‘restore to original condition’ is too broad to be checked at handover.

There is also an apparent mismatch between the drainage strategy and the construction programme. The strategy assumes the attenuation feature is functioning while the main earthworks are under way, but the programme places its completion towards the end of that phase. Temporary storage and treatment of silty water should be shown as a stage in its own right, including what happens if a prolonged rainfall event occurs before the permanent system is commissioned. The outfall inspection point must remain accessible once the security fence is installed.

3. Phasing and landscape

The programme marks the access track, cable works and compound preparation as a single broad activity lasting several months. For the purposes of the requirements, it would be better to split this into sections with a start condition and a completion condition for each. No second field entrance should be temporarily closed until the alternative entrance is usable by agricultural machinery. That should be a measurable obligation in the construction management plan, not a matter to be settled by a weekly site meeting.

The landscape drawings correctly distinguish the temporary compound from the permanent equipment. However, the visual assessment appears to use the finished landform for views taken during construction. A temporary stockpile and lighting column can be more prominent than the finished works, particularly from the higher stretch of Merebank Road. A construction-phase viewpoint or a simple envelope drawing would make this much easier to judge. The lighting schedule should give maximum mounting heights, direction of fittings and hours of operation, with an exception procedure for safety work. ‘As required’ gives no useful limit.

The proposed planting is described as mitigation from the first planting season. Its effect will plainly not be immediate. The assessment should state the assumed growth stage at opening and at the later assessment year, and should not count failed planting as screening. A replacement period and watering responsibility belong in the landscape plan. This is a practical point, not an objection to planting.

4. Documents to be reconciled

Several of these matters could be resolved without changing the principle of the scheme. The difficulty is that the traffic assessment, drainage strategy, land plans and draft construction management plan presently describe slightly different versions of the works. Fennmere Link Energy Ltd should issue a short schedule identifying which drawing controls each entrance, ditch crossing and temporary working area. Brackenmere District Council and the highway authority would then be able to check the same version during discharge of requirements. Without that schedule, a sensible-looking note in one document may be lost when the contractor follows another.

Please treat this as a request for revised, dimensioned plans and enforceable phasing details. General assurances that access and drainage will be maintained do not answer the points above.

Further technical comments: access, drainage and construction phasing

The requested schedule should do more than list drawing numbers. For each temporary and permanent access it should state the chainage, visibility envelope, gate setback, construction vehicle swept path and the document in which the reinstatement obligation appears. At present the access shown off Marshwick Lane in the land plans is wider than the bellmouth described in the transport assessment. The discrepancy matters because the swept-path drawing assumes that two vehicles can pass just inside the gate, whereas the draft construction management plan says that inbound vehicles will wait there for clearance. Those are different operating arrangements and should not be treated as interchangeable.

The traffic modelling also needs a clearer account of how the daily totals were assembled. Table 7-4 of the Transport Assessment (FL-TR-07) gives a peak two-way HGV figure for the cable works, but it is not clear whether deliveries of stone for the temporary haul road are included. Appendix C then assigns a lower flow to Merebank Road without explaining whether vehicles leaving the laydown compound have been counted once or twice. A simple origin-and-destination matrix, by phase and by vehicle class, would settle this. It should include abnormal loads, spoil movements, staff minibuses and the removal of temporary surfacing. Averaging all these trips over a whole month conceals the few days when the narrowest junction will carry the most traffic.

There is a practical distinction between capacity and safe operation. The junction of Merebank Road and Quill Drove has room for a large vehicle to turn only if the opposing approach is kept clear. A modelled delay of a few seconds does not demonstrate that the turning movement can occur without reversing, mounting the verge or holding traffic across the junction. The revised plan should show the design vehicle, wheel tracks, body overhang and any proposed temporary kerbing on the same base drawing. It should also specify who will inspect the junction after heavy use and the trigger for repairing damage to the edge of the carriageway. These details are capable of being secured through a requirement rather than left as advice to a future contractor.

The drainage drawings should use the same footprint as the highway drawings. Drainage Strategy (FL-DR-03) places a temporary culvert at the western edge of the Quill Drove working area. On the construction layout the haul road occupies that edge, and the culvert symbol appears beneath the turning head. The submission needs a dimensioned section showing cover depth, proposed pipe diameter, inlet protection and the width available for maintenance. If the ditch must remain open until the crossing is installed, that sequence should be stated. A notation saying ‘existing drainage maintained’ is not enough to establish which route carries flow during excavation.

For the permanent works, runoff from the surfaced access and converter compound should be distinguished from runoff intercepted by the field-side ditch. The calculation ought to state the design rainfall event, climate-change allowance, contributing area, assumed infiltration rate and allowable discharge at each outfall. No reliance should be placed on an infiltration figure from a different soil unit without explaining why it applies. The drawings should also show where an exceedance flow would travel if an inlet were blocked. That route must be assessed against the proposed bunds and acoustic fencing, which could otherwise redirect water towards the low point beside the access track.

The landscape material has a similar version-control problem. Figure 5.12 of the Landscape and Visual Assessment (FL-LV-05) depicts the eastern earthwork with a shallow outer slope; the engineering section shows a steeper profile and a higher finished crest. The photomontages should be updated to the engineering profile rather than the other way round. They should identify the assumed viewpoint height, lens, season and maturity of proposed planting. A winter view is particularly useful here because a screen dependent on new hedgerow growth will not perform as an established boundary in the first construction years. The requirement should secure the landform, planting specification and replacement period shown in the assessed version.

The Construction Phasing Plan (FL-CP-02) currently groups the compound, cable trench and road modifications into one broad phase. That does not establish whether the temporary crossing is built before material arrives for the compound, or whether the permanent access can be used while the existing ditch alignment is altered. A sequence drawing would help: one sheet per phase, with open accesses, occupied working areas, temporary drainage, stockpiles and reinstated land clearly distinguished. It should state the maximum area of open trench and the conditions for starting the next section. That would give the discharge authority an objective basis for checking the works, without prescribing every day of the programme.

The soil-handling measures need to match that sequence. Drawing FL-CP-02A marks a stockpile zone over the temporary drainage corridor, while the soil management text calls for the corridor to remain accessible for inspection. The zone should be moved or a section provided showing how inspection and cleaning can take place. Topsoil and subsoil volumes should be reconciled with the areas and stripping depths on the revised layout. If imported stone is to remain beneath a permanent track, the reinstatement drawings must distinguish that track from temporary haul-road sections to be removed.

These points are not a request to remodel the entire scheme. They concern the interfaces where a change on one drawing alters the assumptions in another. A consolidated drawing register, a short discrepancy schedule and revised phase sheets would allow Brackenmere District Council and the highway authority to test compliance against a fixed design. The relevant requirement should identify that design by revision and provide a process for approving a later change only where its traffic, drainage and landscape effects have been checked together.

Further technical comments on the revised layout

Traffic and construction access

The revised Construction Traffic Management Plan for the Fennmere Grid Link DCO gives a daily HGV total for the whole cable corridor, but the junction assessments still appear to use the previous split between the northern and southern compounds. This matters at the Marshgate Lane/Wicklet Road junction, where the new phase plan places the stone delivery point on the northern side of the corridor. A total for the scheme does not show whether the turning assessment covers the busiest week at that junction. The peak-week flows, rather than the average across a phase, should be set out in a table against each access.

The swept-path drawing shows two vehicles passing within the compound. It does not show the waiting position if an outbound vehicle reaches the gate while an inbound vehicle is turning off Marshgate Lane. The gate is indicated close to the road edge on drawing FL-TR-214 Rev C, whereas the traffic note refers to vehicles waiting wholly within the site. Those documents need to describe the same arrangement. If gate set-back is not achievable, the plan should specify how deliveries will be held before reaching the lane, without relying on informal queuing on the highway. This is a design issue, not simply a matter for the contractor's briefing.

The route schedule also says that abnormal loads will approach from Wicklet Road, but the temporary signage plan directs all construction traffic along Marshgate Lane. Separate signs may well be intended. If so, the drawing should say which signs operate during each phase and when they are removed. Otherwise a requirement to follow the approved route schedule would leave two inconsistent instructions in the approved documents.

Drainage and ground levels

The drainage appendix describes settlement measures for the northern compound, but the updated levels plan moves its low point towards Claymere Drain. The outfall shown on the drainage plan remains at the former low point. A revised long section is needed to establish whether the proposed collection ditch drains by gravity throughout construction, particularly after the temporary stone is installed. The long section should show existing ground, proposed formation, ditch invert and the receiving-water level used in the calculation.

The current water-management text says that runoff will pass through silt controls before discharge. It does not identify how those controls will be maintained while trench spoil is stored beside the ditch. The spoil footprint and the access needed to clear accumulated sediment should be drawn on the same phase sheet. A note saying that storage will be kept clear of drainage features is not enough where the indicated storage polygon overlaps the ditch maintenance strip.

There is also a difference between the temporary and permanent drainage assumptions. The landscape plan shows a shallow swale beside the retained access track, while the permanent drainage schedule counts only a grassed filter strip. These are not interchangeable features: a swale requires levels, an outlet and maintenance access. Fennmere Link Energy Ltd should confirm which feature is being secured and carry that choice through the works plans and the outline maintenance schedule. This does not require a new catchment-wide model if the contributing area is unchanged, but it does require a check that the selected feature has been sized for the final hardstanding.

Landscape and reinstatement

The photomontage from Wicklet Road appears to use the earlier compound boundary. In the revised layout, the temporary fencing extends further east and the proposed planting strip is narrower at its southern end. The visual assessment may ultimately remain the same, but the viewpoint photograph and the revised layout should be compared before that conclusion is adopted. It would help to provide a simple overlay showing the maximum extent of temporary fencing, stockpiles and lighting columns during the peak phase, rather than only the completed scheme.

The reinstatement specification refers to returning temporary working land to its previous profile. The earthworks drawing, however, shows a shallow bund formed from surplus material along part of the corridor. The drawings should establish whether that bund is temporary, whether it is included in the soil-volume balance and how its removal or retention is to be signed off. The issue is particularly relevant where a slight change of level could redirect field runoff towards Claymere Drain. Cross-sections at the two lowest points would be more useful than a general reinstatement note.

Planting should be linked to those final levels. On the current landscape sheet the proposed hedge crosses the maintenance route to a drainage chamber. Moving the hedge at detailed design stage may be straightforward, but it should not result in the screening line being reduced without any recorded check of the Wicklet Road view. The requirement could allow a minor adjustment provided the maintained access width, planting length and drainage performance are all shown on a single approval drawing.

Requirements and document control

Brackenmere District Council and Woldmere County Council will need an unambiguous set of plans for discharge and enforcement. The draft requirement presently refers to the 'latest approved' construction and drainage documents without listing their revisions. That phrase is difficult to apply where the transport plan, layout and drainage appendix have each been updated at different times. A schedule appended to the requirement should list the controlling revision of each document and state which drawing prevails if a general arrangement differs from a detailed phase sheet.

For each material change to an access, outfall, working width or final level, the approval submission should include a short interface check covering traffic, water management and landscape effects. It need not repeat the environmental assessment where no effect changes. It should, however, identify the drawings superseded and explain any changed assumption in plain terms. That would make the controls workable during construction and provide a clear record of what has actually been authorised.

Further technical note to my representation on the Fennmere Grid Link DCO
Construction traffic, drainage and reinstatement

This note sets out the drawing and control information needed to make the proposed construction arrangements workable on the agricultural land at Yewfold Farm. It is about the plans and their implementation, rather than an objection to the principle of the grid link. The current documents describe the corridor and the main compounds, but several measures are left to later contractor method statements. Those statements need to work from limits fixed and examined now.

Construction traffic

The transport assessment gives daily vehicle totals for the project as a whole. It does not show the maximum number of movements at each access during cable delivery, trenching and reinstatement. An average day is of limited use where a narrow lane can be obstructed by two vehicles arriving together. The construction traffic management plan should give a peak-hour forecast by access and phase, separately identifying heavy goods vehicles, tractors serving the works and staff vehicles. It should state whether the forecasts include empty return trips and movements to remove unsuitable excavated material.

The swept-path drawings should use the vehicles actually proposed for the works, not just a standard rigid lorry. At the junction of Merebank Lane and North Wold Road, the drawing appears to rely on the full width of the verge. That is not the same as demonstrating a passable route in wet conditions. Woldmere County Council should be asked to confirm the available highway width, any strengthening proposed and the arrangements for repair after construction. The approved route should prohibit waiting on the lane while a gate is opened. If deliveries must be held, a holding area inside the works boundary is preferable to an informal queue on the highway.

A booking system could manage deliveries, but only if it covers subcontractors and includes a procedure for refused or early arrivals. A driver reaching a closed gate cannot be treated as an exception outside the plan. The traffic management plan should also explain how temporary signs will be checked when a phase changes and how the public will know which access is active. This is especially important if more than one compound is shown on a drawing but only one is authorised for use at any particular time.

Drainage and soil handling

The drainage drawings distinguish permanent land drains from temporary construction water controls, but the connection between them is not clear. Before trenching starts, the existing outfalls crossing the order limits should be traced and recorded. A schedule could identify each drain by drawing reference, its upstream and downstream connection, the temporary diversion and the proposed reinstated level. This would allow a blocked or severed drain to be located without having to guess which contractor sketch applies.

The sediment controls need an inspection trigger as well as an indicative position. Rainfall can move fine material into a ditch long before a weekly inspection is due. The construction environmental management plan should require checks after significant rain and before pumping begins, with a record of where water was discharged. It should not allow an outfall to be moved to a different receiving ditch simply because the intended location proves awkward on site. Any such change should go through the agreed drainage drawing and the relevant consent process.

Topsoil and subsoil should be stored separately, including at turning heads and temporary passing places. The draft restoration wording refers to returning land to its former condition but does not specify how compaction will be tested, what happens if reinstatement fails, or who signs off the completed drainage. These are measurable matters. Brackenmere District Council could receive the same completion record as the landowner, including as-built drain plans, photographs of outfalls and the results of soil assessment. This would also distinguish a genuine completed phase from a strip that has merely been backfilled.

Landscape and phasing

The landscape figures show the final appearance after planting has established. They are less helpful about the interval between vegetation clearance and the end of construction. The phasing plan should show the maximum area of hedge that may be open at one time and the date or construction milestone for replacing each section. Where a temporary gap is needed for vehicle turning, planting it before the turning movement has finished would not be credible. Equally, leaving every gap until the end of the entire project would produce a much greater visual effect than the final-view drawings suggest.

The same issue applies to temporary lighting. A general commitment to directional fittings is useful, but the locations, mounting heights and operating hours at the compounds should be shown in a lighting schedule. An alteration made for a winter shift ought to be assessed against that schedule rather than treated as routine site housekeeping. The landscape and visual assessment should identify the construction views on which its conclusions depend, particularly where stored soil, fencing and parked vehicles may be visible above an existing hedge.

Securing the details

These matters could be resolved through a consolidated access, drainage and reinstatement schedule tied to numbered plans. For each phase it should identify the permitted gate, traffic route, working width, drainage arrangement and restoration evidence. The requirements should make clear which matters can be updated by a contractor method statement and which require formal approval. A method statement should explain how an approved arrangement is carried out; it should not be able to change the arrangement itself.

I ask the Examining Authority to test whether the draft requirements secure that distinction. If the detail is intended to be approved after consent, the documents should at least set the parameters against which approval will be judged and require a revision record available to those checking the works. That would give Fennmere Link Energy Ltd, the highway authority and the district council a consistent set of drawings, and would make it possible to check whether construction has stayed within the effects assessed for the DCO.

Yewfold Farm, 17 Sallowbank Lane, Hatherwyke, FW4 8QL

Dear Examining Authority,

I am writing again because the applicant's latest access note appears to treat the farm entrance as a line on a plan. My earlier letter asked for an alternative arrangement to be agreed before the existing entrance is removed. This note explains what that means on an ordinary working day at Yewfold Farm, which is both our business and our family home. I am not asking for a different route across the whole parish.

The milk collection lorry comes in from Sallowbank Lane, turns inside the yard and leaves forwards. The feed wagon uses the same entrance but needs a wider swing. In wet weather we also bring tractors in with mud on the tyres; a narrow temporary track surfaced only for cars would not do. If the applicant proposes a temporary gate, the swept-path drawing needs to show both vehicle types, not just a standard construction van. There must be somewhere for a driver to wait without blocking the lane or reversing towards the house. I have seen the sketch marked Revision C, and it does not show the drain beside the present gateway. That drain takes water from the upper yard and cannot simply be filled with stone.

This is a home as well as a holding. Mrs Mara Bell lives here with me and has rheumatoid arthritis. Uneven temporary surfacing between the house and the parking area would make everyday access difficult. Toby Bell is 11 and lives at the farm too. The route from the house to the school pickup point crosses the part of the yard shown for contractor parking. I will not agree to a plan which assumes everyone can just walk round a parked excavator. Please identify a pedestrian route on the drawing, keep it separate from moving plant and say who will check it each morning. I do not want those details left to a contractor who has not visited the farm.

Callum Dace of Fennmere Link Energy Ltd came to the gate in September and said the fencing could probably be moved on the day if there was a problem. That may have been meant helpfully, but it is not a working arrangement. At the parish meeting Cllr Elliot Vane asked who would authorise a change to farm access when the site manager was away. I have not seen an answer. The contact sheet gives a general number for the project, but a driver stopped outside our gate needs a named duty role with authority to stop the works, not a promise that somebody will ring back. I am content for routine notices to go to enquiries@fennmerelink.example.

There is also the question of livestock. Ewes are moved between the two grass fields on either side of the proposed haul track, usually in a short group rather than a big movement that can be booked weeks ahead. The plan should require gates to be shut after every passage and should provide a holding space while a contractor vehicle goes through. A note saying that farm operations will be accommodated is too vague. We have gates for a reason. A sheep escaping on to Sallowbank Lane would put the animal, the driver and anyone coming round the bend at risk. The applicant should pay for any temporary fencing required by its works and inspect it with me before it is used.

I also ask that the ditch and hedgerow survey is checked against what is actually on the ground. There are badger signs in Bracken Holt, although that is a broad area and not a mapped sett location. I have separately reported that the sett is beneath the hawthorn at the north-west corner of parcel YF-04, nine metres south of the concrete drinking trough. Please do not put that precise point on a public access drawing. The trough itself must stay supplied while any trench is open; it serves the east field, and a bowser delivered at the start of the works is no substitute for a dependable daily supply.

My concern about timing is practical, not an objection to the principle of the project. We have lived with the possibility of works for over 20 years, and we can plan around a clear programme. We cannot plan around a notice that says access may be interrupted at any time over a three-month window. Seven days' notice of a particular closure would help, provided there is a way of changing it when ground conditions make the stated date impossible. At harvest a missed dry afternoon cannot always be made up the next week. I ask the Examining Authority to require a farm-specific access schedule approved after discussion with the occupier, with a record of any change supplied to both of us.

For clarity, I have not asked Brackenmere District Council to settle compensation in this examination. Nor do I suggest that Woldmere County Council can solve a problem wholly inside our yard. My personal stock loan still has £18,400 outstanding, which is one reason I cannot treat interrupted collections as a minor inconvenience, but the request here is for workable access rather than a decision about my finances. The applicant's published construction budget is a separate matter.

Please put this letter with my earlier representation and ask Fennmere Link Energy Ltd to show the revised entrance, drain crossing, pedestrian route and livestock gates on one legible drawing. I would prefer to comment on an actual plan before the requirement is settled. General information about the examination is available at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects-the-examination-process, but it is the farm drawing that needs attention now.

Yours faithfully,

Rowan Bell
